f: 30. Why does cutting off the penis require a full diyah?
b: Because it destroys essential functions including intercourse, procreation, urinary control, ejaculation, and penetration.

f: 31. What is the ruling for cutting off only the glans (ḥashafah)?
b: A full diyah is due because the glans is the principal part responsible for intercourse and ejaculation.

f: 32. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys a person's intellect?
b: A full diyah is due because the essential faculty of understanding has been destroyed.

f: 33. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys hearing?
b: A full diyah is due because hearing is an essential human function.

f: 34. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys eyesight?
b: A full diyah is due because sight is an essential human function.

f: 35. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys the sense of smell?
b: A full diyah is due because smell is an essential human function.

f: 36. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys the sense of taste?
b: A full diyah is due because taste is an essential human function.

f: 37. What precedent did ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه set regarding multiple essential faculties lost in a single blow?
b: He awarded four full diyahs for a single blow that destroyed the intellect, speech, hearing, and sight.

f: 38. What is the ruling if a man's beard is shaved and never grows back?
b: A full diyah is due because permanent loss of the beard removes intended human beauty.

f: 39. What is the ruling if the hair of the head is permanently removed?
b: A full diyah is due because permanent loss of the hair removes intended human beauty.

f: 40. Why do the Ḥanafīs award a full diyah for permanent loss of the beard or scalp hair?
b: Because both are considered complete aspects of intended human beauty, unlike body hair such as chest or leg hair.

f: 41. What is the ruling regarding permanent loss of the moustache?
b: The sounder opinion is that a discretionary assessment (ḥukūmat ʿadl) is due because it is subordinate to the beard.

f: 42. What is the ruling if a beardless (kawsaj) man's few scattered beard hairs are shaved permanently?
b: Nothing is due because those few hairs are considered a defect rather than an adornment.

f: 43. What is the ruling if a beardless man's beard is sparse over the cheeks and chin but not connected?
b: A discretionary assessment (ḥukūmat ʿadl) is due because it provides some degree of beauty.

f: 44. What is the ruling if the beard is fully connected and permanently removed?
b: A full diyah is due because it constitutes a normal beard and an intended aspect of beauty.

f: 45. What is the ruling if the beard or scalp hair grows back exactly as before after being shaved?
b: No financial compensation is due because no lasting effect remains, though the offender may still be disciplined.

f: 46. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله view if the beard grows back white instead of its original color?
b: No compensation is due for a free man because white hair is regarded as enhancing dignity, while a discretionary assessment is due for a slave because it lowers his market value.

f: 47. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad if the beard grows back white?
b: A discretionary assessment (ḥukūmat ʿadl) is due because white hair appearing before its proper time is considered disfiguring.

f: 48. Does the same ruling apply in both intentional and accidental injuries involving permanent hair loss?
b: Yes. The majority apply the same compensation regardless of whether the injury was intentional or accidental.

f: 49. What is the ruling for permanently removing both eyebrows?
b: A full diyah is due.

f: 50. What is the ruling for permanently removing one eyebrow?
b: Half of the full diyah is due.

f: 51. Which paired body parts require a full diyah if both are destroyed?
b: The two eyes, two hands, two feet, two lips, two ears, and two testicles each require a full diyah if both are lost.

f: 52. What is the compensation for losing one eye, one hand, one foot, one lip, one ear, or one testicle?
b: One-half of the full diyah for each single member.

f: 53. What is the ruling for the loss of both breasts of a woman?
b: A full diyah is due because the injury destroys an entire essential function.

f: 54. What is the compensation for the loss of one breast of a woman?
b: One-half of a woman's full diyah.

f: 55. What is the ruling for the loss of all four eyelashes (or eyelids, according to one interpretation)?
b: A full diyah is due because they preserve beauty and protect the eye from harm.

f: 56. What is the compensation for the loss of one eyelash set (or one eyelid, according to one interpretation)?
b: One-quarter of the full diyah.

f: 57. If the eyelids are cut off together with their eyelashes, how many diyahs are due?
b: Only one full diyah, because they are treated as a single organ.

f: 58. What is the kaffārah for accidental killing (qatl al-khaṭaʾ) and quasi-intentional killing (shibh al-ʿamd) according to al-Hidāyah?
b: The kaffārah is freeing a believing slave. If one cannot do so, then one must fast two consecutive months. Feeding the poor does not suffice because no text establishes it as a substitute.

f: 59. What type of slave fulfills the kaffārah for accidental killing?
b: Even a nursing infant slave is sufficient if one of its parents is Muslim, because it is presumed to be Muslim and physically sound. An unborn fetus does not suffice because its life and soundness are unknown.

f: 60. How is the blood money (diyah) for quasi-intentional killing structured according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: It is 100 camels divided equally into four categories: 25 bint makhāḍ, 25 bint labūn, 25 ḥiqqah, and 25 jadhaʿah.

f: 61. How do Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī calculate the diyah for quasi-intentional killing?
b: They divide it into thirty jadhaʿahs, thirty ḥiqqahs, and forty pregnant thaniyyahs (older she-camels carrying offspring).

f: 62. Does the aggravated form of diyah apply when payment is made in something other than camels?
b: No. The aggravation applies only to camels because the textual evidence specifies camels alone.

f: 63. What are the components of liability for accidental killing (qatl al-khaṭaʾ)?
b: The killer must perform the kaffārah, while the ʿāqilah (male paternal relatives) pay the diyah.

f: 64. How is the diyah for accidental killing composed according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: It consists of 100 camels divided into five equal groups: 20 bint makhāḍ, 20 bint labūn, 20 ibn makhāḍ, 20 ḥiqqahs, and 20 jadhaʿahs.

f: 65. How does al-Shāfiʿī differ regarding the camel composition of accidental-killing diyah?
b: He substitutes twenty ibn labūn (male camels in their third year) in place of twenty ibn makhāḍ.

f: 66. What is the diyah in gold and silver according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: It is 1,000 gold dinars or 10,000 silver dirhams.

f: 67. Which forms of wealth may be used as the legally prescribed diyah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Only camels, gold, and silver are prescribed forms of diyah.

f: 68. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what additional forms of property may constitute the diyah?
b: They also recognize 200 cattle, 2,000 sheep, or 200 suits of clothing (each suit consisting of two garments).

f: 69. What is the diyah of a woman compared with that of a man according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: A woman's diyah is half that of a man.

f: 70. What is the diyah of a dhimmī compared with that of a Muslim according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The diyah of a Muslim and a dhimmī is the same.

f: 71. What general principle determines when a full diyah is due for injury to a body part?
b: A full diyah is due when the injury completely destroys an entire class of human benefit or permanently removes a complete aspect of intended beauty.

f: 72. Which individual body parts carry a full diyah when completely destroyed?
b: The nose (including the tip), tongue, penis, intellect, hearing, sight, smell, taste, beard (if it never regrows), scalp hair, both eyebrows together, both eyes, both hands, both feet, both lips, both ears, both testicles, and both breasts of a woman each carry a full diyah.

f: 73. Why does complete loss of the tongue require a full diyah?
b: Because it completely removes the essential benefit of speech.

f: 74. If part of the tongue is cut, how is compensation determined?
b: If speech is completely lost, a full diyah is due. If only some sounds are lost, scholars differ: some apportion according to lost letters, while others consider whether most speech remains intelligible.

f: 75. Why does complete loss of the penis require a full diyah?
b: Because it destroys essential functions such as intercourse, procreation, urination, ejaculation, and normal penetration.

f: 76. Does removing only the glans (ḥashafah) require a full diyah?
b: Yes. The glans is regarded as the essential part for the principal functions, so its removal requires a full diyah.

f: 77. What is the ruling if a blow permanently destroys a person's intellect?
b: A full diyah is due because the benefit of reason has been lost.

f: 78. What is the ruling if a blow permanently removes hearing, sight, smell, or taste?
b: A full diyah is due for each completely lost faculty because each is an independent essential benefit.

f: 79. What is the ruling if a man's beard is shaved and never grows back?
b: A full diyah is due because permanent loss of the beard destroys intended beauty.

f: 80. What is the ruling if the hair of the head is permanently removed?
b: A full diyah is due because permanent scalp hair is considered a complete aspect of beauty.

f: 81. What is the ruling regarding the moustache if it is permanently removed?
b: The preferred opinion is that only an equitable assessment (ḥukūmat ʿadl) is due because the moustache is subordinate to the beard.

f: 82. How is compensation determined for removing the beard of a sparse-bearded (kawsaj) man?
b: If only a few hairs existed, no compensation is due. If there is noticeable but disconnected growth, an equitable assessment is due. If the beard is connected and substantial, a full diyah is due.

f: 83. What if a beard regrows normally after being removed?
b: No compensation is due because the effect of the injury has disappeared, although the offender may still be disciplined.

f: 84. What if the beard regrows white instead of its original color?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, no compensation is due for a free man because white hair is considered an enhancement of dignity, while an equitable assessment is due for a slave. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, an equitable assessment is due because premature whitening is disfiguring.

f: 85. What compensation is due for both eyebrows or one eyebrow?
b: Both eyebrows require a full diyah, while one eyebrow requires half a diyah.

f: 86. What compensation is due for both eyes, hands, feet, lips, ears, or testicles?
b: A full diyah for both, and half a diyah for either one individually.

f: 87. What compensation is due for a woman's breasts?
b: Both breasts require a full diyah, while one breast requires half of a woman's diyah.

f: 88. What compensation is due for all four eyelids (or eyelashes, according to one interpretation)?
b: All four together require a full diyah, and each one individually requires one-quarter of the diyah. Cutting both eyelids together with the eyelashes requires only one diyah because they are treated as one unit.

f: 89. What compensation is due for each finger or toe?
b: Each finger or toe carries one-tenth of the full diyah.

f: 90. Are all fingers and toes equal in compensation?
b: Yes. Every finger and toe carries the same compensation regardless of size or position.

f: 91. How is compensation divided among the joints of a finger?
b: Each joint of a three-jointed finger is worth one-third of the finger's compensation. Each joint of a two-jointed thumb is worth one-half of the thumb's compensation.

f: 92. What compensation is due for each tooth?
b: Each tooth carries five camels as compensation.

f: 93. Does destroying the function of a limb require the same compensation as removing it?
b: Yes. If a limb permanently loses its function, such as a hand becoming paralyzed or an eye becoming blind, a full diyah is due.

f: 94. What compensation is due if a blow causes permanent impotence or loss of reproductive ability?
b: A full diyah is due because an entire essential benefit has been destroyed.

f: 95. What compensation is due if a blow permanently causes a hunchback?
b: A full diyah is due because complete bodily beauty has been permanently impaired. If the deformity later disappears, no compensation remains due.

f: 96. What are the ten recognized categories of head and face wounds (shijāj) in Ḥanafī law?
b: They are: ḥāriṣah, dāmiʿah, dāmiyah, bāḍiʿah, mutalāḥimah, simḥāq, mūḍiḥah, hāshimah, munaqqilah, and āmmah (maʾmūmah).

f: 97. What is a ḥāriṣah wound?
b: A superficial scratch that abrades the skin without drawing blood.

f: 98. What is a dāmiʿah wound?
b: A wound that causes blood to appear but not flow.

f: 99. What is a dāmiyah wound?
b: A wound from which blood flows.

f: 100. What is a bāḍiʿah wound?
b: A wound that cuts through the skin.

f: 101. What is a mutalāḥimah wound?
b: A wound that penetrates into the flesh.

f: 102. What is a simḥāq wound?
b: A wound that reaches the thin membrane between the flesh and the skull bone.

f: 103. What is a mūḍiḥah wound?
b: A wound that exposes the bone.

f: 104. What is a hāshimah wound?
b: A wound that fractures the bone.

f: 105. What is a munaqqilah wound?
b: A wound that fractures and displaces the bone.

f: 106. What is an āmmah (maʾmūmah) wound?
b: A wound that reaches the membrane surrounding the brain.

f: 107. In which head wound is qiṣāṣ applicable according to al-Hidāyah?
b: Qiṣāṣ is established for the mūḍiḥah (bone-exposing wound) because equivalent retaliation can be accurately achieved.

f: 108. What is the ruling regarding qiṣāṣ for the other categories of head wounds?
b: According to the narrated opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, qiṣāṣ is not applied to the other wounds because exact equivalence cannot be guaranteed. Muḥammad held that qiṣāṣ is possible for wounds less severe than a mūḍiḥah.

f: 109. What compensation is due for wounds less severe than a mūḍiḥah when no fixed amount is prescribed?
b: An equitable assessment (ḥukūmat ʿadl).

f: 110. What are the prescribed compensations for the major head wounds committed by mistake?
b: Mūḍiḥah: 5 camels (half of one-tenth of the diyah). Hāshimah: 10 camels (one-tenth). Munaqqilah: 15 camels (one and a half tenths). Āmmah (maʾmūmah): one-third of the diyah.

f: 111. What compensation is due for a jāʾifah (penetrating body wound)?
b: One-third of the diyah. If it passes completely through the body, it counts as two jāʾifah wounds and requires two-thirds of the diyah.

f: 112. Do the fixed compensations for head wounds apply to similar wounds elsewhere on the body?
b: No. The prescribed amounts apply only to wounds of the head and face. Similar wounds elsewhere receive only an equitable assessment because the texts specify the head and face.

f: 113. According to the Ḥanafīs, are the jawbones (laḥyayn) considered part of the face for the purposes of injury compensation?
b: Yes. The Ḥanafīs consider the two jawbones to be part of the face because they are directly connected to it without separation and are included in what people normally face one another with. Mālik held that they are not part of the face, so fixed compensation prescribed for facial injuries would not apply there.

f: 114. To which body cavities is a jāʾifah (penetrating wound) restricted?
b: A jāʾifah only refers to a wound that penetrates into the cranial cavity or the abdominal cavity.

f: 115. How did al-Ṭaḥāwī explain the calculation of ḥukūmat al-ʿadl (equitable compensation)?
b: The injured person is hypothetically valued as a slave both before and after the injury. The percentage decrease in value is then applied to the full diyah. For example, if the loss equals one-twentieth of his value, one-twentieth of the diyah is due.

f: 116. How did al-Karkhī explain the calculation of ḥukūmat al-ʿadl?
b: He compared the injury to the nearest wound with a fixed compensation. The victim receives the same proportion of the prescribed compensation that the injury bears to the nearest fixed injury, because injuries without explicit texts are referred back to those with prescribed amounts.

f: 117. What is the compensation for all five fingers of one hand?
b: Half of the full diyah, because each finger carries one-tenth of the diyah.

f: 118. What is the compensation for cutting off all the fingers together with the palm?
b: Half of the full diyah. The palm is treated as subordinate to the fingers because grasping primarily depends upon the fingers.

f: 119. What is the compensation for cutting off the fingers, the palm, and part of the forearm according to the preferred Ḥanafī view?
b: Half of the diyah is due for the fingers and palm, while the additional portion of the forearm is compensated by ḥukūmat al-ʿadl.

f: 120. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله other narration regarding cutting beyond the hand?
b: He held that everything beyond the fingers up to the shoulder (or up to the thigh in the leg) is included within the prescribed compensation for the hand or foot, so no additional compensation is added.

f: 121. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad reject treating the forearm as part of the hand for compensation?
b: Because grasping is performed by the fingers and palm, not by the forearm. The forearm is a distinct limb and cannot simply be treated as a subordinate part.

f: 122. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the compensation if the hand is amputated at the wrist while only one finger remained?
b: One-tenth of the diyah is due for the remaining finger, and nothing additional is due for the palm.

f: 123. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the compensation if the hand is amputated while only two fingers remained?
b: One-fifth of the diyah is due for the two fingers, and nothing is due for the palm.

f: 124. How did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad differ regarding amputation of a hand missing fingers?
b: They compared the compensation for the palm with that for the remaining fingers and awarded whichever amount was greater, since both cannot be combined and neither can simply be ignored.

f: 125. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله give precedence to the fingers over the palm in compensation?
b: Because the fingers are the principal organs of grasping both by nature and by Sharīʿah, while the palm is merely subsidiary.

f: 126. What is the ruling if a hand containing only three fingers is amputated?
b: Compensation is only for the three fingers, and nothing additional is due for the palm by consensus, because the majority of the fingers assume the ruling of the whole hand.

f: 127. What compensation is due for cutting off an extra finger?
b: Only ḥukūmat al-ʿadl, because although it is part of the human body, it provides neither significant benefit nor beauty.

f: 128. What compensation is due for removing a supernumerary (extra) tooth?
b: Only ḥukūmat al-ʿadl, for the same reason as an extra finger.

f: 129. What is the ruling if a young child's eye, tongue, or penis is destroyed before its normal function can be confirmed?
b: Only ḥukūmat al-ʿadl is due, because full compensation depends on certainty that the organ possessed its intended function.

f: 130. Why does the Ḥanafī school not award a full diyah for destroying an infant's eye, tongue, or penis before their function is established?
b: Because the primary consideration is the organ's function, and that function has not yet been proven. Mere probability is insufficient to establish full compensation.

f: 131. Does an infant's first cry (istihlāl) establish the normal function of the tongue?
b: No. A newborn's cry is merely a sound and does not establish the ability to speak. Normal speech must later become apparent.

f: 132. How is the function of a child's eye, tongue, and penis determined?
b: The tongue is judged by the child's later ability to speak, the penis by its normal function and movement, and the eye by evidence of sight. Once established, the rulings become those of an adult.

f: 133. If a mūḍiḥah (bone-exposing wound) causes permanent loss of intellect, does the compensation for the wound remain separate?
b: No. The compensation for the mūḍiḥah is absorbed into the full diyah because the loss of intellect destroys the benefit of the entire body, making the lesser compensation merge into the greater.

f: 134. Why does the compensation for a mūḍiḥah merge into the diyah when the victim loses his intellect?
b: Because both injuries arose from one cause, and the greater compensation for the complete loss of intellect encompasses the lesser compensation for the wound itself.

f: 135. How did Zufar differ regarding the merger of a mūḍiḥah compensation into the full diyah?
b: Zufar held that they remain separate because each is an independent injury below the level of homicide.

f: 136. If a mūḍiḥah causes permanent loss of hearing, sight, or speech, does its compensation merge into the diyah?
b: No. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, the compensation for the mūḍiḥah remains in addition to the full diyah for the lost faculty, because each concerns a distinct bodily benefit.

f: 137. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله second opinion regarding a mūḍiḥah that causes loss of hearing or speech?
b: He held that the compensation for the wound merges into the diyah for hearing or speech because those faculties are internal like the intellect, whereas it does not merge into the diyah for sight because sight is associated with a visible organ.

f: 138. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a person intentionally inflicts a mūḍiḥah (bone-exposing head wound) that later causes the victim to lose both eyes?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ for either the mūḍiḥah or the blindness because the injury spread (sarāyah) beyond the original wound. Instead, the victim is entitled to the full diyah for the loss of both eyes.

f: 139. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the ruling if a person intentionally inflicts a mūḍiḥah that later causes the victim to lose both eyes?
b: Qiṣāṣ is carried out for the mūḍiḥah itself, and the victim is also entitled to the full diyah for the loss of both eyes.

f: 140. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a person amputates another person's finger at its upper joint and the remainder of the finger or even the entire hand later becomes paralyzed?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ for any part of the injury. The victim is entitled to the prescribed compensation for the amputated joint and ḥukūmat al-ʿadl for the remaining paralyzed portion.

f: 141. According to al-Hidāyah, what is the ruling if a person's tooth is broken and the remaining portion later turns black?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ because exact equivalence cannot be achieved. Instead, the victim is entitled to the full prescribed compensation for the tooth.

f: 142. Can a victim request qiṣāṣ only for the original injury while leaving the later effects caused by the injury untouched?
b: No. Since the original injury and its spread are legally treated as one act, qiṣāṣ cannot be limited to only the initial injury while ignoring its later consequences.

f: 143. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله rule that qiṣāṣ is not available when an injury spreads from the original wound to additional connected body parts?
b: Because the original wound and its spread are treated as one continuous act affecting one connected body, creating doubt that prevents qiṣāṣ and requires financial compensation instead.

f: 144. Why is the case of an arrow passing through one victim and killing a second person different from an injury that spreads through the same victim's body?
b: Because the arrow causes two legally distinct injuries to two separate people, whereas a spreading injury is treated as one continuous injury to a single connected body.

f: 145. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a person's finger is amputated and a neighboring finger later becomes paralyzed because of that injury?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ for either finger. Instead, financial compensation is due because the paralysis resulted from the spread of the original injury.

f: 146. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, Muḥammad, Zufar, and al-Ḥasan, what is the ruling if a person's finger is amputated and a neighboring finger later becomes paralyzed?
b: Qiṣāṣ is carried out for the finger that was directly amputated, while financial compensation (arsh) is due for the neighboring finger that became paralyzed.

f: 147. According to Muḥammad's narration through Ibn Samāʿah, what is the ruling if a mūḍiḥah causes the victim to lose his eyesight?
b: Qiṣāṣ is carried out for both the mūḍiḥah and the blindness because eyesight itself is subject to qiṣāṣ and the spreading injury is treated like a direct act.

f: 148. According to the dominant Ḥanafī opinion, why is qiṣāṣ not imposed when a mūḍiḥah later causes blindness?
b: Because the blindness results indirectly through causation (tasabbub), not through a direct injury, and qiṣāṣ is not imposed for such indirect causation in this case.

f: 149. According to the dominant Ḥanafī opinion, what is the ruling if part of a person's tooth is broken and the remainder later falls out?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ. An exception is reported in the narration of Ibn Samāʿah.

f: 150. According to al-Hidāyah, what is the ruling if two mūḍiḥah wounds merge together through deterioration?
b: The ruling follows the same two narrations discussed regarding injuries whose effects spread beyond the original wound.

f: 151. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if an adult's knocked-out tooth is later replaced by a new tooth?
b: The compensation (arsh) is cancelled because no lasting loss of function or beauty remains after the new tooth grows.

f: 152. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, does compensation remain due if a replacement tooth grows after an adult's tooth is knocked out?
b: Yes. The original injury remains legally established, while the replacement tooth is regarded as a new blessing from Allah that does not erase liability.

f: 153. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله cancel compensation when an adult's knocked-out tooth is replaced by a new tooth?
b: Because the legal injury is considered to have disappeared once the lost function and appearance are fully restored, just as with a child's tooth.

f: 154. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion if an adult's knocked-out tooth is later replaced by a new tooth?
b: He held that ḥukūmat al-ʿadl is still due because of the pain suffered, even though the tooth regrew.

f: 155. If a knocked-out tooth is reinserted into its place and heals, is the attacker still liable for full compensation?
b: Yes. Full compensation remains due because the tooth does not truly return to its original state, as its roots do not regenerate.

f: 156. If a severed ear is reattached and heals, does this remove the attacker's liability for compensation?
b: No. Full compensation remains due because the ear does not return to its original condition.

f: 157. What is the ruling if someone knocks out another person's tooth, the victim retaliates by knocking out the attacker's tooth, and the victim's original tooth later grows back?
b: The victim who retaliated must pay the attacker 500 dirhams because it becomes clear that the original injury no longer justified retaliation.

f: 158. Why does Islamic law require the court to wait one year before ordering qiṣāṣ for a knocked-out tooth?
b: Because a replacement tooth normally appears within a year if it is going to regrow, and waiting helps prevent unjust retaliation.

f: 159. Why does the court not wait indefinitely before deciding whether qiṣāṣ should be carried out for a knocked-out tooth?
b: Because indefinite delay would result in the loss of legal rights, so one year is treated as the normal period for possible regrowth.

f: 160. Why is qiṣāṣ not imposed upon a person who lawfully retaliated by knocking out a tooth if the victim's original tooth later grows back?
b: Because he acted under a valid judicial ruling based on the available evidence, creating doubt that prevents qiṣāṣ, although financial compensation becomes due.

f: 161. What should a judge do if a person's tooth has merely become loose after being struck?
b: The judge should wait one year before deciding the case in order to determine whether the injury causes the tooth to fall out.

f: 162. If a loosened tooth falls out during the one-year waiting period and the parties dispute whether the blow caused the tooth to fall out, whose statement is accepted?
b: The injured person's statement is accepted so that the judicial waiting period serves its intended purpose.

f: 163. If a loosened tooth falls out after the one-year waiting period and the parties dispute whether the blow caused the tooth to fall out, whose statement is accepted?
b: The attacker's statement is accepted because the period set for the appearance of the injury's effects has already expired.

f: 164. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a loosened tooth never falls out?
b: No compensation is due because no lasting injury has occurred.

f: 165. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a loosened tooth never falls out?
b: Ḥukūmat al-ʿadl is due for the pain suffered, even though the tooth remained in place.

f: 166. What is the ruling if a person's tooth turns black after being struck?
b: There is no qiṣāṣ because the injury cannot be replicated exactly. Compensation is due instead.

f: 167. Who pays the compensation if a person's tooth turns black as the result of an accidental injury?
b: The offender's ʿāqilah (male agnatic relatives) pays the compensation.

f: 168. Who pays the compensation if a person's tooth turns black as the result of an intentional injury?
b: The offender personally pays the compensation from his own wealth.

f: 169. What is the ruling if part of a person's tooth is broken and the remaining portion later turns black?
b: The ruling is the same: there is no qiṣāṣ, and financial compensation is due instead.

f: 170. What is the ruling if a person's tooth turns red or green after being struck?
b: The ruling is the same as when it turns black: there is no qiṣāṣ, and financial compensation is due.

f: 171. Is there a single agreed-upon ruling if a person's tooth turns yellow after being struck?
b: No. Two different narrations are reported regarding that situation.

f: 172. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a wound heals completely, leaves no scar, and the hair grows back?
b: All compensation is cancelled because the disfigurement that justified compensation has completely disappeared.

f: 173. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله cancel compensation when a wound heals completely without leaving any scar?
b: Because compensation for such wounds is based on permanent disfigurement, and once no trace remains, the legal basis for compensation no longer exists.

f: 174. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is the ruling if a wound heals completely without leaving any scar?
b: Ḥukūmat al-ʿadl remains due because of the pain caused by the injury.

f: 175. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling if a wound heals completely without leaving any scar?
b: The attacker must reimburse the cost of medical treatment, since those expenses were caused by the injury.

f: 176. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject compensation for pain or medical treatment when a wound heals completely without leaving any trace?
b: Because, in the Ḥanafī school, benefits and services are not independently compensable unless protected by a contract or quasi-contract, and neither exists in this case.

f: 177. According to al-Hidāyah, what compensation is due if a person strikes another one hundred times, causing wounds that later heal but leave permanent marks?
b: Compensation (arsh) is due for the injuries, provided the marks or effects remain.

f: 178. According to al-Hidāyah, what is the ruling if a person strikes another one hundred times, the wounds heal completely, and no trace remains?
b: The ruling follows the earlier disagreement regarding a wound that heals without leaving any trace: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله holds that no compensation is due, while Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad differ.

f: 179. What is the ruling if someone accidentally cuts another person's hand and, before it heals, accidentally kills the same person?
b: Only the full diyah for the person's life is due. Compensation for the hand is absorbed into the diyah because both injuries are of the same type (accidental) and the diyah covers the whole person.

f: 180. Why is compensation for an accidentally severed hand cancelled if the victim later dies accidentally from the same injury before healing?
b: Because both injuries are accidental, the legal obligation is a single diyah for the entire person, and compensation for the limb is included within it.

f: 181. According to the Ḥanafī school, when may qiṣāṣ for a wound be carried out?
b: Qiṣāṣ is delayed until the wound has fully healed and its final outcome is known.

f: 182. Why does the Ḥanafī school delay qiṣāṣ for wounds until healing occurs?
b: Because the final consequences of a wound are uncertain. It may heal, worsen, or spread and cause death, so its legal ruling is not settled until healing occurs.

f: 183. What evidence do the Ḥanafīs cite for delaying qiṣāṣ in wound cases?
b: They cite the report: "Wounds should be left for a year (yustaʾnā fī al-jarāḥāt sanah)," and argue that the ultimate outcome of the wound must first become clear.

f: 184. Why does al-Shāfiʿī permit immediate qiṣāṣ for wounds?
b: Because he considers the intentional injury already established, so the right of qiṣāṣ should not be delayed, by analogy with intentional homicide.

f: 185. According to the Ḥanafīs, who pays the diyah whenever qiṣāṣ for an intentional killing is cancelled because of a legal doubt (shubhah)?
b: The killer personally pays the diyah from his own wealth.

f: 186. According to the Ḥanafīs, who pays compensation agreed upon through a settlement (ṣulḥ) for an injury?
b: The offender personally pays it from his own wealth because it arises from a contract, not from the original criminal liability.

f: 187. Why is the diyah for an intentional killing in which qiṣāṣ is prevented by shubhah paid over three years, while compensation agreed by settlement is due immediately?
b: The diyah arises directly from the killing and therefore follows the payment schedule of homicide compensation, whereas settlement compensation arises from a contract and is due immediately like a sale price.

f: 188. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a father intentionally kills his son, how is the diyah paid?
b: The father pays the diyah from his own wealth over three years.

f: 189. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله require the diyah of a father who intentionally kills his son to be paid over three years?
b: Because it is compensation arising from homicide, and all such compensation follows the legislated deferred payment schedule rather than immediate payment.

f: 190. Why does al-Shāfiʿī hold that a father who intentionally kills his son must pay the diyah immediately?
b: Because intentional destruction of life normally creates an immediately payable financial obligation, and deferred payment is a concession only for accidental killings.

f: 191. According to the Ḥanafīs, what is the ruling if a person admits to committing an injury or homicide that would normally be paid by the ʿāqilah?
b: The financial liability falls upon the offender himself, and his admission does not bind the ʿāqilah.

f: 192. Why does a person's confession not bind his ʿāqilah according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because a confession is legally effective only against the confessor himself and cannot impose liability on other people.

f: 193. According to the Ḥanafīs, how are intentional injuries committed by a child or an insane person legally classified?
b: They are treated as accidental injuries.

f: 194. Who pays the diyah for an intentional killing committed by a child or an insane person according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Their ʿāqilah pays the diyah, just as in accidental homicide.

f: 195. According to the Ḥanafīs, what is the ruling for injuries committed by a mentally disabled person (maʿtūh)?
b: They are treated the same as injuries committed by an insane person.

f: 196. According to al-Shāfiʿī, how are intentional killings committed by a child or an insane person treated financially?
b: They remain intentional acts, so the diyah is paid immediately from the offender's own wealth, although qiṣāṣ is not imposed.

f: 197. Why do the Ḥanafīs treat intentional acts of children and insane persons as accidental?
b: Because true legal intent depends upon complete intellect. A child has deficient understanding, and an insane person lacks it altogether.

f: 198. What report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib supports the Ḥanafī ruling on intentional acts committed by the insane?
b: He said that the diyah of an insane person is borne by the ʿāqilah and that "his intentional act and his accidental act are the same."

f: 199. According to the Ḥanafīs, are children and insane persons liable for kaffārah when they cause death?
b: No, because they are not legally accountable (mukallaf) and the Pen has been lifted from them.

f: 200. According to the Ḥanafīs, do children and insane persons lose inheritance rights because of homicide?
b: No. Disqualification from inheritance is a punishment, and they are not legally subject to punishment.

f: 201. What compensation is due if a pregnant woman is struck and miscarries a dead fetus?
b: A ghurrah is due, equal to one-twentieth of the full diyah (500 dirhams).

f: 202. What is a ghurrah in Islamic law?
b: It is the fixed compensation payable for causing a pregnant woman to miscarry a dead fetus, traditionally valued at 500 dirhams or a slave of equivalent value.

f: 203. Why is a ghurrah payable for a miscarried fetus even though its independent life cannot be proven with certainty?
b: Because this ruling is established by prophetic tradition (istiḥsān based on textual evidence), which overrides analogical reasoning.

f: 204. Who pays the ghurrah according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The offender's ʿāqilah, provided the amount reaches the minimum for which the ʿāqilah is responsible.

f: 205. Why do the Ḥanafīs require the ʿāqilah to pay the ghurrah?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ ruled that the ghurrah is borne by the ʿāqilah, and it is treated as compensation for a human life.

f: 206. Over what period is the ghurrah paid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It is paid within one year.

f: 207. Why is the ghurrah paid over one year instead of three years?
b: Because although it resembles compensation for a human life, it also resembles compensation for a bodily part connected to the mother, so it follows the shorter payment period.

f: 208. Does the amount of the ghurrah differ according to whether the fetus is male or female?
b: No. The ghurrah is the same for both because no legal distinction exists between male and female fetuses at that stage.

f: 209. What is the ruling if the child is born alive after the injury and later dies from it?
b: The full diyah for a living person is due because the injury caused the death of someone who had been born alive.

f: 210. What compensation is due if a pregnant woman miscarries a dead fetus because of an assault and then later dies from the same assault?
b: The offender owes the full diyah for the mother and a separate ghurrah for the fetus.

f: 211. What compensation is due if the mother dies from the assault, the child is later delivered alive, and then dies?
b: The offender owes two full diyahs: one for the mother and one for the child, since two separate lives were lost.

f: 212. What is the ruling if the mother dies from the assault and the fetus is later delivered dead?
b: Only the mother's diyah is due; no ghurrah is payable for the fetus according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 213. Why do the Ḥanafīs not require a ghurrah when the mother dies first and the fetus is later delivered dead?
b: Because the fetus may have died as a result of the mother's death rather than directly from the assault, and compensation cannot be imposed when the cause is uncertain.

f: 214. Why does al-Shāfiʿī require a ghurrah even when the mother dies before delivering a dead fetus?
b: Because he presumes that the assault caused the fetus's death unless proven otherwise.

f: 215. Who inherits the compensation (ghurrah) due for a fetus that is killed before birth?
b: The compensation is inherited from the fetus itself, so it is distributed among the fetus's legal heirs.

f: 216. Does the person who caused the death of a fetus inherit from the compensation due for that fetus?
b: No. The person who caused the fetus's death is treated as its killer and is barred from inheriting from its compensation.

f: 217. If a man strikes his pregnant wife, causing her to miscarry their child, does he inherit from the ghurrah due for the fetus?
b: No. A ghurrah is due from the father's ʿāqilah, but the father inherits nothing from it because he caused the death of the fetus.

f: 218. According to the Ḥanafīs, how is compensation calculated for a male fetus belonging to a female slave (janīn al-amah)?
b: The compensation is one-twentieth (half of one-tenth) of the value the slave fetus would have had if born alive.

f: 219. According to the Ḥanafīs, how is compensation calculated for a female fetus belonging to a female slave?
b: The compensation is one-tenth of the value the slave fetus would have had if born alive.

f: 220. According to al-Shāfiʿī, how is compensation calculated for the fetus of a slave woman?
b: It is one-tenth of the value of the mother, because the fetus is treated as part of her.

f: 221. Why do the Ḥanafīs calculate compensation for the fetus of a slave according to the fetus's own value rather than the mother's value?
b: Because they regard the compensation as payment for the fetus itself rather than compensation for part of the mother's body.

f: 222. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding injury to a pregnant slave that harms her fetus?
b: He held that compensation equals the reduction in the mother's value, by analogy with the fetus of livestock.

f: 223. If a slave owner emancipates the fetus after it is injured in the womb, the child is born alive and later dies from that injury, what compensation is due according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The offender must pay the child's market value as a living slave, not a full diyah, because the injury occurred while the child was still a slave.

f: 224. Why is the value of the slave child due instead of a full diyah if the child was emancipated after the injury but before death?
b: Because liability is determined by the child's status when the injury was inflicted, and at that time the child was still a slave.

f: 225. What was Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's opinion regarding a slave fetus injured before emancipation and later dying after emancipation?
b: He held that only the reduction in value caused by the injury is payable, because emancipation cuts off the legal effect of the previous injury.

f: 226. Is kaffārah (expiation) required for causing the death of a fetus according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. Kaffārah is not required.

f: 227. Why do the Ḥanafīs not require kaffārah for causing the death of a fetus?
b: Because kaffārah has the nature of a punishment and is legislated only for complete human lives, while a fetus does not receive the full legal rulings of a born person.

f: 228. According to the Ḥanafīs, is it still recommended for someone who caused the death of a fetus to seek Allah's forgiveness?
b: Yes. Although kaffārah is not obligatory, it is recommended to seek forgiveness and perform acts of worship voluntarily because a prohibited act was committed.

f: 229. When does a fetus receive the same legal rulings as a fully formed fetus regarding compensation?
b: Once some of its human features have become clearly formed.

f: 230. Why is a partially formed fetus treated like a fully formed fetus in these rulings?
b: Because it has become distinguishable as a human being and already receives similar legal rulings in matters such as lineage, waiting periods (ʿiddah), and postnatal bleeding (nifās).

f: 231. According to the Ḥanafīs, who has the right to remove an unlawful structure built on a public road, such as a latrine, waterspout, platform, or bench?
b: Any member of the public who uses the road has the right to remove it because everyone shares the right of passage.

f: 232. Why may any member of the public remove an obstruction built on a public road?
b: Because the right of passage belongs jointly to all users of the road, just as co-owners may remove unauthorized alterations in jointly owned property.

f: 233. May a person benefit from an installation placed on a public road if it causes no harm to others?
b: Yes. It is permissible so long as it causes no harm to the public.

f: 234. What legal principle limits a person's use of public roads according to al-Hidāyah?
b: The Prophetic principle: "There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm (lā ḍarar wa lā ḍirār)."

f: 235. May a resident of a private dead-end street build a waterspout or latrine projecting into that street without the consent of the other residents?
b: No. The consent of all the residents is required because the street belongs collectively to them.

f: 236. Why is unanimous consent required before making alterations in a private dead-end street?
b: Because it is jointly owned by its residents, so no one may dispose of part of it without the permission of the other owners.

f: 237. Why are installations on a public through-road treated differently from those on a private dead-end street?
b: Because obtaining the consent of every member of the public is impossible, so beneficial use is permitted unless it causes harm.

f: 238. Who bears liability if a projecting balcony, waterspout, or similar structure extending into a public road falls and kills someone?
b: The builder's ʿāqilah bears the diyah because the builder created a harmful and unlawful cause.

f: 239. Why is liability imposed when a projection over a public road falls and causes death?
b: Because unlawfully occupying public airspace creates a negligent cause of injury for which the builder is responsible.

f: 240. If someone is injured after tripping over debris unlawfully left in a public road, who is liable?
b: The person who placed the debris there is liable.

f: 241. If a person trips over an unlawful obstruction in the road, falls onto another person, and both die, who is liable?
b: The one who created the obstruction is liable for both deaths because he is treated as though he pushed the first person onto the second.

f: 242. If a waterspout falls and only the portion attached inside the owner's wall strikes and kills someone, is the owner liable?
b: No. That part was within his own property and was not an unlawful encroachment.

f: 243. If only the projecting part of a waterspout extending beyond the wall falls and kills someone, who is liable?
b: The person who installed it is liable because the projecting portion unlawfully occupied public space.

f: 244. If both the lawful and unlawful parts of a waterspout contribute to a person's death, how much liability is imposed?
b: One-half of the diyah is payable and the other half is disregarded because one cause is lawful and the other unlawful.

f: 245. If it is unknown whether the lawful or unlawful part of a waterspout caused the fatal injury, how much liability is imposed?
b: One-half of the diyah is still payable, based on the legal assessment of probabilities.

f: 246. If a homeowner builds a projecting balcony over a public road and later sells the house, who remains liable if the balcony later falls and kills someone?
b: The original builder remains liable because his unlawful act created the dangerous condition.

f: 247. If someone places a beam or timber in a public road, sells it, and the buyer leaves it there until it causes a fatal accident, who is liable?
b: The seller remains liable because he was the one who unlawfully placed it in the road.

f: 248. Why does selling an unlawfully placed object not transfer liability for injuries caused by it?
b: Because the original unlawful act of placing it there remains legally attributable to the person who created the hazard.

f: 249. If someone places burning coals in a public road and they burn another person's property, is he liable?
b: Yes. He is liable because placing burning coals in a public road is an unlawful and harmful act.

f: 250. If a person unlawfully places burning coals on a public road, but the wind blows them elsewhere before they ignite property, is the person liable according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. The wind is considered to have interrupted and replaced the person's act, so liability no longer attaches to the original placement.

f: 251. What alternative opinion is mentioned regarding burning coals moved by the wind?
b: If it was a windy day and the person knowingly placed the coals despite foreseeing that the wind would spread them, he is liable because his act is treated like direct causation.

f: 252. If a homeowner hires workers to remove a projecting balcony or awning, and it falls and kills someone before the work is finished, who is liable?
b: The workers are liable because the fatal act occurred through their own actions while they were still performing the work.

f: 253. Why are hired workers liable if a structure falls and kills someone before they complete its removal?
b: Because the work had not yet been delivered back to the homeowner, and the death resulted directly from the workers' actions.

f: 254. If a projecting balcony falls and kills someone after hired workers have finished removing or repairing it, who is liable according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The homeowner is liable according to istiḥsān.

f: 255. Why does liability shift to the homeowner after workers complete their work on a projecting structure?
b: Because the work is considered complete and accepted, so the workers' actions are legally attributed to the homeowner.

f: 256. If someone pours water onto a public road and a person or animal slips and is injured or killed, is the person who poured the water liable?
b: Yes. He is liable because he unlawfully created a hazard on the public road.

f: 257. Does liability also apply if someone sprinkles water or performs wuḍūʾ on a public road and someone slips because of it?
b: Yes, if doing so creates a dangerous condition for passersby.

f: 258. If a resident sprinkles water, sits, or places belongings in a private dead-end street where he is one of the residents, is he liable for resulting accidents?
b: No, because such acts are regarded as ordinary necessities of living in property jointly shared by the residents.

f: 259. Does sprinkling a small amount of water that normally does not cause slipping create liability?
b: No. Liability applies only when the amount is sufficient to create the usual risk of slipping.

f: 260. If someone knowingly walks over a wet area that another person created on part of a public road and slips, is the person who poured the water liable?
b: No, because the injured person voluntarily chose the dangerous path even though a safe route remained available.

f: 261. When does the person who poured water on a public road remain liable even if the injured person knew about the danger?
b: If the water covered the entire road, leaving no safe alternative, because the injured person was forced to pass through it.

f: 262. Does the same distinction apply to timber or other objects left on a public road?
b: Yes. Liability depends on whether a safe alternative route remained available.

f: 263. If someone sprinkles water in front of a shop with the shop owner's permission and an accident occurs, who is liable?
b: The shop owner (the one who gave the instruction) is liable according to istiḥsān.

f: 264. If a builder finishes construction in front of a shop at the owner's request and someone later trips and dies, who is liable?
b: The person who ordered the work (the shop owner) is liable according to istiḥsān.

f: 265. If a person orders a builder to construct something in the middle of a public road, who is liable for injuries caused by it?
b: The builder is liable because the order itself was invalid and could not transfer responsibility.

f: 266. If someone digs a well in a public road and a person falls in and dies, who bears liability?
b: The digger's ʿāqilah pays the diyah because the digging unlawfully created the cause of death.

f: 267. If an animal falls into an unlawfully dug well and dies, who pays compensation?
b: The digger personally pays the animal's value from his own wealth, because the ʿāqilah bears liability only for human life.

f: 268. Is placing stones, timber, earth, or mud in a public road treated like digging a dangerous hole?
b: Yes. These are all unlawful obstructions that create liability for resulting harm.

f: 269. If someone merely sweeps a public road and another person slips where it was swept, is the sweeper liable?
b: No. Sweeping removes harm from the road and does not create a new hazard.

f: 270. When does sweeping a road become a source of liability?
b: If the person gathers the rubbish into a pile that obstructs the road and someone is injured because of it.

f: 271. If one person places a stone in the road and another later moves it elsewhere before an accident occurs, who is liable?
b: The person who moved the stone is liable because his act replaced the legal effect of the original placement.

f: 272. If the ruler orders someone to dig a drain or pit in a public road and someone is later injured by it, is the digger liable?
b: No. Acting under the lawful order of the ruler removes liability because the act is not considered unlawful.

f: 273. If someone digs a drain or pit in a public road without the ruler's permission, is he liable for resulting injuries?
b: Yes. He is liable because he unlawfully interfered with public rights.

f: 274. Does the same rule apply to all other alterations made in a public road?
b: Yes. Permission from the lawful authority removes liability; acting without it creates liability.

f: 275. If someone digs a pit inside his own private property and another person is harmed by it, is he liable?
b: No, because he is acting within his own property and is not committing an unlawful act.

f: 276. If someone digs in the open space immediately outside his house (fanāʾ al-dār), is he liable?
b: Generally no, because he has the right to use that area for the benefit of his house, provided he has lawful rights over it.

f: 277. When is a person liable for digging in the area outside his house?
b: If that space belongs to the public or is jointly owned, such as in a private dead-end street, because he has no exclusive right to dig there.

f: 278. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if someone falls into an unlawfully dug well but later dies from hunger or grief rather than the fall itself, is the digger liable?
b: No. The death is attributed to another cause rather than the fall.

f: 279. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding someone who falls into a well and later dies from grief?
b: The digger is liable because the grief resulted directly from falling into the well.

f: 280. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion if the person trapped in the well dies from hunger?
b: The digger is not liable because hunger is not uniquely caused by the well.

f: 281. What was Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan's opinion regarding a person who dies from hunger or grief after falling into a well?
b: The digger is liable in every case because the victim would not have been deprived of food or safety had he not fallen into the well.

f: 282. If a landowner hires workers to dig a pit outside his property and the workers do not know they are digging outside his lawful area, who is liable if someone later dies?
b: The employer is liable because the workers were deceived into believing the work was lawful.

f: 283. Why are workers not liable when they unknowingly dig outside the employer's lawful property?
b: Because the employer misled them, making the act legally attributable to him rather than to them.

f: 284. If workers know they are digging outside the employer's lawful property, who is liable for resulting injuries?
b: The workers themselves are liable because they knowingly carried out an unlawful act.

f: 285. If the employer says, "This is the area in front of my house, but I have no legal right to dig here," who is liable according to qiyās if the workers proceed?
b: The workers are liable because they knew the employer lacked the legal authority to order the digging.

f: 286. According to istiḥsān, who is liable if workers dig in front of a person's house after he says he has no right to dig there?
b: The employer is liable because the area in front of his house outwardly appears to be under his control, making the workers' reliance on his instructions legally reasonable.

f: 287. If someone builds a bridge over a public road without the ruler's permission and another person knowingly crosses it and dies, is the builder liable?
b: No. The injured person deliberately chose to use the bridge, so his direct action takes precedence over the builder's earlier indirect act.

f: 288. If someone places a plank across a public road and another person knowingly walks on it and is injured, is the person who placed the plank liable?
b: No. The injured person's voluntary act of walking on it is the direct cause, which overrides the earlier indirect cause.

f: 289. Why is the person who created an unauthorized bridge or plank on a public road not liable when someone knowingly uses it and is injured?
b: Because a voluntary act by a competent person intervenes between the original cause and the injury, severing legal attribution to the earlier act.

f: 290. If someone is carrying an object along a public road and it falls onto another person, causing injury or death, is the carrier liable?
b: Yes. The carrier is liable because he is expected to keep the object under control while carrying it.

f: 291. If an object falls from a person's hands onto the road and another person later trips over it, is the carrier liable?
b: Yes. He is liable because he was responsible for preventing the object from falling.

f: 292. If a person's cloak or garment accidentally falls off while he is wearing it, and someone is injured because of it, is the wearer liable?
b: No. Wearing clothing is not legally conditioned upon guaranteeing that it never falls.

f: 293. Why does the Ḥanafī school distinguish between carrying an object and merely wearing clothing?
b: Carrying an object requires actively preserving control over it, whereas clothing is worn for normal use and not primarily for safeguarding it.

f: 294. According to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, when is a person wearing an item treated like someone carrying it?
b: When he wears something that people do not normally wear, because there is no customary need for wearing it.

f: 295. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a member of the local community hangs a lamp, lays mats, or places pebbles in the community mosque and someone is injured because of them, is he liable?
b: No. Members of the mosque's community have authority over its ordinary management and use.

f: 296. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a person who is not from the mosque's local community hangs a lamp or places items in the mosque and someone is injured, is he liable?
b: Yes. He is liable because he acted without the authority reserved for the mosque's community.

f: 297. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding non-members placing beneficial items in a mosque?
b: They held that no liability exists, because acts such as hanging lamps or placing mats are charitable acts that everyone is generally permitted to perform.

f: 298. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between members and non-members of a mosque's local community?
b: Because matters relating to the mosque's administration belong to its local community, such as appointing its imam, choosing its caretaker, and managing its affairs.

f: 299. Does the charitable nature of an act automatically remove liability if it causes harm?
b: No. A charitable intention does not prevent liability if the act was performed without proper authority or in an improper manner.

f: 300. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a member of the mosque's local community is sitting in the mosque praying and someone trips over him, is he liable?
b: No. Sitting for prayer is the primary purpose for which the mosque was built.

f: 301. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, if a member of the mosque's local community sits in the mosque for a purpose other than prayer and someone trips over him, is he liable?
b: Yes. Activities other than actual prayer are only secondarily connected to the mosque and are therefore subject to the condition of avoiding harm.

f: 302. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, is a person liable if someone trips over him while he is sitting in the mosque, whether for prayer or another religious purpose?
b: No. They held that waiting for prayer and similar religious activities are all included within the mosque's intended use.

f: 303. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does the same ruling apply to sitting in the mosque for Qur'an recitation, teaching, waiting for prayer, sleeping, walking through the mosque, or ordinary conversation?
b: Yes. These activities follow the same legal distinction: actual prayer is exempt, while other uses are subject to liability if harm results.

f: 304. According to one opinion, how is a person in iʿtikāf treated if someone is injured because of him in the mosque?
b: He follows the same legal disagreement regarding other non-prayer activities.

f: 305. According to another opinion, is a person performing iʿtikāf liable if someone is injured because of him?
b: No. According to that opinion, there is no liability by consensus because iʿtikāf is a special act of worship.

f: 306. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad exempt waiting for prayer from liability?
b: Because a person waiting for prayer is regarded by Prophetic tradition as being "in prayer," making his presence equivalent to actual prayer.

f: 307. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish actual prayer from other beneficial religious activities in the mosque?
b: Because the mosque was fundamentally established for prayer, while other activities are secondary and therefore remain subject to the condition of avoiding harm.

f: 308. Can an act that is permissible or even recommended still create liability if it causes harm?
b: Yes. Many lawful or recommended acts remain conditioned upon avoiding harm, such as hunting, fighting in lawful combat, or walking in public places.

f: 309. According to the text, should a Muslim from outside the local mosque community be liable if someone trips over him while he is praying there?
b: It should be said that he is not liable, because every Muslim has the right to pray in a mosque even if he is not from its local community.

f: 310. If a wall leans toward a public road and its owner is warned to demolish it but fails to do so until it falls and causes damage, is the owner liable?
b: Yes. Once he has been notified and given time to remove it, he is liable for all resulting injuries and damage.

f: 311. Why does the owner become liable after being warned about a leaning wall?
b: Because once he is informed and able to remove the danger, his failure to act becomes wrongful and he is responsible for the continuing hazard.

f: 312. Why is the owner not liable before receiving notice that his wall has become dangerous?
b: Because before being informed he is not considered to have wrongfully maintained the danger, since the original construction was lawful.

f: 313. What analogy does al-Hidāyah use to explain liability after notice regarding a leaning wall?
b: It is like someone refusing to return another person's property after being asked; the wrongful retention begins only after the demand is made.

f: 314. What public interest supports imposing liability on the owner of a dangerous leaning wall after notice?
b: Without liability, owners might ignore dangerous walls, causing public roads to become unsafe for everyone.

f: 315. If a leaning wall falls after notice and kills a person, who pays the diyah?
b: The owner's ʿāqilah pays the diyah because the case resembles accidental homicide.

f: 316. If a leaning wall destroys property such as animals or merchandise, who pays compensation?
b: The owner personally pays the compensation from his own wealth because the ʿāqilah bears only liability for human life.

f: 317. Is formal witness testimony (ishhād) itself a condition for liability regarding a dangerous wall?
b: No. Liability depends upon the owner being notified and requested to remove the wall; witnesses merely help prove that notice occurred if it is later denied.

f: 318. How should witnesses be used when notifying the owner of a dangerous leaning wall?
b: The person giving notice should have witnesses testify that he demanded the owner demolish the dangerous wall.

f: 319. Can witnesses be called before a wall has actually become dangerous and leaning?
b: No. Before the wall becomes dangerous there is no wrongful conduct, so such testimony has no legal effect.

f: 320. If a person originally builds a wall leaning toward a public road and it later falls causing injury or damage, is prior notice required before he is liable?
b: No. He is liable without prior notice because the wall was unlawfully built in a dangerous manner from the outset.

f: 321. Why is prior notice unnecessary when a wall is built leaning over a public road from the beginning?
b: Because the initial construction itself was a wrongful act, just like unlawfully projecting a balcony over the road.

f: 322. What evidence is sufficient to prove that a property owner was warned to remove a dangerous leaning wall?
b: The testimony of either two men or one man and two women, since this is not testimony concerning homicide but about giving notice.

f: 323. Besides giving notice, what additional condition must exist before the owner of a leaning wall becomes liable for failing to remove it?
b: The owner must have been given enough time to remove the wall, so that failing to act can legally be regarded as negligence.

f: 324. Who may legally notify the owner to remove a wall leaning over a public road?
b: Any person who has the right to use the road, whether Muslim or dhimmī, man or woman, free person or mukātab (contract slave).

f: 325. Must the warning to remove a dangerous wall be given before a judge or ruler?
b: No. The warning may be given before or outside the ruler because every person sharing the public right of passage may demand removal of the obstruction.

f: 326. If a wall leans toward a private house instead of a public road, who has the right to demand its removal?
b: The owner of the affected house has that exclusive right because the harm concerns his private property.

f: 327. If tenants occupy a house toward which a wall is leaning, may they demand its removal?
b: Yes. They may demand removal because they have the right to prevent interference with the use and airspace of the house they occupy.

f: 328. If the owner or occupants of a private house forgive or delay the removal of a wall leaning toward their property, is the wall's owner still liable for later damage?
b: No. Since the right belongs to them personally, they may waive or postpone it, removing liability.

f: 329. Why can private homeowners waive their right regarding a leaning wall, while the public cannot?
b: Because the right belongs exclusively to the private property holders, whereas the right to a public road belongs collectively to all Muslims and cannot be waived by individuals.

f: 330. Can a judge or the witnesses who gave notice waive the public's right by granting extra time for a dangerous wall over a public road?
b: No. Neither can invalidate the public's collective right.

f: 331. If the owner sells a dangerous leaning wall after receiving notice and the buyer takes possession, does the seller remain liable?
b: No. The seller is no longer liable because he has lost the ability to remove the wall, and liability was based upon failing to act while able.

f: 332. Why is selling a leaning wall different from selling a projecting balcony that was unlawfully constructed?
b: Liability for the leaning wall arises from failing to remove it after notice, whereas liability for the balcony arose from the original unlawful construction, which is not undone by sale.

f: 333. Is the purchaser of a leaning wall automatically liable after buying it?
b: No. The purchaser becomes liable only after receiving notice and then failing to remove the danger despite being able to do so.

f: 334. What general principle determines who may validly receive notice regarding a dangerous wall?
b: Notice is effective only against someone who has the legal ability to remove the wall and clear the obstruction.

f: 335. Can a mortgagee (murtahin), tenant, borrower, or ordinary occupant validly receive notice requiring removal of a dangerous wall?
b: No. They cannot because they lack the legal authority to demolish the wall.

f: 336. Can the owner (rāhin) of mortgaged property validly receive notice regarding a dangerous wall?
b: Yes. He can redeem the property and remove the wall, so notice to him is valid.

f: 337. Can a guardian (waṣī), a minor's father, or a minor's mother receive valid notice concerning a dangerous wall owned by the minor?
b: Yes. Their guardianship gives them authority to act, while liability ultimately falls upon the minor's estate.

f: 338. Why does liability fall upon the minor's estate when his guardian fails to remove a dangerous wall?
b: Because the guardian acts on behalf of the minor, making the omission legally attributable to the minor's property.

f: 339. Can a mukātab (contract slave) receive valid notice to remove a dangerous wall?
b: Yes. A mukātab has legal authority over his own affairs and property.

f: 340. Can a slave engaged in trade (ʿabd tājir) receive valid notice regarding a dangerous wall?
b: Yes. Whether indebted or not, he has authority over such commercial matters.

f: 341. If a trading slave's dangerous wall causes property damage after notice, who pays compensation?
b: The compensation for property damage is paid from the slave's own assets.

f: 342. If a trading slave's dangerous wall causes the death of a person after notice, whose ʿāqilah bears the diyah?
b: The master's ʿāqilah bears the diyah because liability for human life is connected to the master.

f: 343. Can notice be validly served upon one co-owner of a jointly owned dangerous wall?
b: Yes. Each co-owner can protect his own share by bringing the matter before a judge, so notice to one owner is effective regarding his share.

f: 344. If a dangerous wall falls after proper notice, killing one person, and another person later trips over the corpse and dies, is the wall owner liable for the second death?
b: No. Responsibility for removing the corpse belongs to the deceased's heirs, not to the wall owner.

f: 345. If a dangerous wall is being demolished after notice and someone is injured during the demolition, is the owner liable?
b: Yes. Demolishing the wall is the owner's responsibility, so harm occurring during that process is attributed to him.

f: 346. If a jar belonging to the wall owner falls from the dangerous wall and injures someone, is the wall owner liable?
b: Yes. Removing his property from the wall was his responsibility.

f: 347. If property belonging to someone else falls from the dangerous wall and injures a person, is the wall owner liable?
b: No. Responsibility for removing that property belongs to its owner.

f: 348. If five people jointly own a dangerous wall but only one owner received notice, and the wall kills someone, how much diyah is that owner liable for according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He is liable for one-fifth of the diyah, borne by his ʿāqilah, corresponding to his ownership share.

f: 349. If three people jointly own a house and one co-owner unlawfully digs a pit without the others' consent, causing a death, how much diyah is he liable for according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He is liable for two-thirds of the diyah, paid by his ʿāqilah.

f: 350. How did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad differ regarding a co-owner who alone creates a dangerous condition on jointly owned property?
b: They held that he is liable for one-half of the diyah rather than in proportion to ownership shares.

f: 351. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allocate liability according to ownership shares in these cases?
b: Because the collapse or dangerous condition is treated as one indivisible cause, which is then apportioned according to each owner's share of ownership.

f: 352. According to the Ḥanafīs, when is the rider of an animal liable for injuries caused by the animal while travelling on a public road?
b: The rider is liable for injuries caused by the animal's trampling, forelegs, hind legs, head, biting, striking with its body, or collision.

f: 353. Is the rider liable if the moving animal kicks backward or strikes someone with its tail?
b: No. While the animal is moving, such actions are ordinarily unavoidable and cannot reasonably be prevented.

f: 354. What legal principle explains why the rider is liable for trampling but not for kicks or tail strikes while travelling?
b: A person's lawful use of a public road is conditioned upon avoiding preventable harm, but not upon avoiding harm that cannot reasonably be prevented.

f: 355. If a rider stops his animal on a public road and it then kicks someone, is the rider liable?
b: Yes. Since stopping the animal was voluntary, the rider could have avoided creating the opportunity for the kick.

f: 356. Why does stopping an animal on a public road create liability for a later kick, whereas merely riding it does not?
b: Because the rider could have avoided obstructing the road by not stopping, making the resulting harm attributable to his voluntary act.

f: 357. If a riding animal kicks up a small pebble, seed, dust, or tiny stone that injures someone or damages clothing, is the rider liable?
b: No. Such small objects are an unavoidable consequence of normal travel, so liability does not arise because avoiding them is not reasonably possible.

f: 358. If a riding animal throws a large stone that injures someone, is the rider liable?
b: Yes. A large stone is not normally thrown during ordinary travel and can generally be avoided, so the rider is liable.

f: 359. Does the same ruling apply to a passenger riding behind the main rider (murtadif)?
b: Yes. The passenger is treated like the rider because the legal reasoning is the same.

f: 360. If an animal defecates or urinates while walking on the road and someone is harmed because of it, is the rider liable?
b: No. Urination and defecation while the animal is moving are unavoidable incidents of travel, so there is no liability.

f: 361. If an animal is stopped specifically so that it can urinate or defecate, and someone is harmed by the waste, is the rider liable?
b: No. Some animals only relieve themselves when stopped, so stopping them for this purpose is considered a necessity of travel.

f: 362. If an animal is stopped for a reason other than relieving itself, and it then urinates or defecates causing harm, is the rider liable?
b: Yes. Since the stop was unnecessary for travel, the rider is considered negligent and is liable for the resulting harm.

f: 363. For what injuries caused by the animal is the driver behind the animal (السائق) liable?
b: The driver is liable for injuries caused by the animal's front feet, hind feet, head, biting, striking, and similar acts that can reasonably be controlled. According to the preferred opinion, he is not liable for hind-leg kicking (نفحة).

f: 364. For what injuries caused by the animal is the leader in front of the animal (القائد) liable?
b: The leader is liable for injuries caused by the animal's front part, such as its front feet or head, because he can generally control these. He is not liable for hind-leg kicking, since he cannot reasonably prevent it.

f: 365. Why is the preferred Hanafi opinion that neither the driver nor the leader is liable for hind-leg kicking (نفحة)?
b: Because even if the kick can be seen, there is no practical means of preventing it while the animal is moving, making it unavoidable.

f: 366. What is Imam al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding liability for an animal's hind-leg kick?
b: He holds that the rider, driver, and leader are all liable because the animal's actions are legally attributed to them.

f: 367. What ḥadīth is used by the Hanafis regarding injury from an animal's hind leg?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The hind leg is exempt (الرجل جبار)." This is understood to mean that injury from an animal's hind-leg kick does not incur liability when it is unavoidable.

f: 368. According to al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, what general rule applies to the liability of the rider, driver, and leader?
b: Whatever injury makes the rider liable also makes the driver and leader liable, since all three contribute causally by bringing the animal to the place where the injury occurs, subject to the same limitations regarding avoidable and unavoidable harm.

f: 369. When is the rider required to offer kaffārah (expiation) for a death caused by the animal?
b: The rider owes kaffārah only when the animal tramples someone with its feet, because the trampling is legally attributed directly to the rider.

f: 370. Do the driver or leader owe kaffārah for a death caused by the animal?
b: No. They are considered indirect causes rather than direct actors, and kaffārah applies only to direct killing.

f: 371. Does the rider owe kaffārah for injuries caused by the animal other than trampling?
b: No. Kaffārah applies only to direct killing through trampling, not to other forms of indirect harm.

f: 372. Does a rider who causes death by trampling lose the right to inherit from the deceased or receive a bequest?
b: Yes. Since trampling is legally attributed directly to the rider, the legal consequences of direct killing, including loss of inheritance and bequest, apply. These consequences do not apply to the driver or leader.

f: 373. If an animal has both a rider and a driver behind it, who is liable if it tramples someone?
b: One opinion says only the rider is liable because he is the direct actor while the driver is only an indirect cause. Another opinion holds that both are liable because both contributed causally.

f: 374. If two mounted riders collide and both die accidentally, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The ʿāqilah (agnatic relatives) of each rider must pay the full diyah of the other rider.

f: 375. What is the opinion of Zufar and Imam al-Shāfiʿī regarding two riders who collide and both die?
