f: 688. According to Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله analogy, what is the ruling if someone accuses a person who is not from the neighbourhood of murder?
b: The normal rules of evidence apply; qasāmah does not apply because there is no specific text establishing it.

f: 689. According to the preferred opinion (istiḥsān), does qasāmah apply if specific people from the neighbourhood are accused?
b: Yes, qasāmah and blood money are still imposed on the people of the neighbourhood.

f: 690. Why does istiḥsān apply qasāmah even when individuals are specifically accused?
b: Because the texts establishing qasāmah do not distinguish between general and specific accusations; therefore it is established by the text, not by analogy.

f: 691. If someone accuses a specific person outside the neighbourhood and has no proof, what happens?
b: The accused person is asked to swear one oath.

f: 692. If the accused person swears the oath in a normal murder claim, what happens?
b: He is cleared of liability.

f: 693. If the accused person refuses to swear in a financial claim, what is the result?
b: The claimant's claim is established through his refusal (nukūl).

f: 694. If the accused person refuses to swear in a case involving retaliation (qiṣāṣ), what happens?
b: The matter follows the disagreement mentioned in the chapter of legal claims.

f: 695. If the people of a neighbourhood are fewer than fifty, what happens in qasāmah?
b: The oaths are repeated among them until fifty oaths are completed.

f: 696. What evidence is mentioned for repeating oaths when fewer than fifty people are available?
b: It is reported that ʿUmar رضي الله عنه completed a qasāmah case with forty-nine men by repeating the oath upon one of them until it reached fifty.

f: 697. Why are the oaths repeated when the number of people is insufficient?
b: Because completing fifty oaths is established by Sunnah, and it should be completed whenever possible.

f: 698. If there are exactly fifty eligible people, can the heir repeat the oath upon one of them to strengthen the number?
b: No, because repetition is only allowed due to necessity when completing the fifty.

f: 699. Can a child participate in qasāmah?
b: No, because a child is not qualified for valid legal speech and an oath is a valid legal statement.

f: 700. Can a mentally insane person participate in qasāmah?
b: No, because he is not qualified for valid legal speech.

f: 701. Can women participate in qasāmah?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafī position mentioned, because they are not among those responsible for communal support (nuṣrah).

f: 702. Can slaves participate in qasāmah?
b: No, because they are not among those who provide communal support and protection.

f: 703. If a dead person is found with no signs of injury, is qasāmah required?
b: No, and no blood money is required.

f: 704. Why is there no qasāmah when there are no signs of injury on the body?
b: Because it is not established that the person was murdered; he may have died naturally.

f: 705. What signs indicate that a person was likely murdered for purposes of qasāmah?
b: Signs such as wounds, marks of beating, strangulation, or similar evidence of killing.

f: 706. Why is blood coming from the eye or ear considered evidence of killing?
b: Because blood normally does not emerge from those places except due to an action caused by a living person.

f: 707. Why is blood coming from the mouth, anus, or private parts not considered evidence of killing?
b: Because blood can naturally emerge from those places without another person's action.

f: 708. If the entire body of a murdered person is found in a neighbourhood, what is required from the people of that neighbourhood?
b: Qasāmah and blood money are required from them.

f: 709. If more than half of the body of the murdered person is found in a neighbourhood, what is the ruling?
b: It has the ruling of the whole body, so qasāmah and blood money are required.

f: 710. If half of the body is found together with the head, what is the ruling?
b: It is treated like the whole body, so qasāmah and blood money apply.

f: 711. If half of the body is split lengthwise, is qasāmah required?
b: No, because it is not considered a complete body in this ruling.

f: 712. If less than half of the body is found together with the head, is qasāmah required?
b: No.

f: 713. If only the hand, foot, or head of the victim is found, is qasāmah required?
b: No.

f: 714. Why does finding only part of a body not require qasāmah?
b: Because otherwise one person's death could lead to repeated qasāmah and blood money obligations, which is not allowed.

f: 715. What principle determines whether a body part is treated as a full body for qasāmah?
b: If the remaining parts, had they been found, would have allowed qasāmah, then the discovered part can also allow it; otherwise not.

f: 716. If a miscarried fetus is found among a neighbourhood with no signs of injury, is anything required from them?
b: No, neither qasāmah nor blood money is required.

f: 717. If a fully formed fetus is found with signs of beating, what is the ruling?
b: Qasāmah and blood money are required because it is likely that the fetus separated alive.

f: 718. If an incompletely formed fetus is found with signs of injury, is qasāmah required?
b: No, because it is assumed to have separated from the mother without being alive.

f: 719. If a murdered person is found on an animal being driven by a man, who is responsible for the blood money?
b: The driver's ʿāqilah pays the blood money, not the people of the neighbourhood.

f: 720. Why are the people of the neighbourhood not responsible when the victim is found on someone's animal?
b: Because the victim is in the possession and control of that person, like someone found inside his house.

f: 721. If the murdered person is found on an animal being led by someone, what is the ruling?
b: The same ruling applies: the person controlling the animal is responsible.

f: 722. If the murdered person is found on an animal with both a rider and a driver, who is responsible?
b: They are both responsible because the victim is under their control.

f: 723. If a murdered person is found on an animal passing between two villages, who is responsible?
b: The people of the nearer village are responsible.

f: 724. What evidence is mentioned for judging responsibility between two villages?
b: The Prophet ﷺ ordered measurement of the distance between the body and the two villages.

f: 725. Why are the people of the closer village held responsible?
b: Because they are considered more capable of providing help and protection, yet failed to do so.

f: 726. If a murdered person is found inside someone's house, who is responsible for qasāmah?
b: The owner or person in control of the house.

f: 727. Why is the person controlling the house responsible when a body is found there?
b: Because the house is under his authority and control.

f: 728. Who pays the blood money when a body is found in someone's house?
b: The person's ʿāqilah pays the blood money because they provide his support and protection.

f: 729. Do residents (sukkān) participate with property owners in qasāmah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: No, the residents do not participate with the owners in qasāmah.

f: 730. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding residents and owners in qasāmah?
b: Both the owners and residents participate in the qasāmah.

f: 731. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله evidence that residents participate in qasāmah?
b: Authority over managing a place can come through residence as well as ownership, and the Prophet ﷺ placed qasāmah and blood money upon the Jews of Khaybar even though they were residents there.

f: 732. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad respond to the example of Khaybar?
b: The Jews of Khaybar were allowed to remain on their lands as owners, and what was taken from them was treated as land taxation (kharāj), not merely because they were residents.

f: 733. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad exclude residents from qasāmah with owners?
b: Because the owner is the one specifically responsible for protecting the area; ownership is more permanent and gives greater authority of management.

f: 734. Who is included in qasāmah when a killing occurs in a planned settlement (khiṭṭah)?
b: The original settlers (ahl al-khiṭṭah), not those who later purchased the properties.

f: 735. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding original settlers and later purchasers?
b: Both groups participate because liability is based on failing to protect the area, and ownership gives authority over protection.

f: 736. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad distinguish between original settlers and purchasers?
b: The original settlers are the original people responsible for the area, while purchasers are newcomers; authority belongs primarily to the original group.

f: 737. What is mentioned regarding Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله basis for this ruling?
b: It is said that he based it on what he observed regarding the settlements of Kūfah.

f: 738. If all the original settlers sell their properties and only purchasers remain, who bears qasāmah responsibility?
b: The purchasers bear responsibility because authority has transferred to them.

f: 739. If a murdered person is found in a house, who bears qasāmah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The owner of the house and his people bear qasāmah.

f: 740. Do the owner's ʿāqilah participate in qasāmah if they are present?
b: Yes, if they are present.

f: 741. If the owner's ʿāqilah are absent, how is qasāmah performed?
b: The owner alone repeats the oaths until the required number is completed.

f: 742. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding the ʿāqilah of the homeowner?
b: The ʿāqilah do not participate in qasāmah because the homeowner has the strongest connection to the house.

f: 743. What is the argument of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad for including the present ʿāqilah?
b: They also have responsibility for supporting and protecting the area, so they share the obligation of qasāmah.

f: 744. If a shared house has one owner with half ownership, another with one tenth, and another with the remainder, how is qasāmah divided?
b: It is divided according to the number of men (heads), not according to ownership shares.

f: 745. Why are co-owners treated equally in qasāmah regardless of ownership percentage?
b: Because even a small owner shares authority over the property and responsibility for protection.

f: 746. What analogy is used for dividing qasāmah among co-owners?
b: It is compared to the right of pre-emption (shufʿah), where participation is based on individuals rather than shares.

f: 747. If someone buys a house but has not yet received possession and a murdered person is found in it, whose ʿāqilah pays the blood money according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The seller's ʿāqilah pays the blood money.

f: 748. What do Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله two companions say regarding a completed sale before possession?
b: They say the buyer's ʿāqilah pays because ownership has transferred to the buyer.

f: 749. In a sale with a cancellation option (khiyār), according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, whose ʿāqilah pays?
b: The ʿāqilah of the person who has possession pays.

f: 750. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, in a sale with khiyār, whose ʿāqilah pays?
b: The ʿāqilah of whoever ultimately becomes the owner pays.

f: 751. What is the reasoning of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding liability in the house sale case?
b: Liability is based on failure to protect, and the person with ownership has the authority of protection.

f: 752. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله reasoning for making possession the determining factor rather than ownership?
b: The ability to protect comes through physical possession, not merely ownership.

f: 753. Why does the seller remain responsible before delivering a sold house according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the seller still has physical control and can protect the property.

f: 754. If the buyer has possession and the option belongs to him, who bears responsibility?
b: The buyer, because he has the strongest control and ability to manage the property.

f: 755. If the seller has the option and the property is in his possession, who bears responsibility?
b: The seller, because his possession makes him responsible for protecting it.

f: 756. If someone possesses a house and a murdered person is found in it, is his ʿāqilah immediately responsible?
b: No, not until witnesses testify that the house belongs to the person in possession.

f: 757. Why is possession alone insufficient to obligate the ʿāqilah?
b: Because possession may indicate ownership but is not certain enough to impose blood money upon the ʿāqilah.

f: 758. What comparison is made to show that possession alone is insufficient?
b: Possession alone is not enough to establish rights such as pre-emption in property disputes.

f: 759. If a murdered person is found on a ship, who performs qasāmah?
b: The passengers and sailors on the ship perform qasāmah.

f: 760. Does qasāmah on a ship include the ship owners?
b: Yes, the wording includes owners who are present on the ship.

f: 761. Are residents and non-resident owners treated equally regarding a ship?
b: Yes, because a ship is movable and responsibility is based on possession rather than ownership.

f: 762. Why is a ship different from a house regarding ownership and possession?
b: A ship moves and changes location, so possession is the relevant factor; a house remains fixed, so ownership is more significant.

f: 763. If a murdered person is found in a neighbourhood mosque, who bears qasāmah?
b: The people of that neighbourhood bear qasāmah.

f: 764. Why do the people of the neighbourhood bear qasāmah for their mosque?
b: Because management and supervision of the mosque belong to them.

f: 765. If a murdered person is found in the main congregational mosque, is there qasāmah?
b: No, there is no qasāmah.

f: 766. Who pays the blood money if a murdered person is found in the main congregational mosque?
b: The public treasury (Bayt al-Māl) pays it.

f: 767. Why does Bayt al-Māl pay for killings in public places like the main mosque?
b: Because such places belong to all Muslims collectively and are not controlled by a specific group.

f: 768. Does the same ruling apply to public bridges and public roads?
b: Yes, blood money comes from Bayt al-Māl.

f: 769. If a murdered person is found in a privately owned marketplace, who bears responsibility according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: The residents of the marketplace bear responsibility.

f: 770. If a murdered person is found in a privately owned marketplace, who bears responsibility according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The owner bears responsibility.

f: 771. If a murdered person is found in an unowned public marketplace or public road, who pays the blood money?
b: Bayt al-Māl pays.

f: 772. If a murdered person is found in a prison, who pays the blood money according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Bayt al-Māl pays.

f: 773. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding a murdered person found in prison?
b: The prisoners are responsible for qasāmah and blood money.

f: 774. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider the prisoners responsible?
b: They are residents of the prison, have control over it, and the killing is likely to have occurred among them.

f: 775. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad reject making prisoners responsible?
b: Prisoners are under restriction and cannot support or protect one another, so the obligation of communal protection does not apply to them.

f: 776. Why does Bayt al-Māl pay for killings in prisons according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The prison exists for fulfilling the rights of Muslims, so its benefits and burdens return to the Muslim community.

f: 777. What general disagreement does the prison issue branch from?
b: The disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding whether liability follows the owner or the resident.

f: 778. If a murdered person is found in a wilderness with no nearby inhabited area, is there qasāmah or blood money?
b: No, the blood is considered wasted (hadar) because no one can be blamed for failing to protect him.

f: 779. How is "nearby inhabited area" defined in this context?
b: It is defined by whether a person could hear the victim's call for help (istimāʿ al-ṣawt).

f: 780. Why is there no liability when a body is found in a remote wilderness?
b: Because help could not have reached him, so no one is considered negligent in protection.

f: 781. What is the ruling if the wilderness where the body is found belongs to someone?
b: Qasāmah and blood money are upon the owner's ʿāqilah.

f: 782. If a murdered person is found between two villages, who bears qasāmah and blood money?
b: The closer village bears responsibility.

f: 783. If a murdered person is found in the middle of the Euphrates where water flows around him, is there liability?
b: No, the blood is wasted because he is not under anyone's possession or ownership.

f: 784. If a murdered person is found stuck near the bank of the river, who bears responsibility?
b: The closest village bears qasāmah and blood money.

f: 785. Why does the nearest village bear responsibility when the body is found by the riverbank?
b: Because they have special responsibility for that location, such as drawing water and bringing animals there.

f: 786. Why is the ruling different between a riverbank and the middle of the river?
b: The riverbank is considered under the practical control of nearby people, while the flowing river itself belongs to no specific group.

f: 787. Does the ruling of a river differ from a place where people have exclusive control, such as property that gives a right of pre-emption (shufʿah)?
b: Yes, exclusive control creates responsibility, while merely passing through a river does not.

f: 788. If the victim's guardian accuses a specific person from the local community, does qasāmah fall from the community?
b: No, qasāmah remains upon them.

f: 789. Why does accusing one specific person from the same community not remove qasāmah?
b: Because the accused person is still part of the community, and the original possibility that the killer is from them remains.

f: 790. If the guardian accuses someone outside the local community, does qasāmah fall from the community?
b: Yes, qasāmah and liability fall from them.

f: 791. Why does accusing someone outside the community remove qasāmah from the community?
b: Because it indicates that the killer is not from them, while their liability is based on the assumption that the killer was among them.

f: 792. Why are the people of a locality only liable after the guardian makes a claim?
b: Because the appearance of a corpse among them alone does not establish liability without the guardian's accusation.

f: 793. If a group of people fight with swords and separate leaving behind a dead person, who bears responsibility?
b: The people of the locality where the dead person was found bear qasāmah and blood money.

f: 794. Why are the people of the locality responsible after a sword fight?
b: Because the dead person was found among them and they were responsible for protection of the area.

f: 795. If the guardians accuse the fighters instead of the locality, does the locality remain liable?
b: No, because the accusation against others implies the locality is free from responsibility.

f: 796. Are the accused fighters liable merely because they are accused?
b: No, they are not liable unless they provide evidence proving their responsibility.

f: 797. If a murdered person is found in a military camp established in an unowned wilderness, what is the ruling if found inside a tent?
b: The residents of that tent bear qasāmah and blood money.

f: 798. If a murdered person is found outside the tents of a military camp, who bears responsibility?
b: The nearest tent group bears responsibility.

f: 799. Why is responsibility in a military camp based on tents rather than ownership?
b: Because there is no ownership, so possession and control determine responsibility.

f: 800. If soldiers fought an enemy and a dead person is found among them, is there qasāmah?
b: No, there is no qasāmah or blood money because the apparent killer is the enemy.

f: 801. If the soldiers did not encounter an enemy and a dead person is found among them, what is the ruling?
b: The normal qasāmah rules apply.

f: 802. If the land where the military camp is established has an owner, who bears responsibility according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The landowner bears responsibility.

f: 803. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding a military camp on owned land?
b: He disagrees and does not assign responsibility to the landowner.

f: 804. If a person taking the qasāmah oath says, "So-and-so killed him," what must he swear?
b: He swears: "By Allah, we did not kill him and we do not know of any killer except so-and-so."

f: 805. Why does the person making the oath still swear regarding himself and others?
b: Because his statement naming another killer is not accepted as removing the claim against himself without oath.

f: 806. If two people from the locality testify that someone outside the locality killed the victim, is their testimony accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, their testimony is not accepted.

f: 807. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding testimony from local people against an outsider?
b: They accept the testimony because they are no longer potential defendants after the guardian accused someone else.

f: 808. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject their testimony?
b: Because they remain potential defendants due to their assumed responsibility for failing to protect the area.

f: 809. What analogy does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use for people who remain liable despite no longer being direct defendants?
b: A trustee (waṣī) who leaves his position after accepting it but whose testimony remains affected by his former role.

f: 810. If the guardian accuses a specific person from the locality and two people from that locality testify against him, is their testimony accepted?
b: No, their testimony is not accepted.

f: 811. Why is testimony from members of the same locality rejected in this case?
b: Because they remain connected to the dispute and are considered potentially biased.

f: 812. What does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله say regarding such witnesses?
b: They should swear that they did not kill him and should not add anything beyond that.

f: 813. If someone is wounded in a tribe's area, taken to his family, and dies from the wound, when is qasāmah and blood money due on the tribe according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: When he remains bedridden because of the wound until he dies.

f: 814. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding a person wounded in a tribe's area who later dies?
b: There is no qasāmah or blood money on the tribe.

f: 815. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله reasoning for denying liability?
b: The tribe only caused a wound, not death, and qasāmah does not apply to non-fatal injuries.

f: 816. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله reasoning for imposing liability when the wounded person remains bedridden?
b: A wound followed by death is considered a killing, and it can establish liability just as it establishes the possibility of retaliation (qiṣāṣ).

f: 817. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish between a bedridden victim and one who is not?
b: If he was bedridden, the death is attributed to the wound; otherwise, there is doubt that death came from another cause.

f: 818. If a person carrying a wounded man who still has signs of life takes him to his family, and he dies one or two days later, is the carrier liable according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: No, the carrier is not liable according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله.

f: 819. According to the apparent reasoning of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is the carrier liable if the wounded person dies after being carried to his family?
b: Yes, according to the analogy (qiyās) of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, he would be liable.

f: 820. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider the carrier liable in this case?
b: Because the carrier's possession is like the possession of a locality; the wounded person being in his hands is treated like the wounded person being in that place.

f: 821. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله not hold the carrier liable?
b: Because merely transporting the wounded person does not make him responsible for the later death, just as the earlier issue of the wounded person taken to his tribe was discussed.

f: 822. What previous issue is this disagreement connected to?
b: The case of a wounded person taken from a tribe's land to his family and later dying.

f: 823. If a man is found killed inside his own house, who pays his blood money according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: His ʿāqilah pays the blood money to his heirs.

f: 824. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, Muḥammad, and Zufar regarding a man found killed in his own house?
b: Nothing is owed; the blood is considered wasted.

f: 825. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, Muḥammad, and Zufar consider the blood wasted in this case?
b: Because the house was under his control, so it is treated as though he killed himself, making the blood unclaimable.

f: 826. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله reasoning for requiring blood money when a person is found killed in his own house?
b: Qasāmah is established based on the appearance of homicide, and at the time the killing becomes apparent the house belongs to the heirs, so their ʿāqilah bears responsibility.

f: 827. Why is this different from a mukātab (contractually freed slave) found killed in his own house?
b: Because when his killing becomes apparent, the house remains under his ownership, so it is as though he killed himself and his blood is wasted.

f: 828. If two men are alone in a house and one is found slaughtered, what is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion?
b: The surviving man is liable for the blood money.

f: 829. What is Muḥammad's opinion if two men are alone and one is found murdered?
b: The surviving man is not liable.

f: 830. Why does Muḥammad not hold the surviving man liable?
b: Because it is possible that the victim killed himself, so liability cannot be established through doubt.

f: 831. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله hold the surviving man liable?
b: Because the normal assumption is that a person does not kill himself, so this possibility is disregarded, similar to finding a murdered person in a locality.

f: 832. If a murdered person is found in a village belonging to a woman, who bears qasāmah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: The woman must perform qasāmah by repeating the oaths.

f: 833. Who pays the blood money when a murdered person is found in a village belonging to a woman according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Her closest male relatives by lineage (the nearest tribal ʿāqilah) pay the blood money.

f: 834. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding a murdered person found in a woman's village?
b: The obligation of qasāmah and payment also falls upon the ʿāqilah, because liability belongs to those capable of providing protection.

f: 835. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله exclude the woman from qasāmah?
b: Because qasāmah belongs to those responsible for protection (ahl al-nuṣrah), and a woman is not considered among them, similar to a child.

f: 836. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad require qasāmah from the woman?
b: Because qasāmah serves to remove suspicion, and suspicion of her involvement in the killing can exist.

f: 837. What did later scholars say regarding the woman's participation with her ʿāqilah in payment?
b: They said the woman also participates with the ʿāqilah in bearing the payment because she is treated as a possible killer in this case.

f: 838. If a man is found killed on another person's land next to a village, but the landowner is not from that village, who bears responsibility?
b: The landowner bears responsibility.

f: 839. Why does the landowner bear responsibility instead of the nearby village?
b: Because the landowner has greater responsibility for protecting his own land than the villagers do.

f: 1. What is the meaning of al-maʿāqil (المعاقل)?
b: Al-maʿāqil is the plural of maʿqilah (معقلة), meaning the blood money (diyah).

f: 2. Why is the diyah called ʿaql (عقل)?
b: Because it restrains bloodshed by preventing the spilling of blood, meaning it "holds back" or "binds" the matter of blood.

f: 3. In which cases is the diyah paid by the ʿāqilah?
b: In شبه العمد (quasi-intentional killing), accidental killing, and every diyah that becomes obligatory due to killing itself, the diyah is paid by the ʿāqilah.

f: 4. Who are the ʿāqilah?
b: They are those who provide the payment of the ʿaql (diyah), meaning those responsible for bearing the blood money.

f: 5. What is the evidence for making the ʿāqilah responsible for diyah?
b: The hadith of Ḥaml ibn Mālik رضي الله عنه, where the Prophet ﷺ told the heirs: “Stand up and let his people pay the ransom.”

f: 6. Why is diyah placed upon the ʿāqilah rather than only the killer?
b: Because the victim's life is respected and cannot be ignored, while the accidental killer is excused; making him pay a large amount alone would cause severe hardship, so responsibility is shared as a form of relief.

f: 7. Why does شبه العمد also not fall entirely upon the killer?
b: Because the consideration is given to the weapon used; it is not treated as deliberate killing deserving full punishment.

f: 8. Why were the ʿāqilah specifically chosen to bear the diyah?
b: Because the killer's shortcoming occurred despite having supporters, and those supporters (the ʿāqilah) are considered to have failed in supervising and restraining him.

f: 9. Who are considered the ʿāqilah if the killer belongs to the military register (dīwān)?
b: His ʿāqilah are the people of the dīwān (the army members whose names are recorded in the register).

f: 10. What are the people of the dīwān?
b: They are the army members organized under military banners whose names are recorded in the official register.

f: 11. What is the opinion of al-Shāfiʿī regarding who bears diyah?
b: He says it is upon the killer's paternal relatives (ʿaṣabah/tribe), because this was the practice during the time of the Prophet ﷺ.

f: 12. What evidence do the Ḥanafīs use for assigning diyah to the dīwān?
b: The action of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه, who established the dīwān and assigned the payment of blood money to its members, with the Companions not objecting.

f: 13. Why do the Ḥanafīs say this was not abrogation of the earlier system?
b: Because the original reason for liability was support (nuṣrah), and support can occur through lineage, alliances, clientage, or military organization.

f: 14. Why did ʿUmar رضي الله عنه assign diyah to the dīwān?
b: Because in his time the system of support had shifted to the dīwān, so he followed the underlying reason behind the rule.

f: 15. If a group today supports each other through a profession, who would be their ʿāqilah?
b: Their fellow professionals would be their ʿāqilah.

f: 16. If people are bound by an alliance (ḥilf), who would be their ʿāqilah?
b: Their allies would be their ʿāqilah.

f: 17. Why is the diyah taken from stipends rather than personal wealth?
b: Because diyah is a form of assistance, and taking it from a source of regular payments is easier and more suitable for reducing hardship.

f: 18. Over what period is the diyah taken from the ʿāqilah?
b: It is taken over three years.

f: 19. What is the evidence for spreading diyah over three years?
b: It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ and narrated from ʿUmar رضي الله عنه.

f: 20. Why is diyah spread over three years?
b: Because taking it gradually from yearly payments reduces hardship.

f: 21. What happens if stipends are paid over more than three years or less than three years?
b: Payment is taken according to when the stipends are issued, as long as the purpose of easing hardship is achieved.

f: 22. If future stipends after the judgment are accumulated and paid after more than three years, are they all taken?
b: No, only the stipends falling within the relevant three-year period after the judgment are considered.

f: 23. If three years' worth of stipends are all issued in one year after the judgment, how much is taken?
b: The entire diyah is taken from them.

f: 24. How is the diyah divided if the full diyah is payable over three years?
b: One-third is paid each year.

f: 25. If the obligation is one-third of the diyah or less, when is it paid?
b: It is paid in the first year.

f: 26. If the obligation exceeds one-third but does not reach two-thirds, when is the remainder paid?
b: The amount exceeding one-third is paid in the second year.

f: 27. If the obligation exceeds two-thirds, when is the remainder paid?
b: The remaining amount up to the full diyah is paid in the third year.

f: 28. If the killer himself must pay a diyah (such as intentional killing of his child where diyah applies), is it paid immediately?
b: According to the Ḥanafīs, it is also spread over three years.

f: 29. What is al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding diyah owed directly by the killer?
b: He says it must be paid immediately because the delay was only intended as relief for the ʿāqilah.

f: 30. What is the Ḥanafī response to al-Shāfiʿī regarding delayed payment?
b: They say the law has specified a delay, so it cannot be restricted only to the ʿāqilah.

f: 31. If ten people accidentally kill one person, how much does each owe?
b: Each owes one-tenth of the diyah, paid over three years.

f: 32. Why is each person's share of diyah calculated proportionally?
b: Because diyah replaces the value of one life, so each person's portion follows the whole.

f: 33. From when are the three years counted for diyah payment?
b: From the time the judge issues the ruling for diyah.

f: 34. Why are the three years counted from the judgment rather than the time of killing?
b: Because the original obligation is the equivalent (mithl), and conversion to a monetary value occurs through the judgment.

f: 35. Who is the ʿāqilah of someone who is not part of the dīwān?
b: His tribe (qabīlah) is his ʿāqilah.

f: 36. Why is a person's tribe responsible if he is not in the dīwān?
b: Because their support and protection is the basis for mutual responsibility.

f: 37. How is diyah distributed among the tribe?
b: It is distributed over three years among them.

f: 38. What is the maximum amount taken from one person each year according to the wording of al-Qudūrī?
b: No more than four dirhams per year.

f: 39. What did Muḥammad رحمه الله clarify regarding the amount each person pays?
b: No individual pays more than three or four dirhams in total over the three years, meaning about one dirham or one and one-third dirham per year.

f: 40. What is the more correct position regarding individual contributions?
b: The amount stated by Muḥammad رحمه الله is considered the stronger position.

f: 41. What happens if the tribe is too small to cover the diyah?
b: The nearest tribes by lineage are added to them.

f: 42. In what order are additional tribes included?
b: According to the order of male relatives: brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and their sons.

f: 43. Are fathers and sons included among the assisting relatives?
b: There are two opinions: some include them due to their closeness, while others exclude them because the purpose is reducing hardship through a larger group.

f: 44. Why do some scholars exclude fathers and sons from the ʿāqilah?
b: Because adding them does not greatly increase the number of contributors, so it does not achieve the purpose of reducing hardship.

f: 45. If a military banner group (dīwān) is too small to pay the diyah, what happens?
b: The nearest groups that provide similar support are added.

f: 46. Who decides which groups are closest in support?
b: The ruler/imām decides because he has knowledge of the relevant relationships and organization.

f: 47. What is al-Shāfiʿī's opinion about the amount each person pays?
b: Each person pays half a dinar, making the contribution equal for everyone.

f: 48. Why does al-Shāfiʿī compare diyah contributions to zakāh?
b: Because both are forms of financial obligation and assistance.

f: 49. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to al-Shāfiʿī's comparison with zakāh?
b: They say diyah is of a lower financial rank than zakāh because it is not taken from the person's principal wealth, showing greater leniency.

f: 50. If a man's ʿāqilah are people who receive stipends (arzāq), how is the diyah taken from them?
b: The diyah is taken from their stipends over three years, with one-third taken each year.

f: 51. Why are stipends treated like military grants (ʿaṭāʾ)?
b: Because both are forms of support from the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl).

f: 52. If the stipends of the ʿāqilah are issued yearly, how is payment taken?
b: One-third of the diyah is taken from each year's stipend.

f: 53. If the stipends are issued every six months, how is the diyah collected?
b: If issued after the judgment, one-sixth of the diyah is taken from each six-month payment.

f: 54. If the stipends are issued monthly, how is the diyah collected?
b: A proportionate amount is taken from each monthly payment so that the total collected each year equals one-third of the diyah.

f: 55. If a monthly stipend is issued one day or more after the judgment, how much is taken from it?
b: The portion corresponding to that month is taken.

f: 56. If a person receives both monthly stipends and yearly grants, from which is the diyah taken?
b: It is taken from the yearly grants rather than the monthly stipends.

f: 57. Why is the diyah taken from yearly grants instead of monthly stipends when both exist?
b: Because it is easier, either because the grant is larger or because monthly stipends are intended for daily expenses while grants are for military service and support.

f: 58. Is the killer himself included among the ʿāqilah?
b: Yes, the killer is included and contributes like one of them.

f: 59. Why is the killer included among the ʿāqilah?
b: Because he is the actual perpetrator, so there is no reason to exclude him while making others responsible.

f: 60. What is al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding the killer contributing to diyah?
b: He says the killer pays nothing from the diyah because the accidental killer is excused.

f: 61. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to al-Shāfiʿī's view?
b: They say making him pay the entire diyah would be excessive, but making him pay a portion is not, since others are even more deserving of being excused.

f: 62. What Qur'anic principle do the Ḥanafīs mention regarding responsibility?
b: The verse: “No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.” (Qur'an 6:164)

f: 63. Do women and children who receive shares from the dīwān contribute to diyah?
b: No, women and children do not contribute to diyah even if they have a share in the dīwān.

f: 64. What statement of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه is used regarding women and children?
b: “A child and a woman do not pay with the ʿāqilah.”

f: 65. Why are women and children excluded from the ʿāqilah?
b: Because responsibility belongs to those who provide protection and support, and women and children are not considered people of military support.

f: 66. Why are women and children not considered part of the support system?
b: Because people do not rely on them for protection in conflicts.

f: 67. Why is jizyah also not placed upon women and children according to this reasoning?
b: Because jizyah is connected to military protection and support obligations.

f: 68. If the killer himself is a child or woman, do they contribute to diyah?
b: No, they do not contribute anything.

f: 69. Why does a male killer contribute but a female or child killer does not?
b: A man contributes because he is one of those responsible for support and protects himself; this does not apply to women and children.

f: 70. Why do women receive stipends from the treasury if not for military support?
b: Their stipends are for assistance and maintenance, not because they provide protection.

f: 71. Are the wives of the Prophet ﷺ an example of stipends given for assistance rather than support?
b: Yes, their provisions were not based on military support.

f: 72. Do people from one city (miṣr) serve as ʿāqilah for people from another city?
b: No, the people of one city do not bear the diyah of another city when each has its own dīwān.

f: 73. Why do people of one city not bear responsibility for another city's people?
b: Because when the dīwān exists, mutual support is based upon that dīwān rather than mere residence.

f: 74. Who bears responsibility for rural people (ahl al-sawād) attached to a city?
b: The people of the city bear responsibility for them.

f: 75. Why do city residents bear responsibility for the rural population attached to them?
b: Because the rural population relies upon the city people for support when difficulties occur.

f: 76. If someone lives in Basrah but his dīwān is in Kūfah, who is his ʿāqilah?
b: The people of Kūfah are his ʿāqilah.

f: 77. Why are the people of his dīwān responsible rather than his neighbors?
b: Because support is connected to the dīwān, and he seeks help from his dīwān rather than his neighbors.

f: 78. What is the general principle regarding the dīwān and other forms of support?
b: Support through the dīwān takes precedence over lineage, clientage, residence, and other forms of support.

f: 79. If there is no dīwān, what becomes the basis for ʿāqilah responsibility?
b: Lineage (nasab) becomes the basis.

f: 80. If a person from a city commits a crime and has no dīwān stipend, but nearby desert tribes are closer to him, who pays his diyah?
b: The dīwān members of that city pay his diyah.

f: 81. Is kinship required between the criminal and the city's dīwān members in this case?
b: Some say no, because the city's dīwān protects all inhabitants; others interpret it as requiring closeness by lineage.

f: 82. Why do some scholars require kinship in the case of city dīwān members?
b: Because the obligation is normally based upon family support, and the text hints at this by mentioning the nearby desert tribes.

f: 83. If a desert dweller settles in a city but has no residence there, do the city people bear his diyah?
b: No, because the city's people do not provide support for someone without residence among them.

f: 84. Why do city people not bear the diyah of a desert dweller living among them temporarily?
b: Because he does not rely upon them for protection.

f: 85. If a desert dweller settles among city people, do his original desert relatives bear the diyah of a city resident?
b: No, because he does not seek their support while residing in the city.

f: 86. If non-Muslims have an established system of mutual responsibility, who pays diyah if one kills another?
b: Their own ʿāqilah pays the diyah, like the system among Muslims.

f: 87. Why do non-Muslims with an established ʿāqilah system have the same ruling?
b: Because they have accepted Islamic civil laws and the meaning of mutual support exists among them.

f: 88. If non-Muslims have no recognized ʿāqilah, who pays the diyah?
b: The killer pays it from his own wealth over three years.

f: 89. Why does a non-Muslim without ʿāqilah pay from his own wealth?
b: Because the original obligation is upon the killer; it only transfers to the ʿāqilah when one exists.

f: 90. What example is given of someone without a supporting group?
b: Two Muslim merchants in enemy territory: if one kills the other, the killer pays because Muslims in the Islamic land do not support him there.

f: 91. Can a non-Muslim bear diyah for a Muslim?
b: No.

f: 92. Can a Muslim bear diyah for a non-Muslim?
b: No.

f: 93. Why can Muslims and non-Muslims not be each other's ʿāqilah?
b: Because mutual support and protection do not exist between them.

f: 94. Can non-Muslims of different religions be each other's ʿāqilah?
b: Yes, because disbelief is considered one category in this ruling.

f: 95. Is there an exception regarding non-Muslims of different religions?
b: If there is obvious hostility between groups, such as Jews and Christians, they should not bear responsibility for each other.

f: 96. What is the position attributed to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding hostile non-Muslim groups?
b: They do not act as ʿāqilah for one another because mutual support is absent.

f: 97. If a killer from Kūfah has a dīwān there but later his dīwān is transferred to Basrah before the case reaches the judge, whose ʿāqilah pays?
b: His ʿāqilah from Basrah pays, because that is his current dīwān.

f: 98. If a person from Kūfah transfers his dīwān to Basrah before the judge rules on the diyah, who bears the diyah according to Zufar رحمه الله?
b: His ʿāqilah from Kūfah bears it because the cause (the crime) occurred while his ʿāqilah were in Kūfah.

f: 99. What narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله agrees with Zufar's opinion?
b: A narration states that the people of Kūfah remain responsible because the obligation originates from the time of the crime.

f: 100. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to Zufar's opinion?
b: They say the diyah only becomes a financial obligation at the time of the judge's ruling, so responsibility belongs to whoever is his ʿāqilah at that time.

f: 101. Why does the obligation of diyah begin at the time of judgment according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because the original obligation is an equivalent (mithl), and through judgment it transfers into a monetary obligation.

f: 102. Who bears the diyah when the killer's dīwān changes before judgment?
b: The new ʿāqilah at the time of judgment bear it.

f: 103. Why does a change of ʿāqilah after judgment not transfer responsibility?
b: Because the obligation has already been established through the judgment and cannot be moved afterwards.

f: 104. If a person's personal share of diyah is taken from his military grant, which grant is used if he moved cities?
b: His grant from the new city is used because payment is taken from his current grant.

f: 105. Why are additional tribes added if the ʿāqilah become too few after judgment, rather than transferring responsibility?
b: Adding others strengthens the original ruling, while transferring responsibility would cancel the first judgment.

f: 106. If a man from Kūfah without a dīwān settles in Basrah before judgment, who pays his diyah?
b: The people of Basrah pay it.

f: 107. If the same man had been judged against before moving to Basrah, who pays?
b: The people of Kūfah remain responsible.

f: 108. If a Bedouin joins the dīwān after committing a killing but before judgment, who bears his diyah?
b: The members of the dīwān bear it.

f: 109. If a Bedouin joins the dīwān after judgment, who remains responsible?
b: His original tribal ʿāqilah remain responsible.

f: 110. If people from the desert were judged to pay diyah from their own wealth and later joined the dīwān, can payment be taken from their grants?
b: Yes, because the payment source changes to the easier form without cancelling the original judgment.

f: 111. Why can diyah move from personal wealth to grants after judgment?
b: Because the judgment was for their wealth generally, and grants are simply an easier form of payment.

f: 112. When does diyah not transfer from wealth to grants?
b: When the original judgment was for a different type of payment, such as camels, while the grant is money.

f: 113. If diyah was originally judged as camels but the people later receive monetary grants, what happens?
b: The judgment remains as camels, but payment may be taken from the grant money because it is easier, without changing the ruling.

f: 114. Who is the ʿāqilah of a person freed by another (a mawlā al-ʿitāqah)?
b: The tribe of his former master is his ʿāqilah.

f: 115. What evidence is mentioned for the responsibility of the master's tribe?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “The ally of a people is from them.”

f: 116. Who bears diyah for a client of alliance (mawlā al-muwālāt)?
b: His ally and his ally's tribe bear responsibility.

f: 117. Why is mawlā al-muwālāt treated like mawlā al-ʿitāqah?
b: Because both forms of allegiance create mutual support and protection.

f: 118. What is the minimum amount of injury that the ʿāqilah must bear?
b: Half of one-tenth of the diyah (nisf ʿushr al-diyah).

f: 119. What injury amount is half of one-tenth of the diyah equivalent to?
b: The compensation for a muḍiḥah wound (a wound exposing the bone).

f: 120. What is the evidence that the ʿāqilah do not bear less than a muḍiḥah's compensation?
b: The narration: “The ʿāqilah do not bear intentional killing, killing of a slave, settlement, confession, or anything less than the compensation of a muḍiḥah.”

f: 121. Why is a minimum amount set for the ʿāqilah's responsibility?
b: Because their burden exists to prevent hardship, and small amounts do not create hardship.

f: 122. Who pays injuries below the minimum amount?
b: The offender pays from his own wealth.

f: 123. Why are smaller compensations treated like ordinary financial damages?
b: Because they are determined by valuation, like compensation for property damage.

f: 124. Do the ʿāqilah bear the crime of a slave?
b: No.

f: 125. Why do the ʿāqilah not bear compensation for a slave's injury?
b: Because there is no system of mutual support through slaves.

f: 126. Do the ʿāqilah bear diyah established through settlement (ṣulḥ)?
b: No.

f: 127. Why do the ʿāqilah not bear a settlement obligation?
b: Because a settlement does not bind them due to the limited authority of the person making it over them.

f: 128. Do the ʿāqilah bear a diyah that the killer admits himself (iqrār)?
b: No.

f: 129. Why does a killer's confession not bind the ʿāqilah?
b: Because his confession does not have authority over them.

f: 130. When would the ʿāqilah bear a confession-based diyah?
b: If they confirm and accept the confession themselves.

f: 131. Why does confirmation by the ʿāqilah make them responsible?
b: Because the refusal to accept responsibility was their right, and they may waive that right.

f: 132. If someone confesses to accidental killing and the case is not taken to court for many years, where is the diyah taken from?
b: From his own wealth over three years from the date of judgment.

f: 133. Why is the three-year period counted from judgment even in confession cases?
b: Because even in proven cases the delay begins from judgment, so it applies even more to confession.

f: 134. If the killer and victim's guardian agree that a judge ruled against the ʿāqilah, but the ʿāqilah deny it, are they liable?
b: No, because their agreement is not proof against the ʿāqilah.

f: 135. If the killer and guardian agree about the judgment against the ʿāqilah, does the killer personally owe anything?
b: No, because the diyah has been assigned to the ʿāqilah.

f: 136. What if the killer has a share in the same dīwān that is denying responsibility?
b: He must pay his own share because his admission is binding upon himself.

f: 137. If a free person accidentally kills a slave, who pays the slave's value?
b: His ʿāqilah pays the slave's value.

f: 138. Why does the ʿāqilah pay for killing a slave according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because the value of the slave replaces the value of life in this case.

f: 139. What is one opinion of al-Shāfiʿī regarding accidental killing of a slave?
b: The value must be paid from the killer's own wealth because it is compensation for property.

f: 140. Why does al-Shāfiʿī consider the slave's compensation a property payment?
b: Because he considers the slave's value to be purely financial.

f: 141. Do the ʿāqilah bear compensation for injuring a slave (not killing him)?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 142. Why do the Ḥanafīs not make the ʿāqilah pay for injuries to a slave?
b: Because such compensation is treated like property damage rather than blood money.

f: 143. What is another opinion of al-Shāfiʿī regarding injuries to slaves?
b: The ʿāqilah bear it just as they bear injuries to free people.

f: 144. If a person who commits accidental killing has no ʿāqilah (group responsible for supporting him), where is the diyah taken from according to the Ḥanafī scholars?
b: The diyah is taken from the Bayt al-Māl (public treasury).

f: 145. Why do the Ḥanafī scholars make the Bayt al-Māl responsible for the diyah of a killer who has no ʿāqilah?
b: Because all Muslims are considered his supporters, and no specific group has greater responsibility than another.

f: 146. What analogy do the Ḥanafī scholars use to support taking diyah from the Bayt al-Māl when a killer has no ʿāqilah?
b: They compare it to inheritance: if he dies without heirs, his inheritance goes to the Bayt al-Māl, so his financial obligations also return to it.

f: 147. What is the rare narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding the diyah of a person who has no ʿāqilah?
b: The diyah is paid from the killer's own wealth.

f: 148. What is the reasoning behind Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله rare narration that the killer without ʿāqilah pays from his own wealth?
b: The original rule is that the person who caused the destruction pays; the ʿāqilah only carry the burden as a means of easing hardship.

f: 149. Who pays the diyah of a son born from liʿān (where the father denied paternity through mutual oaths)?
b: The mother's ʿāqilah pay the diyah.

f: 150. Why does the mother's ʿāqilah pay the diyah of a son born from liʿān?
b: Because the child's lineage is established through the mother and not through the father.

f: 151. If the mother's ʿāqilah paid the diyah of a son born from liʿān and the father later acknowledges him, who reimburses the mother's ʿāqilah?
b: The father's ʿāqilah reimburse the mother's ʿāqilah.

f: 152. Why do the father's ʿāqilah reimburse the mother's ʿāqilah after the father acknowledges a son of liʿān?
b: Because the father's acknowledgement cancels the effect of liʿān and proves that the child's paternal lineage existed originally.

f: 153. Over what period do the father's ʿāqilah reimburse the mother's ʿāqilah after the father's acknowledgement of a son of liʿān?
b: Over three years from the date the judge rules that the father's ʿāqilah must reimburse them.

f: 154. Why can the mother's ʿāqilah recover the diyah they paid for a son of liʿān after the father acknowledges him?
b: Because they paid a liability that originally belonged to the father's side.

f: 155. If a mukātab (a slave with a contract of emancipation) dies leaving enough wealth to complete his emancipation, but his free son commits a killing before the emancipation payment is completed, who initially pays the diyah?
b: The mother's ʿāqilah initially pay the diyah.

f: 156. If a mukātab's son commits a killing and the mukātab later completes his emancipation, who reimburses the mother's ʿāqilah for the diyah they paid?
b: The father's ʿāqilah reimburse them.

f: 157. Why does responsibility transfer to the father's ʿāqilah after a mukātab becomes free?
b: Because the father's الولاء (relationship of clientage) transfers to his paternal side once his freedom is established.

f: 158. At what point does a mukātab's الولاء transfer to his paternal relatives after emancipation?
b: At the final moment of his life when his freedom becomes established.

f: 159. If a person orders a child to kill someone and the child's ʿāqilah pay the diyah, who can they recover the payment from?
b: They can recover it from the commander's ʿāqilah if the command is proven by witnesses.

f: 160. If a person orders a child to kill someone and the command is only proven through the commander's confession, who pays the reimbursement?
b: The commander pays from his own wealth.

f: 161. Over what period does the commander pay reimbursement when he ordered a child to kill someone?
b: Over three years from the day the judge rules against him or his ʿāqilah.

f: 162. Why is the reimbursement period three years when a person must repay diyah because he ordered a child to kill someone?
b: Because diyah obligations are delayed as a form of easing hardship.

f: 163. What is the general principle when a killer's legal status changes and his الولاء transfers because of a new event?
b: The original ʿāqilah remain responsible for the crime, whether judgment has already occurred or not.

f: 164. If a killer's الولاء transfers to another group after the killing because of a new event, does the diyah move to the new group?
b: No, the original group remains responsible.

f: 165. What type of change causes the diyah responsibility to move to another group according to the principles of Imām Muḥammad?
b: A hidden condition becoming apparent, such as a father later acknowledging a child of liʿān.

f: 166. If a hidden fact later reveals that another group was originally responsible for a diyah, does responsibility transfer to that group?
b: Yes, because the new information reveals who was responsible from the beginning.

f: 167. If the killer's personal status does not change but his ʿāqilah changes, what determines which group pays the diyah?
b: The group that is his ʿāqilah at the time of the judge's ruling.

f: 168. If a killer's ʿāqilah changes after the judge already ruled against the first group, does responsibility transfer to the new ʿāqilah?
b: No, the first ʿāqilah remain responsible.

f: 169. If a killer's ʿāqilah changes before the judge rules on the diyah, which group pays?
b: The new ʿāqilah pay.

f: 170. If the number of members of a person's ʿāqilah increases or decreases while remaining the same group, does responsibility change?
b: They continue sharing responsibility according to their current number, except for amounts already paid.

f: 171. What principle allows scholars to derive rulings for other diyah cases involving changing relationships of responsibility?
b: The principle that changes in the killer's legal status, changes in ʿāqilah, and hidden discoveries each have different effects on liability.

f: 1. Is making a waṣiyyah (bequest) legally obligatory according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No. A waṣiyyah is not obligatory; it is recommended (mustaḥabb).

f: 2. Why would analogy (qiyās) initially reject the validity of a waṣiyyah?
b: Because it is a transfer of ownership attributed to a time when the owner no longer possesses ownership (after death).

f: 3. Why did the scholars allow waṣiyyah despite the objection of analogy?
b: Because of people's need for it, as a person may realize at the end of his life that he neglected good deeds and needs a way to rectify this through his wealth.

f: 4. What need of people does the institution of waṣiyyah address?
b: It allows a person facing death to allocate some wealth toward beneficial purposes that he intended but had neglected.

f: 5. How does a waṣiyyah benefit a person if he recovers from illness?
b: If he recovers, he can use his wealth for his current needs and goals; if he dies, the waṣiyyah fulfills his intended purpose.

f: 6. What Qur'ānic verse is used as evidence for the validity of waṣiyyah?
b: Allah's statement: “After any bequest that is made or debt” (Qur'an 4:12).

f: 7. What prophetic ḥadīth is mentioned as evidence for waṣiyyah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has given people charity from a third of their wealth at the end of their lives, allowing them to place it wherever they wish.

f: 8. What is the ruling of the الأمة (Muslim community) regarding the permissibility of waṣiyyah?
b: There is consensus that waṣiyyah is permissible.

f: 9. Can a person make a waṣiyyah to a non-heir from one-third of his wealth without the heirs' approval?
b: Yes, it is valid without the heirs' approval.

f: 10. What is the maximum amount that a person may bequeath without heirs' approval?
b: One-third of his wealth.

f: 11. What evidence is used to prohibit a waṣiyyah exceeding one-third?
b: The Prophet's ﷺ statement to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ: “One-third, and one-third is much.”

f: 12. Why is a waṣiyyah exceeding one-third restricted?
b: Because the remaining wealth is connected to the rights of the heirs.

f: 13. When do the heirs' rights become attached to the deceased's wealth?
b: When the person dies, because ownership transfers to the heirs at that time.

f: 14. Why did the Sharīʿah allow a person to dispose of up to one-third despite the heirs' rights?
b: To allow him to fulfill his purposes and leave beneficial acts after death.

f: 15. What does the ḥadīth “al-ḥayf fī al-waṣiyyah min akbar al-kabāʾir” (injustice in a bequest is among the greatest sins) refer to?
b: It refers to exceeding one-third and making a bequest for an heir.

f: 16. Can heirs approve a waṣiyyah exceeding one-third after the testator dies?
b: Yes, if they are adults and legally competent.

f: 17. Why is heirs' approval after the death valid?
b: Because the restriction exists due to their rights, and they may waive their own rights.

f: 18. Is heirs' approval of an excessive waṣiyyah during the testator's lifetime valid?
b: No, because their right has not yet been established.

f: 19. Why is heirs' approval during the testator's lifetime not binding?
b: Because ownership of the inheritance only becomes established after death, so they may reject it later.

f: 20. If heirs approve a waṣiyyah after the testator's death, can they revoke their approval?
b: No, because they have waived an established right.

f: 21. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, from whom does the beneficiary receive ownership when heirs approve a waṣiyyah?
b: The beneficiary receives ownership from the testator (the original owner).

f: 22. According to al-Shāfiʿī, from whom does the beneficiary receive ownership when heirs approve a waṣiyyah?
b: From the heirs.

f: 23. Why do the Ḥanafīs say the beneficiary receives ownership from the testator after heirs approve?
b: Because the cause of ownership originated from the testator, and the heirs' approval merely removes the obstacle.

f: 24. Does a beneficiary need to take possession (qabḍ) for an approved waṣiyyah to become valid?
b: No.

f: 25. Can a person who directly killed the testator receive a waṣiyyah from him?
b: No, whether the killing was intentional or accidental.

f: 26. What prophetic ḥadīth is used to prohibit a killer from receiving a waṣiyyah?
b: “There is no waṣiyyah for a killer.”

f: 27. Why is a killer prevented from receiving a waṣiyyah?
b: Because he hastened something that Allah delayed, so he is deprived of the bequest just as he is deprived of inheritance.

f: 28. According to al-Shāfiʿī, is a killer allowed to receive a waṣiyyah?
b: Yes.

f: 29. If a person makes a waṣiyyah for someone and that person later kills him, does the waṣiyyah become invalid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Yes.

f: 30. If a person makes a waṣiyyah for someone and that person later kills him, does al-Shāfiʿī consider the waṣiyyah valid?
b: Yes.

f: 31. Can heirs approve a waṣiyyah made for a killer after the killer is excluded?
b: Yes, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad.

f: 32. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله not allow heirs to approve a waṣiyyah for a killer?
b: Because the reason for prohibition (the killing) still exists.

f: 33. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow heirs to approve a killer's waṣiyyah?
b: Because the prohibition exists due to the heirs' rights, and they may waive their own benefit.

f: 34. Can a person make a waṣiyyah for one of his heirs?
b: No.

f: 35. What prophetic ḥadīth prohibits making a waṣiyyah for an heir?
b: “Indeed Allah has given every person entitled to a right his right; there is no waṣiyyah for an heir.”

f: 36. Why is a waṣiyyah for an heir prohibited?
b: Because favoring one heir harms the others and may lead to breaking family ties.

f: 37. When is a person's status as heir or non-heir considered for the ruling of a waṣiyyah?
b: At the time of death, not at the time the waṣiyyah was written.

f: 38. Why is heir status considered at the time of death rather than when the waṣiyyah is made?
b: Because ownership from the waṣiyyah only begins after death.

f: 39. What is the ruling of a sick person's gift to an heir according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It has the same ruling as a waṣiyyah and is only effective from one-third.

f: 40. Why is a sick person's gift to an heir treated like a waṣiyyah?
b: Because it functions like a waṣiyyah in effect.

f: 41. When is a sick person's admission (iqrār) in favor of an heir evaluated?
b: At the time of the admission, because it is an immediate transaction.

f: 42. Can heirs approve a waṣiyyah made for one heir?
b: Yes.

f: 43. If some heirs approve a waṣiyyah for an heir and others reject it, what happens?
b: It is valid only regarding the approving heirs' shares and invalid regarding the rejecting heirs' shares.

f: 44. Can a Muslim make a waṣiyyah for a non-Muslim?
b: Yes.

f: 45. What evidence is used to allow a Muslim's waṣiyyah to a non-Muslim?
b: Allah's statement: “Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion…” (Qur'an 60:8).

f: 46. Can a non-Muslim make a waṣiyyah for a Muslim?
b: Yes.

f: 47. Why can a non-Muslim make a waṣiyyah for a Muslim?
b: Because protected non-Muslims (dhimmīs) are treated equally with Muslims in financial transactions.

f: 48. Is a Muslim allowed to make a waṣiyyah for a person from a hostile non-Muslim state (dār al-ḥarb)?
b: No, according to the narration in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr.

f: 49. What verse is used to prohibit a waṣiyyah to hostile non-Muslims?
b: Allah's statement: “Allah only forbids you from those who fought you because of religion…” (Qur'an 60:9).

f: 50. When does the person receiving a waṣiyyah (bequest) accept it?
b: Acceptance occurs after the death of the person making the waṣiyyah.

f: 51. Is accepting or rejecting a waṣiyyah during the lifetime of the person making it valid?
b: No. Acceptance or rejection during the testator's lifetime is invalid.

f: 52. Why is acceptance or rejection of a waṣiyyah during the testator's lifetime invalid?
b: Because the legal effect of the waṣiyyah only begins after death, so actions before that time are not considered.

f: 53. Is accepting a waṣiyyah before the contract or legal cause exists considered valid?
b: No, just as acceptance before a contract exists is not considered valid.

f: 54. Is it recommended for a person to make a waṣiyyah for his entire one-third share?
b: No. It is recommended to make a waṣiyyah for less than one-third.

f: 55. Why is making a waṣiyyah for less than one-third recommended?
b: Because leaving some wealth for heirs is a form of kindness toward relatives by not taking all of one's permissible bequest amount.

f: 56. Why is making a waṣiyyah for the full one-third not considered as great a favor to relatives?
b: Because it is merely taking one's full legal allowance rather than showing generosity toward relatives.

f: 57. If a person's heirs are poor and cannot live sufficiently from their inheritance, is making a waṣiyyah or leaving the wealth to heirs preferred?
b: Leaving the wealth to heirs is preferred.

f: 58. Why is leaving wealth to poor heirs preferred over making a waṣiyyah?
b: Because it combines charity toward relatives and concern for the poor.

f: 59. What prophetic ḥadīth supports giving charity to relatives?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “The best charity is that given to a relative who is hostile toward you.”

f: 60. If a person's heirs are wealthy and do not need their inheritance, is making a waṣiyyah preferred?
b: Yes, making a waṣiyyah is preferred.

f: 61. Why is making a waṣiyyah preferred when heirs are wealthy?
b: Because it becomes charity toward others, whereas leaving wealth to relatives is only a gift to family members.

f: 62. What did some scholars say regarding whether to make a waṣiyyah or leave wealth to wealthy heirs?
b: They said a person may choose either because both contain virtue: charity and maintaining family ties.

f: 63. When does the person receiving a waṣiyyah become the owner of the bequeathed item according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and the Ḥanafīs?
b: He becomes owner after accepting the waṣiyyah.

f: 64. Who disagrees with the view that ownership through waṣiyyah requires acceptance?
b: Zufar and one opinion of al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 65. Why does Zufar argue that acceptance is not required for a waṣiyyah?
b: Because he considers waṣiyyah similar to inheritance, and inheritance transfers ownership without acceptance.

f: 66. Why do the Ḥanafīs distinguish waṣiyyah from inheritance regarding acceptance?
b: Because waṣiyyah establishes new ownership, while inheritance is a legal succession established by Sharīʿah.

f: 67. Why does a person receiving a waṣiyyah need to accept it before becoming owner?
b: Because no one can establish ownership for another person without that person's acceptance.

f: 68. Why does inheritance not require acceptance while waṣiyyah does?
b: Because inheritance is forced transfer by law, while waṣiyyah is a new voluntary transfer of ownership.

f: 69. What is the one exception where the recipient of a waṣiyyah becomes owner without explicitly accepting it?
b: If the testator dies and the recipient dies before accepting, the bequeathed property enters the recipient's estate and is inherited by his heirs.

f: 70. What is the normal analogy (qiyās) regarding a recipient who dies before accepting a waṣiyyah?
b: The waṣiyyah should become invalid because ownership was dependent on acceptance.

f: 71. Why did the Ḥanafīs make an exception when the recipient dies before accepting the waṣiyyah?
b: Because the testator's side of the waṣiyyah was completed at death and cannot be cancelled; the remaining suspension was only due to the recipient's right.

f: 72. What example is used to support the exception where a recipient dies before accepting a waṣiyyah?
b: A sale with an option (khiyār) where a party dies before exercising the option.

f: 73. If a person dies owing debts that completely consume his wealth, is his waṣiyyah valid?
b: No, the waṣiyyah is not carried out.

f: 74. Why does debt take priority over a waṣiyyah?
b: Because paying debt is an obligation while waṣiyyah is a voluntary charity.

f: 75. What principle determines priority between debt and waṣiyyah?
b: The more important obligation is fulfilled first.

f: 76. When can a waṣiyyah still be carried out despite debts covering the deceased's wealth?
b: If the creditors forgive the debts.

f: 77. Why does a waṣiyyah become valid after creditors forgive the debt?
b: Because the debt no longer exists, leaving the wealth available for the waṣiyyah.

f: 78. Is the waṣiyyah of a child valid according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: No, a child's waṣiyyah is not valid.

f: 79. What is al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding a child's waṣiyyah for charitable purposes?
b: He considers it valid if it is for acts of goodness.

f: 80. What evidence does al-Shāfiʿī use to support the validity of a child's waṣiyyah?
b: The report that ʿUmar رضي الله عنه allowed the waṣiyyah of a young person close to puberty.

f: 81. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject the validity of a child's waṣiyyah?
b: Because waṣiyyah is a voluntary donation, and a child is not legally qualified for such transactions.

f: 82. How do the Ḥanafīs interpret the report that ʿUmar رضي الله عنه approved a young person's waṣiyyah?
b: They interpret it as referring to someone close to or having reached maturity, or to instructions regarding burial arrangements.

f: 83. Is a child's instruction regarding his burial expenses and funeral arrangements valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Yes.

f: 84. Why does a child not gain the reward of charity through making a waṣiyyah?
b: Because he can still gain reward by leaving wealth to his heirs, as explained in inheritance matters.

f: 85. If a child makes a waṣiyyah and reaches adulthood before dying, is the waṣiyyah valid?
b: No, because he lacked legal capacity when he made it.

f: 86. If a child says, “When I become an adult, one-third of my wealth is for so-and-so as a waṣiyyah,” is this valid?
b: No, because he lacks the legal capacity to make the waṣiyyah, whether immediately or conditionally.

f: 87. Why is a child's conditional waṣiyyah after reaching adulthood invalid?
b: Because lack of legal capacity prevents both immediate and future conditional ownership transfers.

f: 88. Why can a slave or mukātab make a waṣiyyah whereas a child cannot?
b: Because their legal capacity exists; the obstacle is only the master's right, which can end later.

f: 89. Is a mukātab's waṣiyyah valid even if he leaves enough wealth to complete his emancipation?
b: According to the stated Ḥanafī position, no.

f: 90. Why is a mukātab's waṣiyyah invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because his wealth cannot be freely donated.

f: 91. What is the alternative opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding a mukātab's waṣiyyah?
b: They consider it valid.

f: 92. Is a waṣiyyah for an unborn child (fetus) valid?
b: Yes, under certain conditions.

f: 93. Under what condition is a waṣiyyah for a fetus valid?
b: If the fetus is delivered less than six months after the waṣiyyah was made.

f: 94. Why is a waṣiyyah for a fetus valid?
b: Because a fetus can inherit, and waṣiyyah resembles inheritance in allowing succession to wealth.

f: 95. Why does a fetus have a legal ability to inherit but not receive a normal gift?
b: Because inheritance is established by Sharīʿah, while a gift requires a recipient with legal authority to own property.

f: 96. Is making a waṣiyyah involving a fetus before its existence allowed?
b: No, except where existence is known at the time of the waṣiyyah.

f: 97. Why is the scope of waṣiyyah broader than ordinary ownership transfers?
b: Because it addresses the needs of the deceased who can no longer act after death.

f: 98. If a person makes a waṣiyyah for a pregnant slave woman excluding her unborn child, is the waṣiyyah valid?
b: Yes, both the waṣiyyah for the mother and the exclusion of the child are valid.

f: 99. Why can the unborn child be excluded from a waṣiyyah for a pregnant slave woman?
b: Because the term “slave woman” does not linguistically include the fetus, even though the fetus follows the mother by default.

f: 100. What general principle allows the exclusion of a fetus from a waṣiyyah for its mother?
b: Anything that can be independently contracted for can also be independently excluded.

f: 101. What is the general rule regarding things that cannot be separately owned in contracts and excluding them from contracts?
b: If something cannot be independently contracted for, it cannot be independently excluded.

f: 102. Is the person who made a waṣiyyah allowed to revoke it?
b: Yes. The person making the waṣiyyah may revoke it.

f: 103. Why may a person revoke a waṣiyyah before death?
b: Because it is a voluntary donation that has not yet been completed, so it resembles a gift that may be revoked before completion.

f: 104. Why is a waṣiyyah not considered fully completed during the lifetime of the testator?
b: Because acceptance of the waṣiyyah only takes place after death.

f: 105. What analogy is used to show that a waṣiyyah can be revoked before completion?
b: A sale where the offer may be cancelled before acceptance.

f: 106. What are the two ways a person can revoke a waṣiyyah?
b: By explicitly stating that he has revoked it or by performing an action that indicates revocation.

f: 107. Why does an action indicating revocation have the same ruling as an explicit statement?
b: Because indications can function like clear statements in legal rulings.

f: 108. What type of action by the testator counts as revocation of a waṣiyyah?
b: Any action that would prevent the owner from reclaiming the property if done by another person on his property.

f: 109. Why does an action that would terminate the owner's rights over property count as revocation when done by the testator?
b: Because it shows that the testator no longer intends the property to remain available for the waṣiyyah.

f: 110. If a person adds something to the bequeathed item that cannot be removed before handing it over, is this a revocation?
b: Yes.

f: 111. Is mixing flour with fat in a bequeathed food item considered revocation?
b: Yes, because the added component becomes inseparable from the item.

f: 112. Is building on a house that was bequeathed considered revocation?
b: Yes, because the addition cannot be removed before delivering the house.

f: 113. Is stuffing cotton into a bequeathed garment considered revocation?
b: Yes.

f: 114. Is adding lining or an outer layer to a bequeathed garment considered revocation?
b: Yes.

f: 115. Why are inseparable additions to a bequeathed item considered revocation?
b: Because the original item cannot be delivered without the added work, and the addition was made by the owner himself.

f: 116. Is decorating or making minor changes to a bequeathed house considered revocation?
b: No, if the action only concerns the additions or accessories rather than the original item.

f: 117. Why does demolishing the structure of a bequeathed house not necessarily count as revocation?
b: Because it is a disposal of the attached parts rather than the original bequeathed property itself.

f: 118. What general type of action always counts as revocation of a waṣiyyah?
b: Any action that removes the testator's ownership of the bequeathed item.

f: 119. If a person sells the item he had bequeathed and later buys it back, is the waṣiyyah revoked?
b: Yes.

f: 120. Why does selling the bequeathed item revoke the waṣiyyah even if it is later repurchased?
b: Because the waṣiyyah can only operate on property still owned by the testator, and he removed his ownership.

f: 121. Is slaughtering a bequeathed sheep considered revocation?
b: Yes.

f: 122. Why is slaughtering a bequeathed animal considered revocation?
b: Because slaughtering normally indicates that the owner intends to use it for his own need.

f: 123. Is washing a bequeathed garment considered revocation?
b: No.

f: 124. Why is washing a bequeathed garment not considered revocation?
b: Because someone intending to give clothing to another person normally washes it as preparation, so it confirms rather than cancels the waṣiyyah.

f: 125. If a person denies having made a waṣiyyah, does this count as revocation according to Muḥammad?
b: No.

f: 126. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding denying a waṣiyyah?
b: He considers it a revocation.

f: 127. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider denial of a waṣiyyah to be revocation?
b: Because denial rejects the existence of the waṣiyyah in both the past and present, making it stronger than simple revocation.

f: 128. Why does Muḥammad not consider denial of a waṣiyyah as revocation?
b: Because denial primarily negates the past, while revocation negates the present intention; therefore it is not a true revocation.

f: 129. Why is denying a waṣiyyah different from revoking it?
b: Revocation confirms that the waṣiyyah existed but cancels it, while denial rejects that it ever existed.

f: 130. Does denying a marriage contract automatically dissolve the marriage?
b: No, just as denying a waṣiyyah does not necessarily revoke it.

f: 131. If a person says, “Every waṣiyyah I made for so-and-so is forbidden and unlawful,” is this a revocation?
b: No.

f: 132. Why is saying a waṣiyyah is “forbidden” not a revocation?
b: Because describing something as forbidden assumes the original thing still exists.

f: 133. If a person says, “The waṣiyyah I made is invalid,” is this a revocation?
b: Yes.
