f: 134. Why does saying a waṣiyyah is invalid count as revocation?
b: Because it removes the existence of the waṣiyyah itself.

f: 135. If a person says, “I have delayed the waṣiyyah,” is this revocation?
b: No.

f: 136. Why does delaying a waṣiyyah not count as revocation?
b: Because postponement does not mean cancellation, just as delaying repayment of a debt does not erase the debt.

f: 137. If a person says, “I abandoned the waṣiyyah,” is this revocation?
b: Yes.

f: 138. Why does saying “I abandoned it” count as revocation?
b: Because it indicates that he has cancelled and removed it.

f: 139. If a person says, “The slave I bequeathed to so-and-so belongs to so-and-so,” is the first waṣiyyah revoked?
b: Yes.

f: 140. Why does saying the slave belongs to another person revoke the first waṣiyyah?
b: Because the statement indicates removal of the first person's share and replacement of ownership.

f: 141. If a person first bequeaths an item to one person and then bequeaths it to another person, is the first waṣiyyah automatically revoked?
b: No.

f: 142. Why does a second waṣiyyah not automatically cancel the first?
b: Because the property can be shared and the wording allows both claims to coexist.

f: 143. If a person says, “The slave is for my heir,” after previously bequeathing it to someone else, is the first waṣiyyah revoked?
b: Yes.

f: 144. Why does making the slave for an heir revoke the first waṣiyyah?
b: Because it indicates transferring the item away from the first beneficiary.

f: 145. What is the ruling if the second person mentioned in the replacement waṣiyyah was already dead when the second waṣiyyah was made?
b: The first waṣiyyah remains valid.

f: 146. Why does the first waṣiyyah remain valid if the second beneficiary was already dead?
b: Because the first waṣiyyah is only cancelled due to the second being valid, which did not occur.

f: 147. What happens if the second beneficiary was alive when the second waṣiyyah was made but dies before the testator?
b: The property goes to the heirs.

f: 148. Why do the heirs receive the property if the second beneficiary dies before the testator?
b: Because the first waṣiyyah was revoked, and the second waṣiyyah became invalid due to the beneficiary's death.

f: 149. If a person makes a waṣiyyah of one-third of his wealth to two people and the heirs do not approve, how is it divided?
b: The one-third is divided equally between them.

f: 150. Why do two people who were each given one-third share equally in the available one-third?
b: Because the total available amount is restricted to one-third and both have equal entitlement.

f: 151. If a person gives one person one-third and another person one-sixth of his wealth by waṣiyyah without heirs' approval, how is the one-third divided?
b: It is divided in three portions: two portions for the one-third beneficiary and one portion for the one-sixth beneficiary.

f: 152. Why is a one-third and one-sixth waṣiyyah divided into three shares?
b: Because the available one-third is divided according to the proportion of their original claims.

f: 153. If a person bequeaths all his wealth to one person and one-third to another person without heirs' approval, how is the one-third divided according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: It is divided equally between the two beneficiaries.

f: 154. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, how is the one-third divided when one person receives all wealth and another receives one-third?
b: The one-third is divided into four shares: three for the first beneficiary and one for the second.

f: 155. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad give preference to the person bequeathed the entire wealth?
b: Because the testator intended both entitlement and preference, and preference remains even when the full entitlement is restricted.

f: 156. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject giving preference in this case?
b: Because the original waṣiyyah exceeds what is legally allowed without heirs' approval, so the entire invalid basis collapses.

f: 157. What three areas does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow preference to be considered despite limits?
b: Muḥābāh (favor in sale), sāʿāyah, and unrestricted monetary bequests.

f: 158. Why can preference be considered in those three cases but not in an excessive waṣiyyah?
b: Because those cases have some validity without heirs' approval, whereas the excessive waṣiyyah has no validity without approval.

f: 159. If a person bequeaths a specific item from his estate worth more than one-third, is the beneficiary limited to one-third of its value?
b: Yes.

f: 160. Why is a specific item treated differently from a general monetary bequest?
b: Because the right is attached to that specific item itself.

f: 161. If the specific item bequeathed is destroyed and the deceased later acquires other wealth, does the waṣiyyah transfer to the new wealth?
b: No.

f: 162. Why does a specific-item waṣiyyah differ from an unrestricted monetary waṣiyyah?
b: Because the specific item itself is the object of the bequest, while general wealth is not tied to a particular asset.

f: 163. If a person makes a waṣiyyah saying “give my son's share to so-and-so,” is the waṣiyyah valid?
b: No, the waṣiyyah is invalid.

f: 164. Why is a waṣiyyah for “the share of my son” invalid?
b: Because it is a bequest of another person's property, since the son's share only becomes his after the testator's death.

f: 165. If a person makes a waṣiyyah saying “give the equivalent of my son's share,” is it valid?
b: Yes, it is valid.

f: 166. Why is a waṣiyyah for “the equivalent of my son's share” valid?
b: Because the equivalent of something is separate from the thing itself, even though it is measured by it.

f: 167. Who disagrees with the invalidity of a waṣiyyah for the son's actual share?
b: Zufar.

f: 168. Why does Zufar consider a waṣiyyah for the son's share valid?
b: He considers the person's current ownership and argues that all the wealth belongs to the testator before death.

f: 169. What is the Ḥanafī response to Zufar regarding a waṣiyyah for the son's share?
b: The son's share is only established after death, so it is not the testator's property to bequeath.

f: 170. If a person says “I bequeath a سهم (share) of my wealth,” what does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله say the beneficiary receives?
b: The smallest share given to any heir, unless that is less than one-sixth, in which case it is completed to one-sixth but not increased beyond that.

f: 171. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what does a person receive if the testator says “a سهم of my wealth”?
b: He receives the same as the share of one of the heirs, but not more than one-third unless the heirs approve.

f: 172. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad interpret سهم as an heir's share?
b: Because in common usage, especially in waṣiyyah matters, سهم refers to one of the shares of the heirs.

f: 173. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله interpret سهم as one-sixth?
b: Because it is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه that سهم means one-sixth, and this meaning was used in Arabic.

f: 174. What is the linguistic meaning of سهم according to the report from Iyās?
b: سهم can mean one-sixth.

f: 175. How did later scholars describe the meaning of سهم in their own usage?
b: They said in their usage سهم means simply a portion or part.

f: 176. If a person says “I bequeath a part (جزء) of my wealth,” is the amount specified?
b: No, it is unspecified.

f: 177. Who decides the amount when someone says “a part of my wealth”?
b: The heirs are asked to determine it.

f: 178. Why can an unspecified waṣiyyah of “a part” still be valid?
b: Because uncertainty does not invalidate waṣiyyah, and the heirs take the place of the testator in clarifying it.

f: 179. If someone says “one-sixth of my wealth belongs to Zayd” and later says “one-third of my wealth belongs to Zayd,” what does Zayd receive if the heirs approve?
b: He receives one-third of the wealth, and the one-sixth is included within it.

f: 180. Why does the second statement of one-third include the first one-sixth?
b: Because the first amount was specified by a known reference, and repeating the known reference refers back to the same thing.

f: 181. If someone says “one-sixth of my wealth belongs to Zayd” and later repeats “one-sixth of my wealth belongs to Zayd,” how much does Zayd receive?
b: He receives only one-sixth.

f: 182. Why does repeating “one-sixth of my wealth” not add another sixth?
b: Because the second definite expression refers to the already known first one.

f: 183. If a person bequeaths one-third of his dirhams and two-thirds of the dirhams disappear, while the remaining third is still enough to come from one-third of the remaining estate, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: He receives all of the remaining dirhams.

f: 184. What is Zufar's opinion regarding a bequest of one-third of a type of wealth where most of it is destroyed?
b: The beneficiary receives only one-third of what remains.

f: 185. Why does Zufar say the beneficiary only receives one-third of what remains?
b: Because the wealth was jointly shared, so what is lost is lost proportionally among the owners.

f: 186. Why do the Ḥanafīs give the beneficiary all of the remaining dirhams in this case?
b: Because items of the same type can be combined and assigned to one party, and the waṣiyyah is given priority.

f: 187. Why is the ruling different for different types of property?
b: Because different types cannot be combined into one unit for compulsory division.

f: 188. If a person bequeaths one-third of his clothing and two-thirds of the clothing are destroyed, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: He receives only one-third of the remaining clothing.

f: 189. When would clothing be treated like dirhams in this ruling?
b: When all the clothing is of the same type.

f: 190. Are measurable and weighable commodities treated like dirhams regarding combining the remaining property?
b: Yes, because they can be combined through division.

f: 191. If a person bequeaths one-third of three slaves and two slaves die, how much does the beneficiary receive?
b: He receives one-third of the remaining slave.

f: 192. Are different houses treated like different slaves in this ruling?
b: Yes.

f: 193. Is the ruling regarding different slaves and houses specifically Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله opinion?
b: Some scholars said it is specific to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله because he does not require forced combination through division.

f: 194. What is the alternative explanation regarding the ruling of different slaves and houses?
b: Some said it is the position of all three imams because the judge may exercise judgment to combine them, but without that it is impossible.

f: 195. If a person bequeaths one thousand dirhams and has both cash and debts, how is the bequest fulfilled if the cash alone covers the one thousand from one-third of the estate?
b: The beneficiary is given the one thousand from the cash.

f: 196. Why is the beneficiary given cash first if it is sufficient?
b: Because each person's right can be fulfilled completely without harming anyone.

f: 197. If the cash does not cover the one thousand dirhams bequest, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: He receives one-third of the available cash, and whenever debt is collected he receives one-third of the collected amount until he reaches one thousand.

f: 198. Why does the beneficiary not receive the full amount from the cash while leaving debts for heirs?
b: Because this would harm the heirs, as cash has more immediate value than debt.

f: 199. Why is debt not treated like present wealth before collection?
b: Because debt only becomes actual wealth when it is received.

f: 200. If a person bequeaths one-third of his wealth to Zayd and ʿAmr, but ʿAmr is already dead, who receives the one-third?
b: Zayd receives the entire one-third.

f: 201. Why does the living beneficiary receive the entire share when the other beneficiary is dead?
b: Because the deceased person cannot receive a waṣiyyah and cannot compete with someone legally capable of receiving it.

f: 202. What is the report from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding a waṣiyyah to a dead person when the testator did not know of the death?
b: The living beneficiary receives only half of the one-third.

f: 203. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله give the living beneficiary only half if the testator did not know the other beneficiary was dead?
b: Because he considers the waṣiyyah to the deceased person valid originally, so the testator only intended half for the living person.

f: 204. If the testator knew the beneficiary was dead when making the waṣiyyah, what would happen according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: The living beneficiary receives the entire one-third because the waṣiyyah to the dead person is meaningless.

f: 205. If a person says “one-third of my wealth is between Zayd and ʿAmr,” and Zayd is dead, what does ʿAmr receive?
b: ʿAmr receives half of the one-third.

f: 206. Why does ʿAmr receive only half when the wording says “between Zayd and ʿAmr”?
b: Because the wording indicates division between two people, unlike a statement giving the entire one-third to Zayd alone.

f: 207. If a person says “one-third of my wealth is for Zayd” without mentioning anyone else, how much does Zayd receive?
b: Zayd receives the entire one-third.

f: 208. If a person says “one-third of my wealth is between so-and-so” without naming another person, does the named person receive the entire one-third?
b: No, because the wording indicates sharing.

f: 209. If a person makes a bequest of one-third of his wealth but has no wealth at the time of making the bequest and later acquires wealth, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: The beneficiary receives one-third of whatever wealth the person owns at the time of death, because the bequest is an ownership transfer attached to the time after death, so the wealth must exist at the time of death.

f: 210. If a person had wealth when making a bequest of one-third of his wealth, but that wealth disappeared and he later acquired new wealth before death, does the bequest apply to the new wealth?
b: Yes. The beneficiary receives one-third of the wealth that exists at the time of death, because consideration is given to the existence of wealth at death, not at the time of making the bequest.

f: 211. If a person makes a bequest of one-third of his sheep and all his sheep die before his death, what is the ruling?
b: The bequest is invalid because it was attached to a specific item, and the item no longer exists at the time when the bequest becomes effective.

f: 212. If a person makes a bequest of one-third of his sheep but originally owns no sheep, then acquires sheep before death, is the bequest valid?
b: The correct view is that the bequest is valid because if a bequest of wealth would be valid, then a bequest mentioning a type of wealth is also valid. What matters is that the item exists at death.

f: 213. If a person says, "I bequeath a sheep from my wealth," but he owns no sheep, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: He receives the value of a sheep, because adding it to "my wealth" indicates that the intended meaning is the monetary value of a sheep, which exists within general wealth.

f: 214. If a person says, "I bequeath a sheep" without adding "from my wealth," and he owns no sheep, is the bequest valid?
b: There are two views: some scholars said it is invalid because the validity comes from connecting it to wealth; others said it is valid because mentioning a sheep without owning one indicates that the intended meaning is its monetary value.

f: 215. If a person says, "I bequeath a sheep from my flock," but he owns no flock, what is the ruling?
b: The bequest is invalid because mentioning the flock indicates that he intended a specific sheep as part of that flock, not merely its monetary value.

f: 216. If a person makes a bequest of one-third of his wealth to his three umm walads (slave mothers of his children) and to the poor and needy, how is the one-third divided according to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله and Abu Yusuf رحمه الله?
b: The three umm walads receive three shares out of five total shares, and the poor and needy receive two shares.

f: 217. Why do Abu Hanifah رحمه الله and Abu Yusuf رحمه الله divide a bequest between umm walads and the poor into five shares?
b: Because the plural form with the definite article ("the poor and needy") is treated as referring to the category itself, so one share is assigned to each group, while the three umm walads receive three shares.

f: 218. How does Muhammad differ regarding a bequest to umm walads and the poor?
b: Muhammad holds that the plural indicates at least two individuals, so the calculation is based on seven shares: three shares for the three umm walads and two shares for each group of the poor and needy.

f: 219. If a person bequeaths one-third of his wealth to a specific person and to the poor, how is it divided according to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله and Abu Yusuf رحمه الله?
b: Half of the one-third goes to the specific person and half goes to the poor.

f: 220. How does Muhammad divide a bequest made to a specific person and the poor?
b: Muhammad gives one-third of the bequest portion to the specific person and two-thirds to the poor because he considers "the poor" to represent at least two individuals.

f: 221. According to Abu Hanifah رحمه الله and Abu Yusuf رحمه الله, can a bequest to "the poor" be given to only one poor person?
b: Yes, because they consider the plural with the definite article to refer to the category, and fulfilling it with one member of that category is sufficient.

f: 222. According to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله, can a bequest to "the poor" be given to only one poor person?
b: No. According to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله, it must be given to at least two poor people because the plural requires a minimum of two.

f: 223. If a person bequeaths one hundred dirhams to one person and one hundred dirhams to another, then tells a third person, "I have made you a partner with them," what does the third person receive?
b: The third person receives one-third of each hundred dirhams, because partnership implies equality and equality can be achieved by dividing each amount equally among the three.

f: 224. If a person bequeaths four hundred dirhams to one person and two hundred dirhams to another, then adds, "I have made another person a partner with them," how is the third person's share determined?
b: Equality between all three cannot be achieved because the original amounts differ, so the third person shares equally with each person by taking half of each person's share.

f: 225. If a person says to his heirs, "So-and-so has a debt owed to him by me; believe him," is the claimant believed?
b: According to the preferred ruling, he is believed up to one-third of the estate.

f: 226. Why is a person's statement, "So-and-so has a debt against me; believe him," accepted only up to one-third of the estate?
b: Because it is treated as a bequest rather than a confirmed debt, allowing the person's intention to be fulfilled while preserving the rights of the heirs beyond one-third.

f: 227. Why would a person declare an unknown debt before death by saying, "Believe him"?
b: He may know that a debt exists but not know its exact amount, and he wants to discharge his responsibility, so the statement is treated like a bequest.

f: 228. If a person makes multiple other bequests besides an unknown debt claim, how is the estate divided?
b: One-third of the estate is reserved for the bequests, and two-thirds goes to the heirs.

f: 229. Why are the known bequests given priority when separating the estate?
b: Because the inheritance shares and known bequests are established, while the unknown claim is uncertain and cannot compete with established rights.

f: 230. After the one-third for bequests has been separated, what is each side asked regarding an unknown claim?
b: The beneficiaries of the bequests are told to accept whatever amount they wish from their portion, and the heirs are told to accept whatever amount they wish from their portion.

f: 231. If the heirs and beneficiaries accept an unknown claim after separation of the estate, how much must each side pay?
b: The beneficiaries of the one-third pay one-third of what they accepted, and the heirs pay two-thirds of what they accepted, according to their shares.

f: 232. If the claimant demands more than what the heirs or beneficiaries accepted, what must happen?
b: The claimant must provide proof, and each group must swear an oath denying knowledge of the additional amount if necessary.

f: 233. What is the ruling if a person makes a bequest to both a non-heir and his heir?
b: The non-heir receives half of the bequest, while the bequest to the heir is invalid. This is because the testator has the right to bequeath part of his wealth but does not have the right to bequeath to an heir unless the other heirs approve.

f: 234. Why is a bequest to an heir invalid unless the other heirs approve?
b: Because allowing preference of one heir over others may cause harm and severance of family ties. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has given every person of right his right, so there is no bequest for an heir.”

f: 235. Why does a bequest to a living person and a deceased person differ from a bequest to an heir and a non-heir?
b: A deceased person is not eligible to receive a bequest, so he does not compete with the living recipient, and the entire bequest goes to the living person. An heir, however, is eligible for a bequest but is prevented from receiving it without approval of the other heirs.

f: 236. What is the ruling if a person bequeaths something to a murderer and a non-murderer?
b: The same ruling applies as with an heir and non-heir: the valid part of the bequest is executed, while the invalid part is cancelled.

f: 237. Why does an admission (iqrār) to both an heir and a non-heir differ from a bequest to both?
b: A bequest is a new legal action, so the share of the person entitled to it can remain valid even if another person's share is invalid. An admission is a statement about a past reality; if it describes shared ownership, it cannot be partially accepted while changing the stated reality.

f: 238. What is the ruling if a person owns three garments (valuable, medium, and poor quality), bequeaths each garment to a different person, then one garment is lost and the heirs deny the bequests?
b: The bequests become invalid because the specific item belonging to each recipient is unknown, and this uncertainty prevents the court from enforcing the bequest.

f: 239. What happens if the heirs accept responsibility for the two remaining garments after one of three bequeathed garments is lost?
b: The bequests become valid because the obstacle of denial is removed. The recipient of the finest garment receives two-thirds of the finest remaining garment, the recipient of the middle garment receives one-third of the finest and one-third of the lowest, and the recipient of the lowest receives two-thirds of the lowest.

f: 240. Why does the recipient of the finest garment receive two-thirds of the finest remaining garment after one garment is lost?
b: Because he cannot have any share in the lower garments with certainty. His only possible entitlement is through the remaining finest garment, so his share is assigned there.

f: 241. Why does the recipient of the lowest garment receive two-thirds of the lowest remaining garment after one garment is lost?
b: Because he cannot have any share in the finest garment with certainty, and his possible entitlement exists only in the lowest garment.

f: 242. If a house is jointly owned by two people and one owner bequeaths a specific room to someone, what happens if the house is divided and the room falls into the testator's share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: The bequest is valid and the recipient receives that specific room because the room became entirely within the testator's ownership after division.

f: 243. If a jointly owned house is divided and the specific room mentioned in the bequest falls into the other owner's share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what does the recipient receive?
b: The recipient receives an equivalent amount of area from the house because the original item was no longer available to him, so the bequest transfers to its equivalent value in measurement.

f: 244. What is Muḥammad's opinion regarding a bequest of a specific room from a jointly owned house?
b: Muḥammad holds that the recipient receives only half of the room if it falls into the testator's share, and if it falls into the other owner's share, he receives an equivalent amount equal to half of the room's area.

f: 245. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider the bequest of the entire room valid after division?
b: Because the testator intended to bequeath a usable property, and division establishes complete ownership. The purpose of the division is separation and clarification of ownership rather than an actual exchange.

f: 246. Why does Muḥammad consider only the testator's original share valid in a bequest of a specific room from jointly owned property?
b: Because the testator only owned half of the room. The other half belonged to someone else, and one cannot bequeath what one does not own.

f: 247. How is the share divided if the bequeathed room falls into the other owner's portion according to Muḥammad?
b: The recipient is treated as having a claim equal to half of the room's area, while the heirs receive the remainder.

f: 248. If a jointly owned house is 100 cubits in area and the bequeathed room is 10 cubits, how is the division calculated according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله when the room falls into the other owner's share?
b: The recipient is given a share based on 10 cubits, while the heirs are given a share based on 45 cubits (the testator's remaining half excluding the room). The estate is divided into 11 shares: 2 shares for the recipient and 9 shares for the heirs.

f: 249. If the same case is calculated according to Muḥammad, how is it divided?
b: The recipient is assigned 5 cubits (half the room), while the heirs receive 45 cubits. The total becomes 10 shares: 1 share for the recipient and 9 shares for the heirs.

f: 250. What is the difference between a bequest and an admission regarding property that belongs to someone else?
b: An admission of another person's ownership can be valid, because a person may acknowledge ownership belonging to someone else. A bequest of property not owned by the testator is invalid because ownership is not established until after death.

f: 251. If someone bequeaths property belonging to another person, then later acquires ownership of that property before death, does the original bequest become valid?
b: No. A bequest of property not owned at the time of the bequest does not become valid merely because the testator later acquires ownership.

f: 252. Why does a bequest of another person's property remain invalid even if the testator later owns it?
b: Because the original bequest was attached to property that the testator did not own, and a bequest only applies to ownership existing at the time when its legal effect begins (after death).

f: 253. What is the ruling on making a will (waṣiyyah) according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: A will is not obligatory, but it is recommended (mustaḥabb). Although analogy would reject it because it transfers ownership after the person's ownership has ended, it was permitted due to people's need for it.

f: 254. Why was the institution of waṣiyyah permitted despite the objection from analogy?
b: Because people are deceived by hopes and may neglect good deeds. When illness approaches and death is feared, a person may need to correct past shortcomings by directing some of his wealth toward beneficial purposes.

f: 255. What evidence establishes the legitimacy of waṣiyyah?
b: The Qur'an mentions inheritance being distributed "after a bequest or debt" (Qur'an 4:12), and the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah gave people permission to give one-third of their wealth at the end of their lives as an increase in their deeds. There is also consensus of the Ummah.

f: 256. How much of one's wealth may be given through a will without the heirs' approval?
b: A person may make a will for up to one-third of his wealth without the approval of the heirs.

f: 257. Why is a will exceeding one-third not valid without heirs' approval?
b: Because the remaining wealth is connected to the rights of the heirs, as the cause of their inheritance has already begun through the person's approaching death and their need for the wealth.

f: 258. What did the Prophet ﷺ say regarding making a will beyond one-third of one's wealth?
b: Regarding Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ رضي الله عنه, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The third, and the third is much."

f: 259. When can a will exceeding one-third become valid?
b: It becomes valid if the heirs approve it after the death of the testator and they are legally competent adults.

f: 260. Is the heirs' approval of an excessive will valid during the testator's lifetime?
b: No. Their approval during his lifetime is not considered because their right only becomes established after his death.

f: 261. If heirs approve an excessive will after the testator dies, can they later withdraw their approval?
b: No. Their right has already been waived after it became established.

f: 262. According to the Ḥanafīs, from whom does the recipient receive ownership when heirs approve a will exceeding one-third?
b: The recipient receives ownership from the original testator, because the heirs' approval only removes the obstacle preventing the will from taking effect.

f: 263. Is a will valid for someone who intentionally or accidentally killed the testator?
b: No. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no will for a killer." This applies whether the killing was intentional or accidental if the person directly caused the death.

f: 264. Why is a killer prevented from receiving a will?
b: Because he hastened something Allah delayed for him, so he is prevented from benefiting through the will just as he is prevented from inheriting.

f: 265. If the heirs approve a will made for the killer, does it become valid?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, yes. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, it does not become valid because the reason for prohibition remains.

f: 266. Is a will valid for one of the testator's heirs?
b: No. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has given every person with a right his right; there is no will for an heir."

f: 267. Why is making a will for an heir prohibited?
b: Because preferring one heir over another may harm family relationships and constitutes injustice in the distribution of wealth.

f: 268. Is the status of being an heir considered at the time of making the will or at death?
b: It is considered at the time of death, because the will only becomes effective after death.

f: 269. Is a gift given by a sick person to an heir treated like a will?
b: Yes. A gift given during terminal illness to an heir is treated like a will and is subject to the same restrictions.

f: 270. Is a sick person's acknowledgement of a debt owed to an heir treated like a will?
b: No. It is the opposite of a will because it is an immediate declaration, so the relevant time is when the acknowledgement is made.

f: 271. Can heirs approve a will made for another heir?
b: Yes. Since the prohibition exists due to their rights, they may waive those rights after the testator's death.

f: 272. If some heirs approve and others reject a will for an heir, what happens?
b: The will is valid only according to the share of those who approved it and invalid according to those who rejected it.

f: 273. Can a Muslim make a will for a non-Muslim?
b: Yes. This is permitted because Allah says that Muslims are not prohibited from being kind and just toward those who do not fight them because of religion.

f: 274. Can a non-Muslim make a will for a Muslim?
b: Yes. A protected non-Muslim (dhimmī) is treated like a Muslim in financial dealings, so gifts and wills between them are permitted.

f: 275. Is a will for people of war (ahl al-ḥarb) valid?
b: No. The will is invalid according to the narration mentioned in al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, based on the verse prohibiting alliance with those who fight Muslims because of religion.

f: 276. When does acceptance of a will occur?
b: Acceptance of a will occurs after the death of the testator.

f: 277. Is acceptance or rejection of a will during the testator's lifetime valid?
b: No. The effect of the will only begins after death, so acceptance or rejection before then has no legal effect.

f: 278. Is it recommended to make a will for the entire one-third of one's wealth?
b: No. It is recommended to make a will for less than one-third.

f: 279. Why is making a will for less than one-third considered better?
b: Because leaving more inheritance for relatives is itself a form of kindness and support toward them, whereas using the full third merely takes one's permitted right.

f: 280. When is leaving a will better than making one?
b: If the heirs are poor and would benefit from inheritance, leaving the wealth to them is better because supporting relatives is a form of charity.

f: 281. When is making a will better than leaving all wealth to heirs?
b: If the heirs are wealthy and do not need the inheritance, making a will for others is better because it becomes charity for those in need.

f: 282. Does the recipient of a will become owner immediately when the will is made?
b: No. Ownership only occurs after the recipient accepts after the testator's death.

f: 283. Why does a will require acceptance unlike inheritance?
b: A will creates new ownership, whereas inheritance is succession from the deceased and therefore transfers automatically without acceptance.

f: 284. What happens if the testator dies and the recipient dies before accepting the will?
b: The bequeathed property enters into the ownership of the recipient's heirs according to an exception based on juristic preference (istiḥsān).

f: 285. If someone dies owing debts that consume all his wealth, is his will executed?
b: No. The debt takes priority over the will because debt is an obligation while the will is a voluntary donation.

f: 286. When can a will be executed despite debts covering all the estate?
b: If the creditors forgive their debts, then the will may be executed within the lawful limit.

f: 287. Is the will of a child valid?
b: No. A child cannot make a valid will because a will is a donation and a child does not have full legal capacity for such transactions.

f: 288. How did al-Shāfiʿī argue for the validity of a child's will?
b: He argued that ʿUmar رضي الله عنه allowed the will of a child close to puberty and that it benefits the child by allowing him to gain reward.

f: 289. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to the evidence of allowing a child's will?
b: They interpret it as referring to someone near adulthood or to instructions regarding funeral arrangements, which are allowed.

f: 290. Is a will made by a mukātab (contracted slave) valid?
b: No, according to the Ḥanafīs, because his wealth is not fully available for voluntary transfer.

f: 291. Is a will valid for an unborn child (fetus)?
b: Yes, if the conditions are met, because the fetus has the capacity to inherit and a will is similar to inheritance in this respect.

f: 292. Under what condition is a will made for a fetus valid?
b: The fetus must have existed at the time of the will, such as being born within less than six months from the time the will was made.

f: 293. Is it valid to make a will excluding the unborn child of a female slave?
b: Yes. If someone says, "I bequeath my female slave except her child," both the will and the exclusion are valid because the child can be separately bequeathed.

f: 294. What is the principle regarding exceptions in contracts and wills?
b: Anything that can be independently transferred through a contract can also be excluded from that contract; anything that cannot be independently transferred cannot be excluded.

f: 295. What is the ruling of a person's actions in his terminal illness, such as freeing a slave, selling with a discount (muḥābāh), or gifting?
b: If a person performs these actions during his terminal illness, they are valid but are counted from one-third of his wealth and compete with other bequests. They are not actual bequests because they are immediate transactions, but they are treated like bequests due to the rights of the heirs.

f: 296. Why are transactions performed during a terminal illness restricted to one-third of the wealth?
b: Because the heirs' rights become attached to the wealth, and the sick person may be suspected of favoring some people over his heirs.

f: 297. What is the difference between a transaction completed during health and one completed during terminal illness?
b: A transaction completed during health is taken from the entire wealth, while one completed during terminal illness is taken only from one-third of the wealth if it involves a voluntary transfer.

f: 298. What happens if a person recovers from an illness after making such a transaction?
b: If the illness is one from which he recovered, the transaction is treated like one made during health because recovery proves that the heirs had no attached right to his wealth.

f: 299. If a sick person sells something at a discounted price and then frees a slave, and the one-third of his wealth is insufficient for both, which takes priority according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The discounted sale (muḥābāh) takes priority if it occurred before the emancipation. If he freed the slave first and then made the discounted sale, both are equal according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله.

f: 300. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, which takes priority when a sick person frees a slave and makes a discounted sale that exceed one-third of his wealth?
b: The emancipation takes priority in both situations, whether it occurred before or after the discounted sale.

f: 301. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله give priority to a previous discounted sale over a later emancipation?
b: Because the discounted sale is considered stronger: it occurs within an exchange contract and is a form of charity in meaning only, while emancipation is charity in both wording and meaning.

f: 302. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad give priority to emancipation?
b: Because emancipation is stronger since it cannot be cancelled by the owner, whereas a discounted sale may potentially be cancelled.

f: 303. If a sick person makes two discounted sales and frees a slave between them, how is the one-third distributed according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The one-third is first divided equally between the two discounted sales because they are equal. Then the share of the later discounted sale is divided between it and the emancipation because the emancipation has priority over it.

f: 304. If a sick person frees a slave, makes a discounted sale, and then frees another slave, how is the one-third divided according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The one-third is first divided between the first emancipation and the discounted sale. Then the share of the first emancipation is divided between it and the second emancipation.

f: 305. What is the ruling if someone bequeaths that a slave should be purchased and freed for one hundred dirhams, but one dirham is lost before execution?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the remaining ninety-nine dirhams are not used to free a slave.

f: 306. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not allow the remaining money to be used for freeing a slave when part of the specified amount is lost?
b: Because the bequest was specifically for freeing a slave purchased with one hundred dirhams. Using a cheaper slave would be carrying out something other than what was specified by the testator.

f: 307. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what happens if part of the money specified for freeing a slave is lost?
b: The remaining amount is still used to free a slave, because the purpose is performing an act of worship as much as possible.

f: 308. Why is a bequest for performing ḥajj different from a bequest to purchase and free a slave?
b: A bequest for ḥajj is a pure act of worship belonging to Allah, so the beneficiary remains the same even if the amount changes. A bequest for freeing a specific slave changes the intended object if the amount changes.

f: 309. If a person leaves two sons, one hundred dirhams, and a slave worth one hundred dirhams, and he had freed the slave during his terminal illness, but the heirs approve it, what happens?
b: The slave does not need to work to compensate for anything because the heirs' approval removes the restriction caused by their rights.

f: 310. If a person bequeaths that his slave should be freed, then the slave commits a crime after the person's death and is handed over as compensation, what happens to the bequest?
b: The bequest becomes invalid because the slave leaves the ownership through the payment of the crime compensation.

f: 311. If the heirs pay compensation for a slave who was bequeathed to be freed, does the emancipation bequest remain valid?
b: Yes. The slave becomes free from the liability of the crime as though he had not committed it, so the bequest can be carried out.

f: 312. If a person bequeaths one-third of his wealth to someone, and both the heir and the beneficiary agree that the deceased freed a slave, but they disagree whether the emancipation occurred during health or terminal illness, whose statement is accepted?
b: The heir's statement is accepted with an oath, because the heir claims that the emancipation occurred during illness and therefore competes with the bequest, while the beneficiary claims that it occurred during health and benefits from a larger inheritance.

f: 313. Why is the heir's statement preferred when there is disagreement about whether an emancipation happened during health or illness?
b: Because emancipation is a new event, and newly occurring events are attributed to the closest possible time. Therefore, the apparent assumption is that it happened during the illness.

f: 314. If the beneficiary proves with evidence that the slave was freed during health, what happens?
b: The emancipation is accepted as having occurred during health, and the beneficiary receives his full right because the emancipation no longer counts against the one-third.

f: 315. If the beneficiary has no evidence but there is remaining one-third after the sick person's emancipation, what happens?
b: The beneficiary receives whatever remains of the one-third after the emancipation because he has no competing claimant over that remainder.

f: 316. If a deceased person leaves a slave, and the slave claims that his master freed him while healthy, while another man claims that the deceased owed him 1000 dirhams and the heir confirms both claims, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the slave becomes obligated to work to pay his value (safāyah).

f: 317. If a deceased person's heir confirms both a claim of a debt and a claim that the deceased freed a slave while healthy, why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say the slave is free without owing anything?
b: They argue that the debt and the healthy-state emancipation appeared together through the heir's confirmation, so they are treated as if both existed simultaneously. Since emancipation during health does not require payment even if the emancipator had debts, the slave is free without liability.

f: 318. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider the debt claim stronger than the claim of emancipation in the case of a deceased person's slave?
b: Because a debt is taken from the entire estate, whereas emancipation during the final illness is treated like a bequest and only applies within the limit of one-third of the estate. The stronger claim overrides the weaker one.

f: 319. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not completely cancel the emancipation of the slave when a debt takes priority?
b: Because emancipation, once established, cannot be completely invalidated. Therefore, its effect is transferred into requiring the slave to pay his value.

f: 320. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله say the debt existed earlier than the emancipation in this case?
b: Because a debt can be traced back to the time of health without preventing such attribution, while emancipation cannot be attributed to health because the debt prevents free emancipation during the final illness.

f: 321. If a deceased person leaves 1000 dirhams, and one person claims a debt of 1000 dirhams while another claims that he had deposited 1000 dirhams with the deceased, which claim is stronger according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the debt claim is stronger.

f: 322. If a deceased person leaves 1000 dirhams, and one person claims a debt while another claims ownership of a deposited item, which claims are equal according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, both claims are equal in strength.

f: 323. When a person makes multiple bequests involving obligations owed to Allah, which obligations are given priority?
b: Obligatory acts are given priority over non-obligatory acts, such as Ḥajj, zakāh, and expiations (kaffārāt).

f: 324. If a person makes several bequests for obligatory acts of worship and the one-third estate is insufficient, how are they prioritized?
b: If the obligations are equal in strength, the obligation mentioned first by the deceased is given priority.

f: 325. Why are obligatory acts prioritized over voluntary acts in fulfilling bequests?
b: Because obligatory acts are more important than voluntary acts, so the more important obligation is fulfilled first.

f: 326. Which obligation does al-Ṭaḥāwī say should be given priority between zakāh and Ḥajj?
b: Al-Ṭaḥāwī says zakāh should be prioritized over Ḥajj because it involves the rights of people.

f: 327. Which obligation does the narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and the view of Muḥammad prioritize between zakāh and Ḥajj?
b: They prioritize Ḥajj because it involves both wealth and physical effort, whereas zakāh only involves wealth.

f: 328. Why are Ḥajj and zakāh prioritized over kaffārāt (expiations)?
b: Because the warnings and emphasis mentioned regarding them are stronger than those mentioned regarding expiations.

f: 329. Why is the kaffārah for killing, ẓihār, and oaths prioritized over zakāt al-fiṭr?
b: Because those kaffārāt are established obligations, while zakāt al-fiṭr is not established in the same way according to this discussion.

f: 330. Why is zakāt al-fiṭr prioritized over udḥiyah (sacrifice) among bequests?
b: Because zakāt al-fiṭr is agreed upon as obligatory through the Qur’an, whereas there is disagreement regarding the obligation of udḥiyah.

f: 331. If a person makes several non-obligatory bequests, how are they prioritized?
b: The non-obligatory bequests are carried out according to the order mentioned by the deceased.

f: 332. How is the one-third portion divided when a deceased person leaves multiple bequests, including acts of worship for Allah and bequests for people?
b: The one-third is divided among all the bequests. The portion assigned to acts of worship is spent according to the order of priority among those acts.

f: 333. Why are all charitable bequests for Allah not treated as one single bequest?
b: Because each act of worship is independently intended and has its own purpose, just as different human bequests remain separate.

f: 334. If someone makes a bequest that his obligatory Ḥajj should be performed after his death, from where should the person performing Ḥajj travel according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: A person should perform Ḥajj from the deceased's hometown.

f: 335. Why should the person performing a deceased person's obligatory Ḥajj travel from the deceased's hometown?
b: Because the obligation of Ḥajj was originally due from that location, so the required expenses are calculated from there.

f: 336. Why is the person performing a deceased person's obligatory Ḥajj instructed to ride rather than walk?
b: Because the deceased was not obligated to perform the journey walking, so the bequest applies according to the manner originally required.

f: 337. If the bequest for performing obligatory Ḥajj is insufficient to cover travel expenses from the deceased's hometown, from where should the Ḥajj be performed?
b: It should be performed from the furthest place that the available money allows.

f: 338. Why is an insufficient bequest for obligatory Ḥajj still carried out rather than cancelled completely?
b: Because the deceased intended that the bequest be fulfilled, so it should be executed as much as possible rather than abandoned entirely.

f: 339. If someone leaves his hometown intending to perform Ḥajj, dies on the journey, and had instructed that Ḥajj be performed on his behalf, where should the substitute pilgrim begin according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the substitute pilgrim should begin from the deceased's hometown.

f: 340. If someone leaves his hometown intending to perform Ḥajj, dies on the journey, and had instructed that Ḥajj be performed on his behalf, where should the substitute pilgrim begin according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, the substitute pilgrim should begin from the place where the deceased died.

f: 341. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say the substitute pilgrim begins from where the deceased died during a Ḥajj journey?
b: Because the deceased had already begun a journey of worship and earned the reward for the distance travelled, so the remaining journey begins from that point.

f: 342. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله disagree and require the substitute pilgrim to begin from the hometown?
b: Because the bequest refers to performing the obligation of Ḥajj in the same manner it was originally required, which was from the deceased's hometown.

f: 343. How does this ruling differ from someone who dies while travelling for trade?
b: Since trade travel is not itself an act of worship, a substitute would begin the journey from the person's hometown rather than the place where he died.

f: 344. What is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله if someone makes a bequest to his "neighbors" (جيران)?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the bequest applies only to those whose houses are directly adjacent (the immediate neighbors).

f: 345. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding the meaning of "neighbors" in a bequest?
b: They hold that it includes both immediate neighbors and those living in the same neighborhood who share the mosque of that area.

f: 346. What is the reasoning of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله that "neighbors" means only those directly adjacent?
b: Because the word neighbor comes from proximity and actual adjacency. This is also the type of neighborhood recognized in rights such as pre-emption (shufʿah).

f: 347. What is the reasoning of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad that neighbors include the wider neighborhood?
b: Because all of them are commonly called neighbors in custom, and the purpose of the bequest is kindness to neighbors, which applies to both the adjacent neighbor and others who share the same community.

f: 348. What condition did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad add for including wider neighbors in a bequest?
b: There must be social connection and mixing, which they considered present when they share the same neighborhood mosque.

f: 349. What is the ruling on whether a neighbor in a bequest includes males and females, owners and renters, Muslims and non-Muslims?
b: All are included because the term "neighbor" applies generally to them.

f: 350. Is a slave who lives in the neighborhood included in a bequest to neighbors according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Yes, because the wording is general and includes him.

f: 351. Is a slave who lives in the neighborhood included in a bequest to neighbors according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: No, because the bequest would effectively be to his master, and the master is not the resident neighbor.

f: 352. Who receives a bequest made to "my in-laws" (aṣhār / أصهار) according to the preferred interpretation?
b: It refers to every person who is a maḥram relative of the wife of the testator.

f: 353. What evidence is mentioned for interpreting "in-laws" as the wife's maḥram relatives?
b: The report that the Prophet ﷺ freed all slaves who were his wife's maḥram relatives after marrying Ṣafiyyah رضي الله عنها as an honor to her.

f: 354. Does a bequest to one's in-laws include the maḥram relatives of one's father's wife or son's wife?
b: Yes, because they are also considered in-laws.

f: 355. When does a wife's relative qualify as an in-law for a bequest?
b: He qualifies if the marriage still exists at the time of the testator's death or if the wife is in a revocable divorce waiting period.

f: 356. Does a wife's relative receive a bequest if she is in the waiting period of an irrevocable divorce when the testator dies?
b: No, because the marital relationship that created the in-law relationship has ended.

f: 357. Who receives a bequest made to "aṭhān" (akhṭān / أختان)?
b: It applies to the husbands of the testator's maḥram female relatives and, according to the broader usage, the maḥram relatives of spouses.

f: 358. What is the difference between the terms "aṣhār" and "akhṭān" in bequests?
b: Aṣhār refers mainly to relatives connected through the wife, while akhṭān refers to relatives connected through female relatives and their husbands.

f: 359. Does a bequest to akhṭān include free people and slaves, close and distant relatives?
b: Yes, because the wording includes all of them.

f: 360. What is the ruling of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding a bequest to "relatives" (aqārib / أقارب)?
b: It goes to the closest maḥram relatives of the testator, excluding parents and children, and it applies to two or more people.

f: 361. What is the view of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding a bequest to relatives?
b: They hold that it applies to everyone connected to the furthest ancestor who entered Islam (according to their detailed discussion).

f: 362. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله exclude parents and children from a bequest to relatives?
b: Because the purpose is repairing neglect in maintaining family ties, and parents and children are not normally called "relatives" in this sense; their connection is direct rather than through another person.

f: 363. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad include wider descendants of an ancestor in the term relatives?
b: Because the word relative comes from kinship, so anyone possessing kinship should be included.

f: 364. What is the Shāfiʿī position regarding a bequest to relatives?
b: According to the Shāfiʿī view mentioned, it refers to the closest father (the nearest ancestor).

f: 365. If someone bequeaths to his relatives and he has two paternal uncles and two maternal uncles, who receives it according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The paternal uncles receive it because they are closer relatives.

f: 366. If someone bequeaths to his relatives and has two paternal uncles and two maternal uncles, what is the view of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: They divide it among all four relatives equally because they do not prioritize closeness.

f: 367. If someone bequeaths to relatives and leaves one paternal uncle and two maternal uncles, how is the bequest divided according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The paternal uncle receives half and the two maternal uncles share the other half.

f: 368. Why does a single paternal uncle not receive the entire bequest in the case of one paternal uncle and two maternal uncles?
b: Because the word implies a group, and the minimum group in bequests is two people.

f: 369. If someone says "my relative" (dhū qarābatī) in a bequest and has only one paternal uncle, who receives the bequest?
b: The paternal uncle receives the entire bequest because the wording refers to an individual.

f: 370. If someone bequeaths to relatives and leaves a paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt, who receives the bequest?
b: The paternal uncle and paternal aunt receive it equally because their relationship is stronger.

f: 371. Do non-inheriting relatives such as a paternal aunt receive a bequest made to relatives?
b: Yes, because eligibility for the bequest is based on being a maḥram relative, not inheritance.

f: 372. What happens if a person has no maḥram relatives when he makes a bequest to relatives?
b: The bequest becomes invalid because the description required for receiving it does not exist.

f: 373. What is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله if someone bequeaths to "the family of so-and-so" (ahl fulān)?
b: It refers to the person's wife.

f: 374. What is the reasoning of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله that "family" means wife?
b: Because this is the literal meaning of the word ahl, as in the Qur'anic usage "he travelled with his family" referring to his wife.

f: 375. What is the view of the other scholars regarding a bequest to "the family of so-and-so"?
b: They interpret it according to common usage as everyone whom the person supports and whose expenses he covers.

f: 376. What is the ruling of a bequest to "the clan/family of so-and-so" (āl fulān)?
b: It applies to the people of his household and lineage.

f: 377. Does a bequest to "the people of the household of so-and-so" include his father and grandfather?
b: Yes, because the father is the foundation of the household.

f: 378. What does a bequest to "his lineage" refer to?
b: It refers to those connected through his fathers, because lineage is traced through the paternal line.

f: 379. Does lineage in a bequest include relatives from the mother's side?
b: No, because lineage is connected through fathers, while general kinship includes both sides.

f: 380. If someone bequeaths to the orphans, blind people, chronically ill, or widows of a specific tribe that can be counted, who receives it?
b: All members of that group receive it, whether rich or poor, male or female.

f: 381. If someone bequeaths to the orphans, blind people, chronically ill, or widows of a tribe that cannot be counted, who receives it?
b: Only the poor among them receive it because these descriptions imply need.

f: 382. Why does a bequest to uncountable orphans, blind people, chronically ill people, or widows go only to the poor?
b: Because the purpose of such a bequest is charity and relieving hardship.

f: 383. Why does a bequest to uncountable young men of a tribe become invalid?
b: Because youth does not imply need, and the group is too large and undefined for ownership to be established.

f: 384. Why does a bequest to uncountable unmarried women (ayāmā) become invalid?
b: Because the term does not indicate poverty, and the recipients cannot be specified due to excessive uncertainty.

f: 385. How many poor people must receive a bequest made to "the poor and needy"?
b: At least two people, because the plural minimum in bequests is two.

f: 386. Does the phrase "sons of so-and-so" (banū fulān) include females according to Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله earlier opinion?
b: Yes, because masculine plurals can include females.

f: 387. What was Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله later opinion regarding "sons of so-and-so"?
b: It refers only to males because the literal meaning of the word is males, while including females would be metaphorical.

f: 388. Why does "sons of so-and-so" include females when it refers to a tribe or clan?
b: Because in that usage it refers to affiliation and lineage, not individual males, similar to "children of Adam عليه السلام."

f: 389. Who is included in a tribal designation such as "Banū so-and-so"?
b: Both males and females, as well as affiliated people such as freed slaves and allies.

f: 390. What is the ruling if someone makes a bequest to the children of a particular person ("ولد فلان")?
b: The bequest is divided among them, and males and females receive equal shares because the term "children" includes all of them equally.

f: 391. What is the ruling if someone makes a bequest to the heirs of a particular person ("ورثة فلان")?
b: The bequest is divided among them with the male receiving the share of two females, because mentioning the term "heirs" indicates the intention of preference as in inheritance.

f: 392. What is the ruling if a person makes a bequest to his mawālī (clients/freedmen), while he has both people he freed and people who freed him?
b: The bequest is invalid because the term "mawālī" refers to two different relationships: the one who grants freedom and the one who receives freedom, making the term ambiguous in a context of granting ownership.

f: 393. Why did al-Shāfiʿī consider a bequest to all types of mawālī valid?
b: Because each group can be called a mawla, so he considered the word inclusive like the word "brothers."

f: 394. Why did the Hanafis say that a bequest to both types of mawālī is invalid?
b: Because the relationships are different: one is the mawla of blessing (the one who freed), while the other is the one upon whom the blessing was bestowed (the freed person), so one term cannot include both in a transfer of ownership.

f: 395. Does the term "mawālī" include those whom the testator freed during his lifetime?
b: Yes, it includes those whom he freed while healthy or during his final illness, because their status as mawālī existed before death.

f: 396. Are a mudabbar slave or an umm walad included in a bequest to the testator's mawālī?
b: No, because their freedom only takes effect after death, while the bequest refers to the state existing before death.

f: 397. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, do mudabbar slaves and umm walads enter into the category of mawālī?
b: Yes, according to one narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, because the cause of their entitlement (the promise of freedom) is already established.

f: 398. Is a slave included among the mawālī if his master said: "If I do not beat you, you are free"?
b: Yes, because his freedom becomes established immediately before death when the condition is fulfilled.

f: 399. If a person has freedmen, their descendants, and mawālī by contractual alliance (walāʾ al-muwālāh), who is included in a bequest to his mawālī according to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله?
b: Those whom he personally freed and their descendants are included, but mawālī by alliance are not included because the relationship differs.

f: 400. Why does Muhammad exclude mawālī by alliance from a bequest to mawālī?
b: Because the basis of the relationship differs: freedmen are connected through the favor of emancipation, while alliance is based on a contractual obligation.

f: 401. Are the descendants of a person's freedmen included in a bequest to his mawālī?
b: Yes, because they are attributed to him through the emancipation he performed.

f: 402. Why are the descendants of a person's mawālī not included in a bequest to his mawālī?
b: Because they are truly the mawālī of another person, not of the testator himself.

f: 403. If a person has one freedman and also has mawālī of mawālī, how is a bequest to his mawālī divided?
b: Half goes to his freedman, and the other half returns to the heirs because the literal meaning and metaphorical meaning cannot both be combined.

f: 404. Are people freed by the testator's father or son included in a bequest to the testator's mawālī?
b: No, because they are not his mawālī either literally or metaphorically.

f: 405. What is the ruling on making a bequest of the usufruct of a slave or the use of a house?
b: It is valid, whether for a specified number of years or permanently, because benefits can be owned and transferred.

f: 406. Why is a bequest of usufruct (such as service of a slave or residence in a house) valid after death?
b: Because benefits may be owned during life through compensation or donation, so they may also be transferred after death due to people's needs.

f: 407. What is the ownership status of the slave or house when its benefit has been bequeathed to someone?
b: The physical property remains held under the ownership of the estate, while the beneficiary owns the right to use its benefits.

f: 408. Is a bequest of the produce or income of a slave or house valid?
b: Yes, because the income is a substitute for the benefit and takes the same ruling.

f: 409. What happens if the value of the slave itself falls within one-third of the estate when the testator bequeaths the slave's service?
b: The slave is handed over to the beneficiary so that he may use the slave's service.

f: 410. What happens if the testator has no other property besides the slave whose service he bequeathed?
b: The heirs receive the slave's service for two days, and the beneficiary receives it for one day, because the beneficiary has one-third and the heirs have two-thirds.

f: 411. Why is a slave divided by alternating days instead of physically divided when only his service is bequeathed?
b: Because a slave cannot be divided into parts, so alternating possession (muhāyaʾah) is used to fulfill both parties' rights.

f: 412. How is a house handled if its use is bequeathed and the house does not fit within one-third of the estate?
b: The house itself is divided into three portions for use because physical division is possible and is more equitable than alternating time.

f: 413. Can heirs sell the portion of the house they possess when another person has been granted residence rights in the whole house through a bequest?
b: No, according to the apparent Hanafi position, because the beneficiary's right may extend to the entire house if additional estate assets appear or if circumstances change.

f: 414. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله allow heirs to sell their portion of the house in this case?
b: Because he viewed their portion as their complete ownership, unaffected by the beneficiary's right.

f: 415. What happens if the person who was granted lifetime use of a slave or house dies?
b: The right returns to the heirs of the testator because the testator granted the benefit specifically to that person, not to his heirs.

f: 416. What happens if the beneficiary of a service or residence bequest dies before the testator?
b: The bequest becomes invalid because the right was attached to the testator's death and the beneficiary no longer exists at that time.

f: 417. If someone is given the income of a slave or house by bequest, may he personally use the slave or live in the house instead of taking the income?
b: According to the stronger view, no, because the bequest is for financial income, not merely for use of the benefit.

f: 418. Why is personally using the slave or house not considered the same as receiving its income?
b: Because income is money, while personal use is a different benefit, and they differ in the rights of the heirs.

f: 419. May a person who receives a bequest of a slave's service or residence in a house rent it out?
b: No, because the bequest grants personal use, not the right to transfer the benefit to another person.

f: 420. Can a person who receives a bequest of the service of a slave rent out that slave's service to another person according to the Hanafi scholars?
b: No. According to the Hanafis, the recipient of a bequeathed service cannot rent out the slave or transfer the service to another person.

f: 421. Why did al-Shāfiʿī allow a person who received a bequest of a slave's service to rent out that service?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī considered the recipient to own the benefit itself, so he may transfer it to another person with or without compensation, just like physical property.

f: 422. Why do the Hanafis reject al-Shāfiʿī's view that a person who receives a bequest of service owns the benefit absolutely?
b: The Hanafis argue that a bequest is ownership without compensation that begins after death, so the recipient cannot transfer the benefit in a way stronger than the ownership he received.

f: 423. What comparison do the Hanafis make between a person who receives a bequest of service and a borrower regarding renting out the benefit?
b: They compare it to a borrower who cannot rent out what he borrowed, because the borrower only received permission to use it, not complete ownership of the benefit.

f: 424. Why do the Hanafis say that ownership without compensation is weaker than ownership through compensation?
b: Because a compensated ownership gives a stronger right, while a gift-based ownership does not allow a person to grant others a stronger right than what he possesses.

f: 425. Why do the Hanafis not consider a benefit (manfaʿah) to be independent wealth?
b: Because benefits are not independent wealth according to the Hanafi school; they become financially recognized through ownership of the object or through a compensatory contract.

f: 426. Who is allowed to transfer a benefit as a financial transaction according to the Hanafi explanation?
b: The owner of the physical object or someone who acquired the benefit through a compensatory contract, because they possess the benefit in a financially recognized manner.

f: 427. Why can a person who received a bequest of a benefit not convert that benefit into a paid transaction?
b: Because he would be transferring the benefit as something more valuable and stronger than the type of ownership he originally received.

f: 428. Can a person who received a bequest of a slave's service remove that slave from Kūfah?
b: No, unless the recipient and his family live outside Kūfah and he takes the slave there to serve them, provided the slave is within the permitted one-third of the estate.

f: 429. Why can a person who received a bequest of a slave's service normally not remove the slave from Kūfah?
b: Because the bequest is interpreted according to the testator's intended purpose, which is assumed to be service in the city where the recipient lives without causing hardship.

f: 430. Why may a person who received a bequest of a slave's service take the slave outside Kūfah if the recipient's family lives elsewhere?
b: Because the purpose of the bequest is understood to be that the slave serves the recipient and his household where they reside.

f: 431. Is a bequest of the income (ghallah) of a slave or house valid according to the Hanafis?
b: Yes. A bequest of income is valid because income is a substitute for the benefit and follows the ruling of the benefit.

f: 432. Why is a bequest of income considered even stronger than a bequest of a benefit according to the Hanafis?
b: Because income is actual physical wealth, such as money, while a benefit itself is not considered independent wealth.

f: 433. If a person bequeaths the income of his slave and leaves no other wealth, what portion of that income does the beneficiary receive?
b: The beneficiary receives one-third of the income of that year because income is divisible wealth.

f: 434. Can a person who was bequeathed the income of a house demand that the house itself be divided so that he can use one-third of the house?
b: No. His right is only in the income of the house, not ownership of the house itself.

f: 435. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله allow a person who received a bequest of house income to request division of the house?
b: Because he considered the beneficiary similar to a partner with the heirs, and a partner may request division.

f: 436. Why does the Hanafi position not allow a person who received a bequest of house income to divide the house?
b: Because the right to request division belongs to someone whose ownership is attached to the property itself, whereas the beneficiary only owns the income.

f: 437. If a person bequeaths the service of a slave to one person and the ownership of the slave to another person, and the value fits within one-third of the estate, who receives each right?
b: The person given ownership receives the slave itself, and the person given service receives the right to use the slave.

f: 438. Why does a person who receives ownership of a slave not prevent another person from receiving the slave's service through a separate bequest?
b: Because the testator assigned two different rights: ownership of the slave to one person and the benefit of service to another.

f: 439. If a person bequeaths a slave woman to one person and the child in her womb to another person, what is the ruling if the bequests fit within one-third of the estate?
b: Both bequests are valid: the first person receives the slave woman and the second person receives the child.

f: 440. If a person bequeaths a ring to one person and the gemstone inside the ring to another person, who receives each part according to the Hanafi position?
b: The first person receives the ring and the second person receives the gemstone.

f: 441. If a person says, "This container belongs to Zayd and the dates inside it belong to ʿAmr," who receives the container and dates?
b: Zayd receives the container and ʿAmr receives the dates.

f: 442. Why does the person who receives a container or ring not automatically receive its contents in these bequest cases?
b: Because the testator separately assigned ownership of the contents to another person.

f: 443. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, if a person first bequeaths a slave woman to someone and later separately bequeaths her child to someone else, how are the bequests understood?
b: The later statement clarifies that the first person was intended to receive only the slave woman, while the second person receives the child.

f: 444. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider a separate later statement to clarify an earlier bequest?
b: Because a bequest is not binding during the testator's lifetime, so a later explanation has the same effect as a connected explanation.

f: 445. According to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله, if a person separately bequeaths a slave woman and her child to different people, how is the child divided?
b: The child is divided equally between the two beneficiaries.

f: 446. Why does Muhammad divide the child or gemstone between two beneficiaries in these bequest cases?
b: Because the original term includes the attached part, so the child or gemstone is included in both bequests.

f: 447. Why is a second bequest not automatically considered a cancellation of the first bequest according to Imam Muhammad رحمه الله?
b: Because the second statement may simply be another independent bequest rather than a revocation.

f: 448. Why is the bequest of a slave's service different from the bequest of a slave woman and her child?
b: Because the word "slave woman" includes what is attached to her, while ownership of the slave itself does not include the service linguistically.

f: 449. If a person bequeaths the fruit of his orchard and dies while fruit already exists on the trees, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: The beneficiary receives only the fruit that already exists at the time of death.

f: 450. If a person says, "I bequeath the fruit of my orchard to this person forever," what does the beneficiary receive?
b: The beneficiary receives the existing fruit and future fruit produced during his lifetime.

f: 451. If a person bequeaths the produce (ghallah) of his orchard to someone, what does the beneficiary receive?
b: The beneficiary receives the existing produce and future produce that comes from the orchard.

f: 452. Why does the word "fruit" normally only refer to existing fruit in a bequest?
b: Because common usage understands "fruit" as something currently present, not future harvests.

f: 453. Why does adding the phrase "forever" to a bequest of fruit make future fruit included?
b: Because the word "forever" indicates continuation, requiring the inclusion of future fruit.

f: 454. Why does the word "produce/income" (ghallah) include future harvests without needing the word "forever"?
b: Because common usage applies "income" to recurring things that continue to appear, whether present or future.

f: 455. If someone makes a bequest to a person of the wool of his sheep forever, or their offspring, or their milk, what does the recipient receive when the testator dies?
b: The recipient receives the offspring that are in the wombs, the milk that is in the udders, and the wool on the backs of the sheep at the time of the testator’s death, whether or not the word “forever” was mentioned.

f: 456. Why does a bequest of sheep wool, offspring, or milk only include what exists at the time of the testator’s death?
b: Because a bequest becomes effective upon death, so the existence of the bequeathed items is considered at that time.

f: 457. Why can existing wool, milk, and offspring be included in a bequest even though they were not originally present as separate property?
b: Because existing wool, milk, and offspring can be acquired through contracts; wool and milk through sale and offspring through certain transactions, so they can also be acquired through a bequest.

f: 458. Why are future unborn offspring, future milk, and future wool not included in a bequest unless they exist at death?
b: Because ownership of non-existent things is generally not valid, and unlike fruits and produce, these things do not have a legal basis allowing contracts to apply to their future existence.

f: 459. Why are future fruits and crops treated differently from future animal offspring in bequests?
b: Because Islamic law allows contracts involving future fruits and produce, such as agricultural partnerships and leases, so allowing them in bequests is even more appropriate because the rules of bequests are broader.

f: 460. What is the ruling if a Jewish or Christian person builds a synagogue or church during their lifetime and dies afterwards?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, it becomes inheritance because it has the ruling of a waqf, and a waqf is inheritable according to him. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, it is invalid because it is an act of disobedience.

f: 461. If a Jewish or Christian person bequeaths that their house should be made into a synagogue or church for specific named people, what is the ruling?
b: The bequest is valid from one-third of the estate.

f: 462. Why is a bequest by a dhimmī to build a synagogue or church for specific people valid?
b: Because a bequest contains both the meaning of appointing a successor and the meaning of transferring ownership, and the person has authority over their property, so it can be validated through these aspects.

f: 463. What is the ruling if a Jewish or Christian person bequeaths their house to become a synagogue or church for unspecified people?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the bequest is valid. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, it is invalid.

f: 464. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad consider a bequest to build an unspecified synagogue or church invalid?
b: Because it is actually an act of disobedience, and carrying out such a bequest would establish and support disobedience.

f: 465. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow a dhimmī’s bequest to build an unspecified synagogue or church?
b: Because it is considered an act of worship according to their belief, and Muslims are commanded to leave them according to their religious practices.

f: 466. What is the difference between building a synagogue or church during life and bequeathing that one should be built after death according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
