f: 256. Why does a dhimmī pay half of a tenth when passing by the ʿāshir?
b: Because it is double the amount collected from Muslims.

f: 257. Why does a ḥarbī pay one tenth when passing by the ʿāshir?
b: Because it is taken as a reciprocal charge for protection.

f: 258. If a ḥarbī passes by the ʿāshir with fifty dirhams, is anything taken from him?
b: No, unless they take an equivalent amount from Muslim merchants in his territory.

f: 259. Why is a small amount not taken from a ḥarbī merchant?
b: Because small amounts are normally exempt, and such wealth does not require protection.

f: 260. If a ḥarbī merchant passes with two hundred dirhams and it is unknown how much they take from Muslims, what is taken from him?
b: One tenth is taken.

f: 261. What was the statement of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه regarding taking from ḥarbīs when their policy is unknown?
b: "If you are uncertain, then take one tenth."

f: 262. If it is known that ḥarbīs take one quarter of a tenth from Muslim merchants, how much is taken from their merchants?
b: The same amount, one quarter of a tenth.

f: 263. If ḥarbīs take half of a tenth from Muslims, how much is taken from their merchants?
b: Half of a tenth.

f: 264. If ḥarbīs take all the wealth of Muslim merchants, do Muslims take all the wealth of their merchants in return?
b: No, because that would be treachery.

f: 265. If ḥarbīs take nothing from Muslim merchants, what do Muslims take from their merchants?
b: Nothing, to encourage them to stop taking from Muslim merchants and because Muslims uphold noble conduct.

f: 266. If a ḥarbī passes by the ʿāshir and pays one tenth, then passes again later, is another tenth taken immediately?
b: No, another tenth is not taken until a full year has passed.

f: 267. Why is a second payment not taken from the same ḥarbī until a year passes?
b: Because taking it each time would completely consume his wealth, while protection is the reason for the payment.

f: 268. If a ḥarbī pays the tenth, returns to his land, and leaves again the same day, is another tenth taken?
b: Yes, because he has received a new guarantee of safety.

f: 269. If a dhimmī passes by the ʿāshir carrying wine and pigs, what is taken from him?
b: The value of the wine is charged, but nothing is taken for the pig.

f: 270. Why is the value of wine charged but not the value of pigs?
b: Because wine has a recognized value as a fungible item, while pigs are not protected property in this context.

f: 271. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding wine and pigs carried by a dhimmī?
b: He said neither should be charged because they have no value.

f: 272. What was Zufar's opinion regarding wine and pigs carried by a dhimmī?
b: He said both should be charged because both have monetary value.

f: 273. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding wine and pigs carried together?
b: He charged for both when they are together, considering the pig secondary to the wine.

f: 274. Why does the Hanafi school consider wine protected property but not pigs?
b: Because Muslims protect their own wine if intended for lawful transformation into vinegar, but they do not protect pigs and instead must remove them.

f: 275. If a child from Banū Taghlib passes by the ʿāshir with wealth, is anything taken from him?
b: No, nothing is taken from the child.

f: 276. If a woman from Banū Taghlib passes by the ʿāshir with wealth, what is taken from her?
b: The same amount taken from the men.

f: 277. If someone passes the ʿāshir with 100 dirhams and says he has another 100 dirhams at home that completed a year, is zakāt taken from the 100 dirhams he carries?
b: No, because the carried amount alone is below the niṣāb.

f: 278. Why is zakāt not taken from wealth kept at home when someone passes the ʿāshir?
b: Because the ʿāshir's protection applies only to the wealth that passes under his authority.

f: 279. If someone passes the ʿāshir with 200 dirhams belonging to another person as merchandise, is the tenth taken?
b: No.

f: 280. Why is zakāt not taken from merchandise carried by someone else?
b: Because the person carrying it has no permission to pay its zakāt.

f: 281. Does the same ruling apply to wealth belonging to a muḍārabah partnership?
b: Yes, the same principle applies when the muḍārib passes with the partnership wealth.

f: 282. What was Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله first opinion regarding a muḍārabah (profit-sharing) partnership passing by the ʿāshir with wealth?
b: He initially held that the wealth should be charged the tenth because of the strength of the muḍārib’s right over the wealth.

f: 283. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله initially consider the muḍārib similar to an owner?
b: Because the owner of the capital could not prevent him from trading with the wealth after it had become trade goods, so he was treated like an owner.

f: 284. What was Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله later and final opinion regarding a muḍārib passing by the ʿāshir?
b: He returned to the view that no tenth is taken, which is also the view of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad.

f: 285. Why is no tenth taken from the wealth of a muḍārabah according to the final Hanafi position?
b: Because the muḍārib is not the owner and is not the owner’s representative in paying zakāt.

f: 286. When is wealth from a muḍārabah charged zakāt when passing by the ʿāshir?
b: If the muḍārib’s share of the profit reaches a complete niṣāb, then zakāt is taken from that share because he owns it.

f: 287. If an authorized slave (ʿabd مأذون) passes by the ʿāshir with two hundred dirhams and has no debt, is the wealth charged?
b: Yes, the tenth is taken from it.

f: 288. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله uncertainty regarding the ruling of an authorized slave passing by the ʿāshir?
b: He was unsure whether Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله had retracted from his earlier opinion regarding this issue.

f: 289. According to the analogy of Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله second opinion on muḍārabah, should wealth held by an authorized slave be charged?
b: According to that analogy, it should not be charged because ownership belongs to the master.

f: 290. Why is an authorized slave compared to a muḍārib regarding wealth passing by the ʿāshir?
b: Because both have control over wealth that they do not fully own.

f: 291. What is the difference between an authorized slave and a muḍārib regarding responsibility for the wealth?
b: The slave acts for himself and does not return liability to his master, whereas the muḍārib acts as an agent and liability returns to the owner of the capital.

f: 292. Why is the muḍārib not treated exactly like the authorized slave?
b: Because the muḍārib acts through representation of the owner, while the slave acts independently for himself.

f: 293. If the master of an authorized slave is accompanying him when he passes by the ʿāshir, is the wealth charged?
b: Yes, because ownership belongs to the master.

f: 294. When is the wealth of an authorized slave not charged when passing by the ʿāshir?
b: When the slave has a debt covering his wealth, because ownership is either absent or restricted.

f: 295. If someone passes by the ʿāshir of the Khawārij in land they control and pays the tenth, does he pay again to the legitimate Muslim authority?
b: Yes, he pays again.

f: 296. What does it mean when someone passes by the ʿāshir of the Khawārij and pays the tenth again?
b: It refers to passing by the ʿāshir of the legitimate authorities, because the person himself was responsible for passing by the wrong collector.

f: 297. What is the ruling on gold, silver, iron, lead, or copper extracted from a mine located in a kharāj or ʿushr land?
b: According to the Hanafi school, one fifth (khums) is due on it.

f: 298. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding minerals extracted from the earth?
b: He held that there is nothing due on them because they are permissible resources like hunting, except gold and silver where zakāt applies.

f: 299. Why does al-Shāfiʿī not require a khums on minerals?
b: Because the person merely obtains something permissible that was not previously possessed by another person.

f: 300. What evidence do the Hanafis use for requiring khums on minerals?
b: The statement of the Prophet ﷺ: “And in rikāz is one fifth.”

f: 301. Why do the Hanafis include minerals under the term rikāz?
b: Because rikāz comes from the meaning of something embedded and fixed in the earth, which applies to minerals.

f: 302. Why do the Hanafis consider minerals similar to war booty?
b: Because they were previously in the possession of non-Muslims and Muslims acquired them through dominance, like spoils of war.

f: 303. Why is hunting different from minerals regarding khums?
b: Because hunting was not previously possessed by anyone, whereas minerals were considered part of the wealth held by previous nations.

f: 304. If someone finds a mineral in his own house, is there khums according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, there is no khums.

f: 305. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding a mineral found in one’s own house?
b: They held that khums is due.

f: 306. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not require khums for a mineral found in one’s house?
b: Because it is part of the earth itself, and other parts of the earth do not require khums.

f: 307. Why is a buried treasure different from a mineral found in the earth?
b: Because the treasure is not naturally part of the earth; it is something stored within it.

f: 308. If someone finds a mineral in his own land, what are the two narrations from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: One narration says khums is due, while another follows the ruling of the house and says it is not due.

f: 309. Why does one narration distinguish between a house and land regarding minerals?
b: Because a house is acquired free of such obligations, whereas land can carry obligations like ʿushr and kharāj.

f: 310. What is the ruling if someone finds rikāz (buried treasure)?
b: Khums is due according to the Hanafis.

f: 311. Why does rikāz include buried treasure?
b: Because the word rikāz refers to something fixed and hidden within the earth.

f: 312. If buried treasure has Islamic markings, such as the testimony of faith, what is its ruling?
b: It is treated like lost property (luqaṭah).

f: 313. If buried treasure has pre-Islamic markings, such as idols or pagan symbols, what is its ruling?
b: Khums is due on it in all cases.

f: 314. If someone finds pre-Islamic treasure in public land, who receives the remaining four-fifths after khums?
b: The finder receives the remaining four-fifths because he completed the possession of it.

f: 315. Why does the finder receive the remaining four-fifths of treasure found in public land?
b: Because no one else had knowledge or possession of it, so he alone acquired it.

f: 316. If someone finds pre-Islamic treasure in privately owned land, who receives it according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: The finder receives it because complete possession occurred through his discovery.

f: 317. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, who owns buried treasure found in privately owned land?
b: The person who originally received ownership of that land from the Muslim ruler at the time of conquest (the mukhaṭṭaṭ lahū).

f: 318. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad give buried treasure to the original land owner?
b: Because his previous ownership extends to what is hidden beneath the surface.

f: 319. If a person finds a pearl inside a fish he caught, who owns the pearl?
b: The person who caught the fish owns the pearl.

f: 320. Why does a pearl found inside a fish belong to the finder?
b: Because the pearl was only stored inside the fish and was not part of its essential body.

f: 321. If the original owner of land containing treasure is unknown, where is the treasure given?
b: It is given to the last known Muslim owner according to the scholars.

f: 322. If it is unclear whether treasure is Islamic or pre-Islamic, what is the default ruling?
b: According to the apparent Hanafi position, it is treated as pre-Islamic.

f: 323. What was another view regarding unidentified treasure in later times?
b: Some held that it should be treated as Islamic because too much time has passed.

f: 324. If a person enters enemy territory with a guarantee of safety and finds treasure inside someone’s house, what should he do?
b: He must return it to them.

f: 325. Why must treasure found inside an enemy’s house be returned when entering under a guarantee of safety?
b: Because the property inside their houses is considered under their possession, and taking it would be treachery.

f: 326. If someone finds treasure in open wilderness in enemy territory while under a guarantee of safety, who owns it?
b: The finder owns it.

f: 327. Why can the finder keep treasure found in the wilderness of enemy territory?
b: Because it is not under anyone’s specific possession, so taking it is not considered betrayal.

f: 328. Is khums due on turquoise stones found in mountains?
b: No, there is no khums on turquoise.

f: 329. What evidence is used that there is no khums on stones like turquoise?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “There is no khums on stones.”

f: 330. Is khums due on mercury according to Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله later opinion?
b: Yes, khums is due according to his later opinion and the opinion of Muḥammad.

f: 331. Is khums due on pearls and amber according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: No, khums is not due on them.

f: 332. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion regarding pearls and amber found from the sea?
b: He held that khums is due on them and on all valuable ornaments extracted from the sea.

f: 333. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad not require khums on pearls and amber?
b: Because the bottom of the sea was not conquered, so what is extracted from it is not considered war booty.

f: 334. What is the ruling of valuable goods found as rikāz in ownerless land?
b: They belong to the finder and khums is due on them.

f: 335. Why are valuable goods found as rikāz treated like gold and silver?
b: Because they are considered booty obtained from hidden wealth.

f: 336. What was Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله opinion regarding the amount of land produce subject to ʿushr (one-tenth)?
b: He held that both a small and large amount of produce from the land is subject to ʿushr, whether irrigated naturally by flowing water or by rain.

f: 337. Which types of produce did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله exclude from ʿushr?
b: Firewood, reeds, and grass.

f: 338. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding ʿushr on agricultural produce?
b: They held that ʿushr is only obligatory on produce that has a lasting fruit when it reaches five awsuq.

f: 339. What is an awsuq (plural of wasq)?
b: A wasq is sixty ṣāʿ according to the ṣāʿ of the Prophet ﷺ.

f: 340. What was the first disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and his two companions regarding agricultural zakāt?
b: Whether reaching the niṣāb (minimum amount) is a condition for ʿushr.

f: 341. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for requiring a niṣāb?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “There is no charity on less than five awsuq.”

f: 342. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad require a niṣāb for crops?
b: Because it is a charity, and charity requires the presence of wealth indicating sufficiency.

f: 343. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to reject the condition of niṣāb for crops?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “Whatever the earth produces, then upon it is one tenth,” without distinction.

f: 344. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله interpret the narration about five awsuq?
b: He interpreted it as referring to zakāt on trade goods, because people used to trade by measures of wasq.

f: 345. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not require wealth or richness of the owner for ʿushr?
b: Because the cause of obligation is the productive land itself, not the owner’s personal wealth.

f: 346. Why is a full year (ḥawl) not required for agricultural zakāt?
b: Because agricultural produce is already growth itself, whereas the ḥawl is only needed for developing wealth.

f: 347. What was the second disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and his companions regarding agricultural zakāt?
b: Whether the produce must be something that remains and lasts after harvesting.

f: 348. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to exclude vegetables from ʿushr?
b: The narration: “There is no charity on vegetables.”

f: 349. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله respond to the narration about vegetables?
b: He interpreted it as referring to charity collected by the ʿāshir (tax collector), not agricultural ʿushr.

f: 350. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله consider vegetables subject to ʿushr?
b: Because the cause is productive land, and land may produce crops that do not remain after harvesting.

f: 351. Why are firewood, reeds, and grass generally not subject to ʿushr according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because they are not normally cultivated in gardens; rather, gardens are cleared of them.

f: 352. When would reeds and grass become subject to ʿushr?
b: If someone intentionally cultivates land for reeds, trees, or grass.

f: 353. What type of reed did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله refer to when excluding reeds?
b: Persian reed.

f: 354. Is sugar cane subject to ʿushr?
b: Yes, because it is cultivated for benefiting from the land.

f: 355. Is sweet-smelling reed (qaṣab al-dharīrah) subject to ʿushr?
b: Yes, because it is cultivated for benefit from the land.

f: 356. Why are palm leaves and straw not separately subject to ʿushr?
b: Because the intended produce is the dates and grain, not the leaves or straw themselves.

f: 357. What is the ʿushr rate for crops irrigated by wells, water wheels, or animal-powered irrigation?
b: Half of one tenth (5%), according to both Hanafi positions.

f: 358. Why is the rate reduced for artificially irrigated crops?
b: Because they require greater expenses, while naturally irrigated crops have fewer costs.

f: 359. If land is irrigated both naturally and artificially, which rate applies?
b: The method used for most of the year is considered.

f: 360. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion regarding crops that are not measured by wasq, such as saffron and cotton?
b: ʿUshr is due if their value reaches the value of five awsuq of the lowest measurable crop.

f: 361. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله use monetary value for crops like saffron and cotton?
b: Because their quantity cannot be measured by the legal measure of wasq.

f: 362. What was Muḥammad’s opinion regarding crops that are not measured by wasq?
b: ʿUshr is due when they reach five units measured by the highest common measure for that type.

f: 363. How did Muḥammad estimate cotton for ʿushr?
b: Five loads, each load being three hundred manns.

f: 364. How did Muḥammad estimate saffron for ʿushr?
b: Five manns.

f: 365. Is honey subject to ʿushr if collected from ʿushr land?
b: Yes.

f: 366. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding zakāt on honey?
b: He held that no ʿushr is due on honey.

f: 367. What evidence did the Hanafis use for ʿushr on honey?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “There is one tenth on honey.”

f: 368. Why did the Hanafis consider honey similar to crops?
b: Because bees take from flowers and fruits, which themselves are subject to ʿushr.

f: 369. Why is silkworm production different from honey according to the Hanafis?
b: Because silkworms eat leaves, and leaves are not subject to ʿushr.

f: 370. Does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله require a minimum amount of honey before ʿushr becomes obligatory?
b: No, he requires ʿushr regardless of whether it is little or much.

f: 371. What was one narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding the minimum amount of honey?
b: That its value should reach five awsuq.

f: 372. What was another narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding honey?
b: That nothing is due until it reaches ten containers (qirbahs), based on the practice of Banū Shabābah.

f: 373. What was another narration regarding the minimum amount of honey?
b: Five manns.

f: 374. What was Muḥammad’s opinion regarding the minimum amount of honey?
b: Five afrāq, each being thirty-six riṭls.

f: 375. Is honey and fruit found in mountains subject to ʿushr?
b: Yes, according to the apparent Hanafi position.

f: 376. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله view regarding honey and fruits found in mountains?
b: He held that no ʿushr is due because the land is not cultivated.

f: 377. Why did the apparent Hanafi position require ʿushr on mountain produce?
b: Because the purpose, namely the produce itself, exists.

f: 378. Are labour wages and expenses for oxen deducted before calculating ʿushr?
b: No, they are not deducted.

f: 379. Why are agricultural expenses not deducted from ʿushr?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ already differentiated the obligation based on irrigation expense.

f: 380. If a Banū Taghlib person owns ʿushr land, what is due from him?
b: Double ʿushr.

f: 381. Why do Banū Taghlib pay double ʿushr?
b: Because this was established by the agreement of the Companions.

f: 382. What was another opinion from Muḥammad regarding land purchased by a Banū Taghlib person from a Muslim?
b: Only one ʿushr is due because the obligation does not change with ownership.

f: 383. If a dhimmī purchases land from a Banū Taghlib person, what is the ruling?
b: The land remains under the same obligation according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and his companions.

f: 384. If a Muslim purchases land from Banū Taghlib or a Banū Taghlib person becomes Muslim, does the double ʿushr remain according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Yes, because the doubled obligation has become attached to the land itself.

f: 385. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare doubled ʿushr to kharāj?
b: Because it becomes a fixed obligation attached to the land and transfers with it.

f: 386. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion when a Banū Taghlib person becomes Muslim or sells the land to a Muslim?
b: The obligation returns to normal ʿushr because the reason for doubling no longer exists.

f: 387. If a Muslim’s ʿushr land is sold to a non-Taghlib Christian (dhimmī), what is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله ruling?
b: It becomes kharāj land.

f: 388. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله make such land subject to kharāj?
b: Because kharāj is more suitable for the condition of a non-Muslim owner.

f: 389. What is Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion regarding a dhimmī purchasing Muslim ʿushr land?
b: It remains subject to double ʿushr, which is spent like kharāj.

f: 390. What is Muḥammad’s opinion regarding a dhimmī purchasing Muslim ʿushr land?
b: The land remains ʿushr land and does not change.

f: 391. If a Muslim takes back ʿushr land through pre-emption (shufʿah), what is its ruling?
b: It returns to being ʿushr land as before.

f: 392. Why does pre-emption restore the land’s original status?
b: Because the transaction is treated as if the pre-emptor bought it directly from the Muslim owner.

f: 393. If a sale is invalid and the land returns to the seller, what is the ruling?
b: It remains ʿushr land as it originally was.

f: 394. Why does an invalid sale not change the land’s status?
b: Because the sale is treated as if it never occurred, and the Muslim owner’s right was never fully removed.

f: 395. If a Muslim has a residential plot and turns it into an orchard, what is due from it?
b: He owes ʿushr if it is irrigated with ʿushr water.

f: 396. What happens if the orchard made from a residential plot is irrigated with kharāj water?
b: Kharāj is due instead of ʿushr.

f: 397. Why does the obligation follow the type of water used?
b: Because the financial obligation in such cases is connected to the type of irrigation.

f: 398. Is anything due from a Magian (Majūsī) for his residential property?
b: No, nothing is due because ʿUmar رضي الله عنه considered residences exempt.

f: 399. What is due if a Magian turns his residence into an orchard?
b: Kharāj is due.

f: 400. Why is kharāj imposed on a Magian’s orchard even if irrigated with ʿushr water?
b: Because ʿushr contains an element of worship, so kharāj, which suits his status, is applied instead.

f: 401. According to the analogy of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what would be due on a Magian’s orchard irrigated with ʿushr water?
b: ʿUshr would be due.

f: 402. According to Muḥammad, how much ʿushr would be due on a Magian’s orchard irrigated with ʿushr water?
b: One ʿushr (normal 10%).

f: 403. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, how much ʿushr would be due on a Magian’s orchard irrigated with ʿushr water?
b: Two ʿushrs (double 10%).

f: 404. What is ʿushr water?
b: Water from rain, wells, springs, and seas that are not under anyone’s control.

f: 405. What is kharāj water?
b: Water from rivers dug by non-Arabs and rivers under human management.

f: 406. Is the water of the Jīḥūn and Sayḥūn rivers considered ʿushr water or kharāj water?
b: According to Muḥammad, it is ʿushr water because nobody protects or controls it.

f: 407. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what type of water are the Jīḥūn and Sayḥūn rivers?
b: Kharāj water because bridges and ships are maintained over them.

f: 408. What type of water are the Tigris and Euphrates according to Muḥammad?
b: ʿUshr water.

f: 409. What type of water are the Tigris and Euphrates according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Kharāj water.

f: 410. What is due on the land of a Banū Taghlib child or woman?
b: The same as on the land of a Banū Taghlib man.

f: 411. What does this mean for Banū Taghlib agricultural land?
b: If it is ʿushr land, double ʿushr is due; if it is kharāj land, normal kharāj is due.

f: 412. Why do Banū Taghlib women and children have the same agricultural obligations as men?
b: Because the treaty doubled their charity obligation, not their purely financial obligations.

f: 413. If a Muslim child or woman owns land, what is due from it?
b: Normal ʿushr.

f: 414. Why is the ʿushr of Banū Taghlib children and women doubled?
b: Because their treaty obligation applies to them as it applies to their men.

f: 415. Is there any obligation on a spring of pitch or petroleum in ʿushr land?
b: No, there is nothing due.

f: 416. Why is there no ʿushr on petroleum or pitch springs in ʿushr land?
b: Because they are not considered produce extracted from cultivation, but a flowing substance like a water spring.

f: 417. What is due from a petroleum or pitch spring in kharāj land?
b: Kharāj is due.

f: 418. When is kharāj due on a petroleum or pitch spring?
b: When the surrounding land is suitable for cultivation.

f: 419. Why does kharāj apply to such land?
b: Because kharāj is connected to the ability to cultivate the land.

f: 420. What is the basis for the recipients of zakāt?
b: Allah’s statement: “Indeed, charities are only for the poor and the needy…” (Qur’an 9:60).

f: 421. How many categories of zakāt recipients are mentioned in the Qur’an?
b: Eight categories.

f: 422. Which category of zakāt recipients no longer applies according to the Hanafis?
b: Those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-muʾallafatu qulūbuhum).

f: 423. Why was the category of those whose hearts are reconciled removed according to the Hanafis?
b: Because Allah strengthened Islam and there was no longer a need for them.

f: 424. What was the consensus regarding the removal of al-muʾallafatu qulūbuhum?
b: Consensus was established upon it according to the author.

f: 425. Who is considered a poor person (faqīr) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Someone who possesses a small amount of wealth.

f: 426. Who is considered a needy person (miskīn) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Someone who possesses nothing.

f: 427. What other opinion exists regarding the difference between faqīr and miskīn?
b: Some held the opposite definition: the faqīr has nothing and the miskīn has something.

f: 428. Is faqīr and miskīn considered two separate categories or one?
b: This discussion is deferred to the Book of Wills.

f: 429. Who is the zakāt worker (ʿāmil)?
b: The person appointed by the Imam to collect and manage zakāt.

f: 430. How much is the zakāt worker given?
b: Enough to cover himself and his assistants according to their work.

f: 431. Is the zakāt worker’s payment fixed according to a percentage or amount?
b: No, it is not fixed according to a specific amount.

f: 432. Why does the zakāt worker receive zakāt even if he is wealthy?
b: Because his entitlement is based on his work, not his poverty.

f: 433. Can a Hāshimī person take payment as a zakāt worker?
b: No, because it contains the suspicion of charity’s impurity, and the Prophet’s ﷺ family is honoured above that.

f: 434. Why can a wealthy zakāt worker receive payment but a wealthy ordinary person cannot?
b: Because the worker’s right comes through service, while the ordinary wealthy person has no such entitlement.

f: 435. What does the category “freeing slaves” (fī al-riqāb) refer to according to the Hanafis?
b: Helping enslaved people who have contracts of manumission (mukātab) to free themselves.

f: 436. Who is a debtor (ghārim) eligible for zakāt?
b: Someone who owes a debt and does not possess surplus wealth reaching a niṣāb after that debt.

f: 437. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s interpretation of the debtor category?
b: Someone who incurs expenses to reconcile people or stop conflict between groups.

f: 438. What does “in the path of Allah” (fī sabīl Allāh) mean according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Soldiers who are cut off and lack resources.

f: 439. What does “in the path of Allah” mean according to Muḥammad?
b: Pilgrims who are cut off and lack resources.

f: 440. What evidence did Muḥammad use for including stranded pilgrims in fī sabīl Allāh?
b: The Prophet ﷺ told someone who dedicated his camel in Allah’s path to use it for carrying pilgrims.

f: 441. Can wealthy soldiers receive zakāt according to the Hanafis?
b: No, because zakāt recipients must be poor.

f: 442. Who is the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl)?
b: Someone who has wealth in his homeland but has nothing available where he currently is.

f: 443. Can a person distribute zakāt to only one category of recipients?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafis.

f: 444. Can a person distribute zakāt among all eight categories?
b: Yes, but it is not required.

f: 445. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding distributing zakāt to only one category?
b: He held that it must be distributed to at least three people from each category.

f: 446. How did the Hanafis respond to al-Shāfiʿī’s argument?
b: The Qur’anic wording identifies categories of recipients, not that each category has an obligatory share.

f: 447. To whom may zakāt not be given?
b: A dhimmī (non-Muslim under Muslim protection).

f: 448. What evidence did the Hanafis use to prohibit giving zakāt to dhimmīs?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ instruction to Muʿādh: “Take it from their wealthy and return it to their poor.”

f: 449. Can voluntary charity (ṣadaqah) other than zakāt be given to a dhimmī?
b: Yes.

f: 450. What evidence allows giving voluntary charity to non-Muslims?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “Give charity to people of all religions.”

f: 451. Why did the Hanafis distinguish voluntary charity from zakāt?
b: Because zakāt has specific recipients, while voluntary charity is broader.

f: 452. Can zakāt money be used to build a mosque?
b: No.

f: 453. Why cannot zakāt money be used to build a mosque?
b: Because zakāt requires transferring ownership to an individual recipient.

f: 454. Can zakāt money be used to shroud a deceased person?
b: No.

f: 455. Why cannot zakāt money be used for shrouding the dead?
b: Because there is no transfer of ownership.

f: 456. Can zakāt be used to pay the debt of a deceased person?
b: No.

f: 457. Why cannot zakāt pay the debt of a deceased person?
b: Because payment of another person’s debt does not establish ownership transfer to the deceased.

f: 458. Can zakāt be used to buy a slave and free him directly?
b: No, according to the Hanafis.

f: 459. What was Mālik’s opinion regarding buying slaves with zakāt?
b: He allowed it based on the verse “and for freeing slaves.”

f: 460. How did the Hanafis interpret “freeing slaves” (fī al-riqāb)?
b: As giving money to mukātab slaves so they can purchase their freedom.

f: 461. Can zakāt be given to a wealthy person?
b: No.

f: 462. What evidence prohibits giving zakāt to the wealthy?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ statement: “Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person.”

f: 463. Who did the Hanafis include among those prohibited from receiving zakāt despite al-Shāfiʿī’s disagreement?
b: Wealthy warriors, because poverty is still required for zakāt recipients.

f: 464. Can a person give his zakāt to his father or grandfather?
b: No, he cannot give zakāt to his father, grandfather, or any ancestor above them.

f: 465. Can a person give zakāt to his child or grandchild?
b: No, he cannot give zakāt to his child, grandchild, or any descendant below them.

f: 466. Why cannot zakāt be given to one's ascendants or descendants?
b: Because their benefits and financial interests are normally connected, so full transfer of ownership (tamlik) is not achieved.

f: 467. Can a husband give zakāt to his wife?
b: No, he cannot give zakāt to his wife.

f: 468. Why cannot a husband give zakāt to his wife?
b: Because spouses usually share benefits and financial interests.

f: 469. Can a wife give zakāt to her husband according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No, according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله she cannot.

f: 470. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to allow a wife to give zakāt to her husband?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “You will have two rewards: the reward of charity and the reward of maintaining family ties.”

f: 471. How did the Hanafis answer the hadith about a wife giving charity to her husband?
b: They said it refers to voluntary charity, not obligatory zakāt.

f: 472. Can zakāt be given to a mudabbar slave?
b: No.

f: 473. Can zakāt be given to a mukātab slave?
b: No.

f: 474. Can zakāt be given to an umm walad (slave woman who bore her master’s child)?
b: No.

f: 475. Why cannot zakāt be given to a mudabbar, mukātab, or umm walad?
b: Because ownership transfer is not complete; the slave’s earnings belong to the master, and the master has rights over the mukātab’s earnings.

f: 476. Can zakāt be given to a slave who has been partially freed?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, no.

f: 477. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not allow giving zakāt to a partially freed slave?
b: Because he considers him similar to a mukātab.

f: 478. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding giving zakāt to a partially freed slave?
b: They allow it because he is considered a free person with debt obligations.

f: 479. Can zakāt be given to a wealthy slave?
b: No.

f: 480. Why cannot zakāt be given to a wealthy slave?
b: Because ownership belongs to the master, not the slave.

f: 481. Can zakāt be given to the young child of a wealthy person?
b: No.

f: 482. Why cannot zakāt be given to a wealthy person’s young child?
b: Because the child is considered wealthy due to the wealth of the father.

f: 483. Can zakāt be given to an adult poor child of a wealthy person?
b: Yes.

f: 484. Why can an adult poor child of a wealthy person receive zakāt?
b: Because an adult child is not considered wealthy merely because of the father’s wealth.

f: 485. Can a poor wife of a wealthy husband receive zakāt?
b: Yes.

f: 486. Why can a poor wife of a wealthy husband receive zakāt?
b: Because she is not considered wealthy by her husband’s wealth; maintenance does not make her wealthy.

f: 487. Can zakāt be given to Banū Hāshim?
b: No.

f: 488. What evidence prohibits giving zakāt to Banū Hāshim?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Banū Hāshim, Allah has forbidden for you the impurities of people’s wealth and has compensated you with one-fifth of the fifth.”

f: 489. Why is voluntary charity allowed for Banū Hāshim but zakāt is not?
b: Because obligatory zakāt is considered like something that becomes impure through removing an obligation, while voluntary charity is like drinking water for refreshment.

f: 490. Which families are included among Banū Hāshim who cannot receive zakāt?
b: The families of ʿAlī, ʿAbbās, Jaʿfar, ʿAqīl, and al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

f: 491. Why are these families considered Banū Hāshim?
b: Because they trace their lineage to Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf.

f: 492. Are the freed clients (mawālī) of Banū Hāshim included in this prohibition?
b: Yes, they also cannot receive zakāt.

f: 493. What evidence prohibits giving zakāt to the mawālī of Banū Hāshim?
b: The Prophet ﷺ told his freed servant: “No, you are our mawla.”

f: 494. If a Qurayshī person frees a Christian slave, does the slave become prohibited from receiving zakāt?
b: No, because the original lineage of the freed person is considered.

f: 495. If someone gives zakāt to a person he believes is poor, then discovers he is wealthy, must he repeat the zakāt?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, no.

f: 496. What is Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion if someone gives zakāt to someone who turns out to be wealthy?
b: He must repeat the payment.

f: 497. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله require repeating the zakāt in such cases?
b: Because the mistake became certain and these matters could potentially have been known.

f: 498. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to excuse the mistake?
b: The hadith of Maʿn ibn Yazīd where the Prophet ﷺ said: “O Yazīd, you have what you intended, and O Maʿn, you have what you took.”

f: 499. How did the Hanafis compare determining zakāt recipients to another legal matter?
b: They compared it to determining the direction of prayer (qiblah) when uncertain.

f: 500. If someone gives zakāt after investigating and believing the recipient is eligible, is it valid if he was mistaken?
b: Yes, according to the preferred Hanafi view.

f: 501. If someone gives zakāt without investigating while uncertain about the recipient, is it valid?
b: No, unless he later knows the person was actually poor.

f: 502. If someone gives zakāt to his slave or mukātab and later discovers this, is it valid?
b: No.

f: 503. Why is zakāt invalid when given to one’s slave or mukātab?
b: Because ownership transfer, which is a pillar of zakāt, does not occur.

f: 504. Can zakāt be given to someone who owns a niṣāb of any type of wealth?
b: No.

f: 505. Why cannot zakāt be given to someone who owns a niṣāb?
b: Because legal wealth is measured by possessing a niṣāb beyond essential needs.

f: 506. Can zakāt be given to someone who owns less than a niṣāb even if he is healthy and able to work?
b: Yes.

f: 507. Why can a healthy working person with less than a niṣāb receive zakāt?
b: Because he is legally poor, and the actual level of need is difficult to determine, so the absence of a niṣāb is used as the indicator.

f: 508. Is it disliked to give one person two hundred dirhams or more in zakāt?
b: Yes, it is disliked.

f: 509. If someone gives two hundred dirhams or more to one person, is the zakāt valid?
b: Yes, it is valid.

f: 510. What was Zafar’s opinion regarding giving two hundred dirhams or more to one person?
b: He said it is not valid because the recipient becomes wealthy at the time of payment.

f: 511. Why did the Hanafis consider such payment valid but disliked?
b: Because wealth is judged after completion of the payment, though it is disliked because it is close to making the person wealthy.

f: 512. What is preferred regarding using zakāt to help someone?
b: It is preferred to make a person independent from asking for that day.

f: 513. Does “making someone rich” mean permanently wealthy?
b: No, it means providing enough for the person’s needs that day.

f: 514. Is completely making someone wealthy through zakāt preferred?
b: No, it is disliked.

f: 515. Is transferring zakāt from one town to another disliked?
b: Yes.

f: 516. Why is transferring zakāt from one place to another disliked?
b: Because local poor people have greater claim and due consideration should be given to neighbours.

f: 517. What evidence supports distributing zakāt locally?
b: The hadith of Muʿādh رضي الله عنه regarding taking from the wealthy of a place and returning it to its poor.

f: 518. When is transferring zakāt to another place allowed?
b: When giving it to relatives or to people who are more needy than the people of one’s own town.

f: 519. Is zakāt valid if transferred to another place for a reason other than relatives or greater need?
b: Yes, but it is disliked.

f: 520. Why is zakāt still valid if transferred elsewhere unnecessarily?
b: Because the Qur’anic category is general: the poor are recipients wherever they are.

f: 521. Who is obligated to give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr according to the Hanafis?
b: A free Muslim who owns a niṣāb beyond his essential needs.

f: 522. What evidence establishes the obligation of ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: The Prophet’s ﷺ instruction: “Give for every free person and slave, young or old, half a ṣāʿ of wheat or a ṣāʿ of dates or barley.”

f: 523. Why is freedom a condition for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because complete ownership is required.

f: 524. Why is Islam a condition for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because it is an act of worship.

f: 525. Why is wealth a condition for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no charity except from one who possesses sufficiency.”

f: 526. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding the wealth requirement for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: It is required from someone who has more than his daily food needs for himself and his family.

f: 527. How did the Hanafis define the wealth requirement for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: By possessing a niṣāb beyond essential needs.

f: 528. What things are excluded from the niṣāb calculation for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Residence, clothing, household furniture, riding animal, weapons, and servants needed for use.

f: 529. Why are these items excluded from the niṣāb calculation?
b: Because they are required due to essential needs and are treated as nonexistent for wealth calculations.

f: 530. Is growth (namāʾ) required for the niṣāb of ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: No.

f: 531. What other rulings are connected to possessing this type of niṣāb?
b: Being prohibited from receiving zakāt and the obligation of udḥiyah (sacrifice) and ṣadaqat al-fiṭr.

f: 532. Who must a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for himself?
b: He must give it for himself.

f: 533. What evidence establishes that a person gives ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for himself?
b: The hadith of Ibn ʿUmar رضي الله عنهما that the Prophet ﷺ obligated ṣadaqat al-fiṭr upon males and females.

f: 534. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr connected to the person himself?
b: Because the cause of obligation is the person (head) who is supported and under authority.

f: 535. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr called “zakāt of the head” (zakāt al-raʾs)?
b: Because the obligation is attached to the individual person, and this indicates the cause of obligation.

f: 536. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr called “the zakāt of breaking the fast” (zakāt al-fiṭr)?
b: Because it is connected to the time of fiṭr (the ending of Ramadan).

f: 537. Does ṣadaqat al-fiṭr increase when the number of people increases?
b: Yes, because it is connected to each individual head, even if the day is the same.

f: 538. Who does a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for besides himself?
b: He gives it for his young children.

f: 539. Why must a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his young children?
b: Because he supports them and has authority over them, making them similar to himself.

f: 540. Why are young children included in ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because they are dependent on him for maintenance and guardianship.

f: 541. Must a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his slaves?
b: Yes, if they are slaves for service and dependent on him.

f: 542. Why does a master give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his slaves?
b: Because he has authority over them and is responsible for their maintenance.

f: 543. If young children own wealth, from where is their ṣadaqat al-fiṭr paid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: It is paid from their wealth.

f: 544. What was Muḥammad’s opinion regarding children who possess wealth?
b: Their ṣadaqat al-fiṭr is still treated like a maintenance obligation and is not paid from their wealth.

f: 545. Must a husband give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his wife?
b: No.

f: 546. Why does a husband not have to give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his wife?
b: Because he does not have complete authority over her and does not maintain her except in matters such as regular expenses.

f: 547. Does a husband have authority over his wife outside marital rights?
b: No.

f: 548. Must a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his adult children?
b: No, even if they live under his care.

f: 549. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr not required for adult children?
b: Because guardianship does not continue over adult children.

f: 550. If a person gives ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his adult child or wife without their permission, is it valid?
b: Yes, according to istihsān (juristic preference).

f: 551. Why is giving ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for one's wife or adult child without permission valid?
b: Because customary practice indicates their permission.

f: 552. Must a person give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his mukātab slave?
b: No.

f: 553. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr not required for a mukātab slave?
b: Because the master no longer has full authority over him.

f: 554. Must a mukātab slave give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for himself?
b: No.

f: 555. Why does a mukātab slave not give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for himself?
b: Because he is financially unable.

f: 556. Must a master give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for a mudabbar slave and an umm walad?
b: Yes.

f: 557. Why does a master give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for a mudabbar slave and umm walad?
b: Because the master's authority over them remains.

f: 558. Must a master give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for slaves owned for trade?
b: No, according to the Hanafis.

f: 559. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding slaves owned for trade?
b: He considered ṣadaqat al-fiṭr obligatory on the slave.

f: 560. Why did al-Shāfiʿī not see a conflict between zakāt and fiṭr obligations for trade slaves?
b: Because he placed the fiṭr obligation on the slave and the zakāt obligation on the master.

f: 561. Why do the Hanafis reject requiring fiṭr from trade slaves?
b: Because they consider the obligation to be on the master due to ownership, similar to zakāt, which would cause double obligation.

f: 562. If a slave is jointly owned by two partners, is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr required from either partner?
b: No.

f: 563. Why is there no ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for a jointly owned slave according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because neither owner has complete authority and responsibility over the slave.

f: 564. What did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say regarding jointly owned slaves?
b: Each owner must pay according to his share of the slave.

f: 565. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad differ from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding jointly owned slaves?
b: Because they consider division of slaves possible, unlike Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله.

f: 566. What is another explanation given for why jointly owned slaves have no fiṭr obligation?
b: Because before division, each owner does not possess a complete share of the slave.

f: 567. Must a Muslim give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr for his non-Muslim slave?
b: Yes.

f: 568. What evidence supports giving fiṭr for a non-Muslim slave?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Give on behalf of every free person and slave, whether Jewish, Christian, or Magian.”

f: 569. Why does a Muslim master give fiṭr for a non-Muslim slave?
b: Because the cause of obligation exists and the master is legally responsible.

f: 570. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding fiṭr for a non-Muslim slave?
b: He did not require it because he placed the obligation on the slave, who is not eligible for worship obligations.

f: 571. If a slave is sold while either buyer or seller has an option to cancel, who pays the slave’s fiṭr?
b: The one who ultimately becomes the owner.

f: 572. When does this ruling apply?
b: When the day of Eid al-Fiṭr arrives while the option period remains.

f: 573. What was Zafar’s opinion regarding a slave sold with an option?
b: The person who has the option pays because authority belongs to him.

f: 574. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding a slave sold with an option?
b: The owner pays because it is connected to ownership like maintenance.

f: 575. Why do the Hanafis say the final owner pays the fiṭr in a sale with an option?
b: Because ownership is suspended; it may return to the seller or become established for the buyer.

f: 576. Why is maintenance different from fiṭr in a sale with an option?
b: Because maintenance is an immediate need and cannot be suspended.

f: 577. Is zakāt on trade goods also affected by a sale option in the same way?
b: Yes, it follows the same principle.

f: 578. What is the amount of ṣadaqat al-fiṭr according to the first Hanafi opinion?
b: Half a ṣāʿ of wheat, flour, roasted flour (sawīq), or raisins, or one ṣāʿ of dates or barley.

f: 579. What was the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding raisins?
b: They considered raisins equivalent to barley, requiring one ṣāʿ.

f: 580. What narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله supports the one ṣāʿ amount for raisins?
b: It is one of the narrations from him.

f: 581. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding the amount of fiṭr?
b: One ṣāʿ from all types of food mentioned.

f: 582. What evidence did al-Shāfiʿī use for one ṣāʿ from all foods?
b: The hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī رضي الله عنه that they used to give one ṣāʿ during the time of the Prophet ﷺ.

f: 583. How did the Hanafis answer the hadith of Abū Saʿīd?
b: They interpreted the extra amount as voluntary charity.

f: 584. Why did the Hanafis differentiate between wheat and other foods?
b: Because wheat and flour are eaten completely, while dates and barley contain parts that are discarded, such as date stones and bran.

f: 585. What is meant by flour (daqīq) in the ruling of fiṭr?
b: Flour made from wheat.

f: 586. What is the ruling of barley flour for fiṭr?
b: It follows the ruling of barley.

f: 587. What is preferable regarding flour and sawīq amounts?
b: To consider both quantity and value as a precaution.

f: 588. What is the ruling regarding giving bread as ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Its value should be considered according to the correct view.

f: 589. According to the narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how much wheat is half a ṣāʿ by weight?
b: Half a ṣāʿ of wheat by weight.

f: 590. What did Muḥammad consider regarding measuring half a ṣāʿ of wheat?
b: He considered it by volume (kīl), not weight.

f: 591. According to Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله reported preference, what is better than wheat flour for fiṭr?
b: Giving money is better because it fulfills the need more effectively and quickly.

f: 592. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله prefer giving money for ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Because it better addresses the poor person’s need.

f: 593. Why did Abū Bakr al-Aʿmash رضي الله عنه prefer giving wheat?
b: Because it avoids disagreement with other scholars, since flour and monetary value are disputed by al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 594. How much is the ṣāʿ according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad رحمهما الله?
b: The ṣāʿ is eight Iraqi ratls (arṭāl).

f: 595. What was Abū Yūsuf’s رحمه الله opinion regarding the size of the ṣāʿ?
b: The ṣāʿ is five and one-third Iraqi ratls.

f: 596. Whose opinion did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله agree with regarding the size of the ṣāʿ?
b: He agreed with al-Shāfiʿī رحمه الله.

f: 597. What evidence did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and al-Shāfiʿī use for their measurement of the ṣāʿ?
b: The hadith: “Our ṣāʿ is the smallest of the ṣāʿs.”

f: 598. What evidence did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for their measurement of the ṣāʿ?
b: The report that the Prophet ﷺ performed wuḍūʾ with a mudd of two ratls and ghusl with a ṣāʿ of eight ratls.

f: 599. What was the size of the ṣāʿ used by ʿUmar رضي الله عنه?
b: It was eight Iraqi ratls.

f: 600. Was the ṣāʿ of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه smaller or larger than the Hāshimī ṣāʿ?
b: It was smaller than the Hāshimī ṣāʿ.

f: 601. Which ṣāʿ did people commonly use despite the existence of the smaller ṣāʿ?
b: They used the Hāshimī ṣāʿ.

f: 602. When does the obligation of ṣadaqat al-fiṭr begin according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: At the rising of dawn on the day of Eid al-Fiṭr.

f: 603. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding when ṣadaqat al-fiṭr becomes obligatory?
b: It becomes obligatory at sunset on the final day of Ramadan.

f: 604. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does a person who accepts Islam on the night of Eid have to pay ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: Yes.

f: 605. According to al-Shāfiʿī, does a person who accepts Islam on the night of Eid have to pay ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: No.

f: 606. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does a child born on the night of Eid have ṣadaqat al-fiṭr due?
b: Yes.

f: 607. According to al-Shāfiʿī, does a child born on the night of Eid have ṣadaqat al-fiṭr due?
b: No.

f: 608. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does the death of a slave or child on the night of Eid remove the obligation of fiṭr?
b: Yes, because the obligation is connected to the time of dawn.

f: 609. What is the reasoning of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله for connecting fiṭr to dawn?
b: Because the wording indicates attachment to the day of Eid, not the night before it.

f: 610. What does the phrase “ṣadaqat al-fiṭr” indicate regarding its timing?
b: It is connected specifically to the day of breaking the fast.

f: 611. When is it recommended for people to give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr?
b: On the day of Eid before going to the prayer area (muṣallā).

f: 612. Why is it recommended to give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr before going to the muṣallā?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ used to give it before leaving for the prayer.

f: 613. Why is giving fiṭr before Eid prayer beneficial for the poor?
b: So the poor person is enriched and does not become distracted by asking people during prayer time.

f: 614. Is it permissible to give ṣadaqat al-fiṭr before Eid day?
b: Yes.

f: 615. Why is early payment of ṣadaqat al-fiṭr permissible?
b: Because the cause of obligation has already occurred, similar to paying zakāt early.

f: 616. Is there a specific maximum period for paying ṣadaqat al-fiṭr early?
b: The correct view is that there is no distinction between different lengths of time.

f: 617. What other opinions exist regarding paying ṣadaqat al-fiṭr early?
b: Some said it may be paid during the last half of Ramadan, and others said during the last ten days.

f: 618. If someone delays ṣadaqat al-fiṭr until after Eid day, is it waived?
b: No, it remains obligatory and must still be paid.

f: 619. Why does delaying ṣadaqat al-fiṭr not remove the obligation?
b: Because the purpose of worship in it is understood rationally, so its performance time is not restricted like the udḥiyah sacrifice.

f: 620. Why is ṣadaqat al-fiṭr different from udḥiyah regarding delayed performance?
b: Because udḥiyah has a fixed ritual time, while fiṭr is connected to helping the needy.

f: 1. What are the two categories of fasting?
b: Obligatory fasting and voluntary fasting.

f: 2. What are the two types of obligatory fasting?
b: Fasting connected to a specific time, and fasting that becomes a debt upon the person.

f: 3. What obligatory fasts are connected to a specific time?
b: The fast of Ramadan and a specified vow (nadhr muʿayyan).

f: 4. What obligatory fasts are considered a debt upon the person?
b: Missed Ramadan fasts (qaḍāʾ), unrestricted vows (nadhr muṭlaq), and expiatory fasts (kaffārah).

f: 5. When may the intention for Ramadan fasting be made according to the Hanafis?
b: It may be made during the night, and if not made until morning, it is valid until before midday (according to their details).

f: 6. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion regarding making the intention for Ramadan after dawn?
b: It is not valid; the intention must be made during the night.

f: 7. What evidence establishes that Ramadan fasting is obligatory?
b: The verse: “Fasting has been prescribed for you” (Qur’an 2:183), and scholarly consensus on its obligation.

f: 8. What is the ruling of someone who rejects the obligation of Ramadan fasting?
b: He becomes a disbeliever because its obligation is established by definitive evidence and consensus.

f: 9. Why is a vowed fast obligatory?
b: Because Allah says: “Let them fulfill their vows” (Qur’an 22:29).

f: 10. What is the cause (sabab) of the obligation of Ramadan fasting?
b: The month of Ramadan.

f: 11. Why is Ramadan fasting attributed to the month?
b: Because its obligation repeats whenever the month returns.

f: 12. What is the cause of obligation for a vowed fast?
b: The vow itself.

f: 13. What is the role of intention in fasting?
b: It is a condition for the validity of fasting.

f: 14. What evidence does al-Shāfiʿī use for requiring the intention from the night?
b: The hadith: “There is no fasting for the one who does not intend the fast from the night.”

f: 15. How do the Hanafis interpret the hadith “There is no fasting for the one who does not intend from the night”?
b: They interpret it as negating perfection and virtue, or meaning the person did not intend that it was a specific obligatory fast from the night.

f: 16. What evidence do the Hanafis use that a Ramadan intention may be made after dawn?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said after the Bedouin testified to seeing the crescent: “Whoever has eaten, let him not eat the rest of the day, and whoever has not eaten, let him fast.”

f: 17. Why can the intention for Ramadan be delayed according to the Hanafis?
b: Because fasting is one continuous act whose pillar extends throughout the day, unlike prayers which have separate pillars.

f: 18. Why is intention required earlier for prayer and pilgrimage than for fasting?
b: Because prayer and pilgrimage contain multiple pillars, so the intention must accompany the beginning of the act.

f: 19. Why can fasting have a later intention while prayer cannot?
b: Because fasting is one extended pillar, whereas prayer and pilgrimage are composed of separate actions.

f: 20. Why is a later intention invalid after midday according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the intention would no longer coincide with the majority of the fasting day.

f: 21. What is the correct time limit for intending a time-specific obligatory fast according to the Hanafis?
b: Before midday (before the major forenoon, ḍuḥā kubrā).

f: 22. Why must the intention be before midday?
b: Because the intention must exist during the majority of the day.

f: 23. What is the difference between the “midday” mentioned in some texts and the “major forenoon”?
b: The intended midpoint is from dawn until ḍuḥā kubrā, not necessarily the legal noon (zawāl).

f: 24. Does the rule of delayed intention differ between a traveler and resident?
b: No, according to the Hanafis.

f: 25. Does a time-specific obligatory fast require a specific Ramadan intention?
b: No, a general intention or even an intention for another obligatory fast is sufficient according to the Hanafis.

f: 26. Can Ramadan fasting be valid with the intention of a voluntary fast?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafis.

f: 27. Why is a general intention sufficient for Ramadan fasting?
b: Because the obligation itself is already specified by the time; the original intention of fasting is enough.

f: 28. Why does intending another obligatory fast still count for Ramadan according to the Hanafis?
b: Because the person intended fasting itself plus an additional purpose, and the extra purpose is ignored.

f: 29. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s view on intending a voluntary fast for Ramadan?
b: He considered it meaningless, and regarding a general intention he had two opinions.

f: 30. Why does al-Shāfiʿī reject using a voluntary intention for Ramadan?
b: Because the person intended a voluntary act instead of the obligatory one.

f: 31. What is the ruling if a sick person or traveler fasts Ramadan intending another obligatory fast?
b: According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, it counts as Ramadan.

f: 32. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say the intention of another obligation still counts?
b: Because the concession exists to remove hardship, but by choosing to fast the person joins the ruling of those without the excuse.

f: 33. What was Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله opinion regarding a sick person or traveler intending another obligatory fast?
b: It counts because he occupied the time with the more immediate obligation.

f: 34. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish the sick person and traveler?
b: Because they have a choice to delay Ramadan until another time, while the other obligation may be immediately binding.

f: 35. What is the second category of obligatory fasting?
b: Fasting that remains as a liability upon the person, such as qaḍāʾ and kaffārah.

f: 36. Why must debt-like fasts have an intention from the night?
b: Because they are not tied to a specific day and require specification from the beginning.

f: 37. Can all voluntary fasts be intended after dawn?
b: Yes, according to the Hanafis, as long as it is before midday.

f: 38. What was Mālik’s opinion regarding delayed intention for voluntary fasting?
b: He did not allow it based on the general wording of the hadith.

f: 39. What evidence do the Hanafis use for allowing a delayed intention in voluntary fasting?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said after waking without fasting: “Then indeed, I am fasting.”

f: 40. Why is voluntary fasting allowed with a later intention?
b: Because outside Ramadan the default fast is voluntary, so the intention makes the remaining abstention into a fast.

f: 41. Is a voluntary fast valid if the intention is made after midday?
b: No, according to the Hanafis.

f: 42. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion about intending voluntary fasting after midday?
b: It is valid.

f: 43. Why does al-Shāfiʿī allow intention after midday for voluntary fasting?
b: Because he considers voluntary fasting divisible and based on personal willingness.

f: 44. Why do the Hanafis reject intention after midday for voluntary fasting?
b: Because fasting is an act of restraining oneself for a measured period, requiring the intention to accompany most of the day.

f: 45. What should people do regarding the crescent of Ramadan?
b: They should seek the crescent on the 29th night of Shaʿbān.

f: 46. What should people do if they see the Ramadan crescent?
b: They should begin fasting.

f: 47. What should people do if the crescent is not visible due to clouds?
b: They should complete Shaʿbān as thirty days and then fast.

f: 48. What hadith establishes completing Shaʿbān when the crescent is not seen?
b: “Fast when you see it and break the fast when you see it; if it is obscured, complete Shaʿbān as thirty days.”

f: 49. What is the legal principle regarding the month of Shaʿbān when the crescent is not seen?
b: The original assumption is that the month continues, so certainty is not abandoned without evidence.

f: 50. Is fasting the day of doubt (yawm al-shakk) allowed?
b: It is only allowed as a voluntary fast.

f: 51. What evidence prohibits fasting the day of doubt as Ramadan?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not fast the day about which there is doubt that it is Ramadan, except as a voluntary fast.”

f: 52. What is the first case regarding fasting on the day of doubt?
b: Intending that it is Ramadan.

f: 53. What is the ruling of intending Ramadan fasting on the day of doubt?
b: It is disliked.

f: 54. Why is intending Ramadan on the day of doubt disliked?
b: Because it resembles the People of the Book, who added to the duration of their fasting.

f: 55. If the day of doubt later turns out to be Ramadan, does the fast count?
b: Yes, because the person encountered Ramadan and fasted it.

f: 56. If the day of doubt turns out to have been Shaʿbān, what is the ruling of that fast?
b: It counts as a voluntary fast.

f: 57. If a person fasted the day of doubt and later it was proven to be Shaʿbān, does he have to make it up?
b: No, because it was treated as a doubtful matter.

f: 58. What is the second case of fasting on the day of doubt?
b: A person intends a different obligatory fast (such as a vow or make-up fast).

f: 59. What is the ruling of intending another obligatory fast on the day of doubt?
b: It is disliked, though its dislike is less than intending Ramadan itself.

f: 60. If a person intended another obligatory fast on the day of doubt and it turns out to be Ramadan, does it count?
b: Yes, because the original intention of fasting existed.

f: 61. If a person intended another obligatory fast on the day of doubt and it turns out to be Shaʿbān, does it count?
b: There are two opinions: one says it becomes voluntary because the act was prohibited; the other says it counts as the intended obligatory fast, which is the stronger opinion.

f: 62. Why does the stronger Hanafi view say another obligatory fast counts if the day of doubt was Shaʿbān?
b: Because the prohibition is specifically about fasting Ramadan before its time, and this does not apply to every type of fast.

f: 63. Why is fasting on Eid different from this issue?
b: The prohibition of Eid fasting applies to every fast because it opposes the command to break the fast.

f: 64. What is the third case of fasting on the day of doubt?
b: Intending a voluntary fast.

f: 65. What is the ruling of intending a voluntary fast on the day of doubt?
b: It is not disliked.

f: 66. What evidence supports the permissibility of voluntary fasting on the day of doubt?
b: The hadith allowing fasting except when intending Ramadan.

f: 67. What did al-Shāfiʿī say regarding voluntary fasting on the day of doubt?
b: He considered it disliked from the outset.

f: 68. How do the Hanafis interpret the hadith “Do not precede Ramadan by fasting a day or two”?
b: It refers to preceding Ramadan by fasting Ramadan itself before its proper time.

f: 69. If the day of doubt coincides with a person’s regular voluntary fast, what is the ruling?
b: Fasting is better according to scholarly consensus.

f: 70. If someone normally fasts three days at the end of every month and one coincides with the day of doubt, what is the ruling?
b: Fasting is better.

f: 71. If someone singles out the day of doubt with voluntary fasting, what opinions exist?
b: Some said breaking the fast is better to avoid the appearance of violating the prohibition; others said fasting is better following ʿAlī and ʿĀʾishah رضي الله عنهما.

f: 72. What is the preferred approach for scholars regarding fasting the day of doubt?
b: The scholar may fast himself as a precaution but should advise ordinary people to wait until midday and then break the fast.

f: 73. Why should scholars advise ordinary people to wait and then break the fast?
b: To avoid accusations or suspicion of claiming knowledge of the unseen.

f: 74. What is the fourth case of fasting on the day of doubt?
b: A person hesitates in the basic intention, saying: “I will fast tomorrow if it is Ramadan, and I will not fast if it is Shaʿbān.”

f: 75. Does a person become fasting in the fourth case?
b: No.

f: 76. Why does the fourth case not count as fasting?
b: Because the person did not firmly resolve to fast.

f: 77. What example is given to explain this hesitation in intention?
b: Someone saying: “If I find food tomorrow I will break my fast; if I do not find food I will fast.”

f: 78. What is the fifth case of fasting on the day of doubt?
b: Hesitation regarding the description of the intention: intending Ramadan if it is Ramadan, and another obligatory fast if it is Shaʿbān.

f: 79. What is the ruling of the fifth case?
b: It is disliked because the intention fluctuates between two disliked possibilities.

f: 80. If the fifth case turns out to be Ramadan, does the fast count?
b: Yes, because the uncertainty was not in the foundation of the intention.

f: 81. If the fifth case turns out to be Shaʿbān, does it count as the other obligatory fast?
b: No, because the specific intention was uncertain and the general intention alone is insufficient.

f: 82. What does the fifth case become if it is Shaʿbān?
b: It becomes a voluntary fast.

f: 83. Does the person need to make up the fifth case if he breaks it?
b: No, because he began it in a manner that removes the obligation of making it up.

f: 84. What is the ruling if someone intends: “If tomorrow is Ramadan, I will fast Ramadan; if it is Shaʿbān, I will fast voluntarily”?
b: It is disliked because he intended an obligatory fast from one perspective.

f: 85. If this intention turns out to be Ramadan, does it count?
b: Yes, as Ramadan fasting.

f: 86. If this intention turns out to be Shaʿbān, does it count as voluntary fasting?
b: Yes.

f: 87. If he breaks this voluntary fast, must he make it up?
b: No, because his intention included the possibility of being released from obligation.

f: 88. What is the ruling of someone who sees the Ramadan crescent alone but whose testimony is not accepted by the ruler?
b: He must fast.

f: 89. What evidence supports fasting based on personal sighting of the crescent?
b: The hadith: “Fast when you see it and break the fast when you see it.”

f: 90. If someone who saw the Ramadan crescent alone breaks his fast, what is required?
b: He must make up the day but does not owe kaffārah.

f: 91. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s opinion if such a person breaks the fast through intercourse?
b: Kaffārah is required because he was truly in Ramadan and obligated to fast.

f: 92. Why do the Hanafis say kaffārah is not required for the person whose testimony was rejected?
b: Because the judge’s rejection creates a legal doubt, and kaffārah is removed by doubts.

f: 93. If the person breaks his fast before the ruler rejects his testimony, what is the ruling?
b: The scholars differed regarding this case.

f: 94. If the person completes thirty days after seeing the crescent alone, when may he end his fast?
b: He should only end it with the community and the ruler.

f: 95. Why does he wait after completing thirty days?
b: Because his obligation was based on precaution, so precaution requires delaying breaking the fast.

f: 96. If he breaks his fast after thirty days, is kaffārah required?
b: No, because according to his own certainty, the month has ended.

f: 97. When there is a cloudy sky, whose testimony for the Ramadan crescent is accepted?
b: The testimony of one upright person, whether male or female, free or slave.

f: 98. Why is one person’s testimony accepted when the sky is cloudy?
b: Because it is a religious report, similar to transmitting hadith.

f: 99. Why is uprightness required for moon sighting testimony?
b: Because the statement of a sinful person is not accepted in religious matters.

f: 100. Does moon sighting testimony require the wording of formal testimony?
b: No, because it is treated like a religious report.

f: 101. Is the testimony of a repentant person previously convicted of false accusation accepted?
b: Yes, according to the apparent Hanafi narration.

f: 102. What was another opinion from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding a previously convicted person?
b: That it is not accepted because it is testimony in one aspect.

f: 103. What was one opinion of al-Shāfiʿī regarding Ramadan crescent testimony?
b: He required two witnesses.

f: 104. What evidence is used against requiring two witnesses?
b: The Prophet ﷺ accepted the testimony of one person regarding the Ramadan crescent.

f: 105. If the ruler accepts one person’s Ramadan crescent testimony and the people complete thirty days, may they break the fast?
b: According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, they should not, as a precaution.

f: 106. What was Muḥammad’s opinion regarding breaking the fast after thirty days in this case?
b: They may break the fast because the establishment of Ramadan through one testimony also establishes its ending.

f: 107. Why does Muḥammad allow breaking the fast after thirty days?
b: Because the ending follows the established beginning, similar to inheritance being established through a confirmed lineage.

f: 108. If the sky is clear, is the testimony of one person accepted for the Ramadan crescent?
b: No.

f: 109. What is required when the sky is clear for accepting the Ramadan crescent?
b: A large group whose report produces certainty must see it.

f: 110. Why is a large group required when the sky is clear?
b: Because an individual sighting in such conditions suggests possible error.

f: 111. Why is one testimony accepted when the sky is cloudy but not when it is clear?
b: Clouds may open only in one place allowing one person to see the moon, while clear skies should allow many people to see it.

f: 112. What number was mentioned by Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله as an example of a large group?
b: Fifty people, by analogy with the number used in oath-related cases (qasāmah).

f: 113. Does it matter whether those who saw the moon are residents or visitors from outside the city?
b: No, there is no difference.

f: 114. What did al-Ṭaḥāwī mention regarding a person arriving from outside the city with a moon sighting?
b: His testimony may be accepted because there are fewer obstacles to his sighting.

f: 115. What is the ruling of someone who sees the Eid al-Fiṭr crescent alone?
b: He should not break his fast as a precaution.

f: 116. Why is precaution different between the beginning and end of Ramadan?
b: At the beginning, precaution means establishing the obligation of fasting; at the end, precaution means avoiding breaking the fast too early.

f: 117. If the sky is cloudy, how many witnesses are required for the crescent of Eid al-Fiṭr?
b: Two men, or one man and two women.

f: 118. Why is the testimony for Eid al-Fiṭr stricter than Ramadan when the sky is cloudy?
b: Because Eid involves a benefit for people (allowing them to break the fast), so it resembles other worldly rights.

f: 119. Is Eid al-Aḍḥā treated the same as Eid al-Fiṭr regarding crescent testimony?
b: Yes, according to the apparent narration, which is the correct view.

f: 120. What was another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding Eid al-Aḍḥā crescent testimony?
b: That it is like Ramadan because it involves the benefit of people through the meat of sacrifices.

f: 121. If the sky is clear, what is required for the crescent of Eid al-Fiṭr and Eid al-Aḍḥā?
b: A large group whose report produces certainty, as previously explained.

f: 122. When does the time of fasting begin and end?
b: It begins at the second dawn (true dawn) and ends at sunset.

f: 123. What Quranic verse establishes the time of fasting?
b: “Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread... then complete the fast until the night.” (Qur’an 2:187)

f: 124. What do the “white thread” and “black thread” refer to?
b: The white thread refers to the brightness of day and the black thread refers to the darkness of night.

f: 125. What is the linguistic meaning of fasting (ṣawm)?
b: Abstaining from eating, drinking, and sexual relations.

f: 126. What additional element does Islamic law add to the definition of fasting?
b: Intention, so that worship is distinguished from ordinary abstention.

f: 127. Why is fasting restricted to the daytime?
b: Because the Quran specifies it, and because when continuous fasting was impossible, the daytime was chosen as it differs from normal habit and better reflects worship.

f: 128. What condition related to women is required for a valid fast?
b: Purity from menstruation and postnatal bleeding.

f: 129. What chapter discusses actions requiring makeup (qaḍāʾ) and expiation (kaffārah)?
b: The chapter of what necessitates makeup and expiation.

f: 130. If a fasting person eats, drinks, or has intercourse during the day forgetfully, does the fast break?
b: No, the fast remains valid.

f: 131. What is the analogy (qiyās) regarding eating or drinking forgetfully while fasting?
b: The fast would be invalid because something contradicting fasting occurred, similar to speaking forgetfully during prayer.

f: 132. Who held that eating forgetfully breaks the fast?
b: Mālik رحمه الله.

f: 133. What evidence supports the Hanafi view that forgetful eating does not break the fast?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said regarding one who ate or drank forgetfully: “Complete your fast, for Allah has fed you and given you drink.”

f: 134. If forgetful eating does not invalidate fasting, does the same apply to intercourse forgetfully?
b: Yes, because both are essential matters related to fasting.

f: 135. Why is forgetfulness treated differently in fasting than in prayer?
b: Prayer has physical forms that remind the person, while fasting lacks such reminders, making forgetfulness more likely.

f: 136. Does the ruling of forgetful eating differ between obligatory and voluntary fasts?
b: No, because the text does not distinguish between them.

f: 137. If someone eats, drinks, or has intercourse while mistaken or forced, does the fast break?
b: Yes, they must make up the fast.

f: 138. Why does a mistake or coercion require makeup but forgetfulness does not?
b: Forgetfulness is common and comes from the person who has the right, whereas coercion comes from another person and is not as common.

f: 139. If a fasting person sleeps and has a wet dream, does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 140. What evidence shows that a wet dream does not invalidate fasting?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Three things do not break the fast: vomiting, cupping, and a wet dream.”

f: 141. Why does a wet dream not invalidate fasting?
b: Because there is neither the physical act of intercourse nor its meaning, which is ejaculation through intentional pleasure.

f: 142. If someone looks at a woman and ejaculates, does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 143. What acts are compared to ejaculation caused by looking?
b: Ejaculation caused by thinking and ejaculation according to some scholars from masturbation.

f: 144. If a fasting person applies oil to his body, does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 145. Why does applying oil not invalidate fasting?
b: Because no invalidating substance enters the body.

f: 146. If a fasting person undergoes cupping, does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 147. If a fasting person uses kohl (eyeliner), does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 148. Why does kohl not invalidate fasting?
b: Because there is no passage between the eye and the brain, and tears are like sweat; what enters through pores does not invalidate fasting.

f: 149. If a fasting person kisses his wife without ejaculation, does his fast break?
b: No.

f: 150. When does kissing become problematic during fasting?
b: When it leads to ejaculation or intercourse.

f: 151. If ejaculation occurs due to kissing or touching, what is required?
b: Makeup of the fast but not kaffārah.

f: 152. Why is kaffārah not required for ejaculation caused by kissing or touching?
b: Because kaffārah requires a complete violation of the fast, and it is avoided when there is doubt, like legal punishments.

f: 153. When is kissing permissible while fasting?
b: When a person is confident he will not have intercourse or ejaculate.

f: 154. When is kissing disliked while fasting?
b: When a person fears he may lose control and cause ejaculation or intercourse.

f: 155. What was al-Shāfiʿī’s view regarding kissing while fasting?
b: He allowed it generally in both situations.

f: 156. What is the ruling of excessive physical contact (mubāsharah fāḥishah) while fasting?
b: According to the apparent narration, it is like kissing; according to Muḥammad it is disliked because it rarely avoids temptation.

f: 157. If a fly enters the throat of a fasting person while he remembers his fast, does the fast break?
b: No.

f: 158. Why does a fly not invalidate fasting?
b: Because avoiding it is impossible, like dust and smoke.

f: 159. What was the analogy regarding a fly entering the throat?
